claims.text: Many apparently random historical events have identifiable biological, political, or social causes, yet their outcomes often appear morally indiscriminate and non-monotonic.
claims.quote: The evidence does not establish that these events are literally random; many have identifiable biological, political, or social causes. Nevertheless, their outcomes frequently appear non-monotonic and morally indiscriminate, with no consistent relationship between moral character and health, longevity, safety, prosperity, or political success.

claims.text: Naturalism explains apparent randomness through impersonal causation and probability, while biblical theology explains it through agency, natural processes, hidden providence, suffering, and delayed judgment.
claims.quote: Naturalism interprets this pattern through impersonal causation and probability, whereas biblical theology appeals to human agency, regular natural processes, hidden providence, suffering, and delayed judgment.

claims.text: Apparent randomness challenges expectations of continuously visible divine control but cannot independently prove or disprove God's existence.
claims.quote: Apparent randomness therefore creates an evidential difficulty for expectations of continuously visible divine control, but it does not independently prove or disprove God because the same observations remain compatible with competing metaphysical interpretations.

claims.text: Political history shows no obvious continuous or monotonic movement toward morally preferable outcomes.
claims.quote: Political history does not exhibit an obvious, continuous, or monotonic movement toward morally preferable outcomes.

claims.text: Good and evil historical outcomes can be assessed morally, even though they cannot be assigned exact numerical values or shown to occur in an equal ratio.
claims.quote: For purposes of this comparison, “balance” does not mean that good and evil can be assigned numerical values or demonstrated to occur in an exact ratio. No comprehensive historical measurement presently establishes that morally good and morally evil outcomes are equally distributed.

claims.text: Conquest, forced population movement, enslavement, and spectacular violence were documented features of several major ancient imperial systems.
claims.quote: Thus, conquest, forced population movement, enslavement, and spectacular violence were not exceptional features invented by later moral critics, but documented components of several major ancient imperial systems (Fagan, 2020).

claims.text: Mixed features of Greek and Persian civilizations make it difficult to classify entire civilizations simply as good or evil.
claims.quote: These mixed cases illustrate the difficulty of assigning entire civilizations to simple categories of “good” and “evil.”

claims.text: Solomon's reign cannot be classified as entirely good because biblical accounts also describe coercive policies and political instability.
claims.quote: Consequently, even a reign remembered for wisdom, prosperity, and relative peace cannot be classified as entirely good without ignoring the coercive policies and political instability also described by the biblical narrative.

claims.text: British imperial political institutions expanded liberty for some populations while denying comparable rights to colonial subjects and coexisting with famine.
claims.quote: The same political system could therefore produce expanding political liberty for some populations while withholding comparable rights from others.

claims.text: The moral character of historical events can depend heavily on the period, actors, and perspective involved.
claims.quote: Thus, even an institution remembered alternately as defensive warfare or religious aggression illustrates how the moral character of historical events can depend heavily upon period, actors, and perspective.

claims.text: Historical evidence alone lacks the directional signature expected if history were steered toward the good.
claims.quote: The historical record does not, on its own, display the directional signature one might expect if history were being steered toward the good.

claims.text: Long-term political cycles involve expansion, stagnation, instability, state failure, and territorial loss rather than a continuously improving political order.
claims.quote: Their findings identify recurring causal mechanisms rather than chance, but those mechanisms do not produce a continuously improving political order.

claims.text: Twentieth-century democratization occurred through expansion, interruption, and reversal rather than continuous global progress.
claims.quote: Political scientists consequently describe democratization as occurring through waves of expansion, interruption, and reversal, not as a continuous global progression (Gunitsky, 2018).

claims.text: If political outcomes are treated as evidence of providential direction, twentieth-century history is ambiguous rather than unmistakably progressive.
claims.quote: If political outcomes alone are treated as evidence of providential direction, the historical record presents an ambiguous rather than unmistakably progressive pattern.

claims.text: Twentieth-century political history contains progress alongside dictatorship, reversal, regime survival, and democratic breakdown.
claims.quote: The twentieth century consequently presents evidence of genuine political progress alongside dictatorship, reversal, regime survival, and democratic breakdown.

claims.text: Political outcomes provide ambiguous rather than unmistakable evidence of providential direction.
claims.quote: If political outcomes alone are treated as evidence of providential direction, the historical record presents an ambiguous rather than unmistakably progressive pattern.

claims.text: Battlefield survival depends on physical conditions that have no observable relationship to moral goodness or evil.
claims.quote: They mean that survival frequently depends upon wound location, proximity to medical assistance, evacuation time, and treatment availability, conditions that bear no observable relationship to whether a person is morally good or evil.

claims.text: The individual victims of Allied bombing were determined by circumstances rather than innocence, guilt, virtue, age, or allegiance.
claims.quote: The bombs therefore were not always randomly aimed, but the identity of the individual who died beneath them often depended upon location, timing, structural protection, and proximity to the point of impact, not upon innocence, guilt, virtue, age, or allegiance.

claims.text: Holocaust victims were selected by group identity or location rather than individualized moral judgment.
claims.quote: The victims were selected because of ancestry, identity, disability, political classification, or location rather than because of any individualized moral judgment.

claims.text: Soviet state policies created and intensified the Ukrainian famine, while its suffering appeared morally random among ordinary people.
claims.quote: Thus, these deaths were not causally random: state policies created and intensified the catastrophe. What appears morally random is the distribution of suffering among ordinary people.

claims.text: If God exists, luck does not exist because God controls events.
claims.quote: If God exists, there is no such thing as luck because God is in control.

claims.text: The apparent prominence of good and bad luck during war calls God's existence into question.
claims.quote: But with everything seemingly about good and bad luck especially during wars, it calls into question whether God exists or not.

claims.text: The morally indifferent distribution of wartime suffering poses an evidential problem for belief in an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, providential God.
claims.quote: This pattern does not logically prove that God does not exist, but it creates an evidential problem: if God is all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, and providentially active, why does the distribution of wartime suffering so often appear indifferent to innocence and guilt?

claims.text: Apparently unnecessary intense suffering can rationally count against an omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good God without logically disproving God.
claims.quote: Rowe (1979) argued that instances of intense suffering that appear to serve no necessary greater good can provide rational evidence against the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly good God, even if they do not produce a strict logical disproof.

claims.text: War does not show that events lack causes, but it makes suffering appear distributed without visible moral governance.
claims.quote: The evidence from war therefore supports a carefully limited conclusion: war does not demonstrate that events are causeless, but it does create the appearance of a world in which suffering is distributed without any visible moral governance.

claims.text: Prayer outcomes show no significant tendency for good people to receive answered prayers.
claims.quote: There is no really significant tilt toward answered prayers for good people.

claims.text: Genetic mutations occur probabilistically and without regard for a person's needs or moral desert.
claims.quote: That's why sometimes genetic experts call it random mutations - not because they have no physical causes, but because they occur probabilistically and without regard for what an individual needs or morally deserves

claims.text: The lack of a visible moral pattern in severe illness raises a serious question if providence should protect good people.
claims.quote: If divine providence is expected to protect good people from severe illness, this absence of a visible moral pattern raises a serious question.

claims.text: The absence of a visible moral pattern in severe illness raises a serious problem for the expectation that divine providence protects good people.
claims.quote: If divine providence is expected to protect good people from severe illness, this absence of a visible moral pattern raises a serious question.

claims.text: Evidence offered for miracles can be interpreted in more than one way.
claims.quote: Do miracles really happen? The evidence can be interpreted in more than one way.

claims.text: It remains open whether medical science will eventually explain currently unexplained recoveries.
claims.quote: So will medical science someday figure out what causes these unexplained recoveries?

claims.text: If science cannot explain unexplained recoveries, they can safely be concluded to be divine intervention.
claims.quote: If not then we can safely conclude that it's divine intervention.

claims.text: Weather conditions during the Dunkirk evacuation restricted German bombing and aided vessels crossing the English Channel.
claims.quote: Low cloud, fog, and overcast conditions repeatedly restricted Luftwaffe operations and visual bombing, while unusually calm seas simultaneously aided the hundreds of vessels crossing the English Channel.

claims.text: The second and third purported miracles at Dunkirk may instead have resulted from tactical blunders and effective resource management.
claims.quote: Miracle number 2 and 3 may not really be real miracles as they were tactical blunders and excellent resource management.

claims.text: The cloud cover at Dunkirk can be interpreted either as coincidence or as divine intervention, and its true explanation cannot be known.
claims.quote: So we can say that this is a coincidence, while we can also argue that God intervened. We will never know.

claims.text: Science can explain minor faith healings, but terminal diseases have not been documented as healed at faith-healing crusades.
claims.quote: So far science today can explain all the minor healings, while fatal diseases and illnesses like terminal cancer were never documented to be healed on any faith healing crusades.

claims.text: Many evil historical rulers died without trial or proportionate suffering while those they governed suffered and died younger.
claims.quote: Countless people governed by these men died younger, suffered more, and possessed far less power over the conditions of their lives.

claims.text: Scripture does not promise that moral character determines health, wealth, longevity, or political success in this life.
claims.quote: The Bible also does not promise that health, wealth, longevity, or political success will be distributed according to moral character during this life.

claims.text: Biblical theology locates complete justice in a future judgment rather than in earthly life.
claims.quote: Biblical theology ultimately places complete justice in a future judgment rather than promising that injustice will be corrected during earthly life.

claims.text: Apparent randomness can support theistic or atheistic interpretations but does not itself determine whether God exists.
claims.quote: But if you are an atheist, the randomness we see is a clear indication that God doesn't exist. but it does not by itself determine whether God exists.

claims.text: Judging God's existence only by apparent worldly randomness yields no clear winner because its meaning depends greatly on worldview.
claims.quote: So if we judge the existence of God only by the apparent randomness of what happens in this world, the evidence does not give us a clear winner. The randomness is real in appearance, but what it ultimately means depends greatly on the worldview through which we interpret it.

claims.text: On the Thomistic model, divine cognition is identical with the divine essence and divine being.
claims.quote: On the Thomistic model, divine cognition is neither discursive nor representational, but identical with the divine essence itself. God knows God through a single timeless act identical with God’s being

claims.text: Classical theists often hold that divine cognition is wholly non-indexical and lacks essentially first-personal or self-locating structure.
claims.quote: Classical theists accordingly often understand divine cognition as wholly non-indexical. On this view, God does not know God by occupying a cognitive standpoint distinct from what is known.

claims.text: Strictly non-indexical accounts of divine cognition may be unable to explain libertarian and morally responsible divine agency.
claims.quote: Taken together, these discussions raise the question whether strictly non-indexical accounts of divine cognition can adequately explain libertarian and morally responsible divine agency.

claims.text: An agent is robustly responsible for an action only if the agent can be identified as its source rather than the source of relevant alternatives.
claims.quote: I adopt a robust contrastive conception of responsibility according to which an agent is responsible for φ only if the agent can be identified as the source of φ rather than relevant alternatives.

claims.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than another, its cognition must represent the first outcome as its own action.
claims.quote: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ, then the agent’s cognitive state must represent φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ.

claims.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives.
claims.quote: where responsibility is understood contrastively, the cognitive state constitutive of responsible agency must itself represent the relevant outcome as issuing from the agent’s own activity rather than the relevant alternatives.

claims.text: Self-ascriptive cognition is constitutive of robust contrastive agency attribution, rather than merely a practical aid for finite agents.
claims.quote: Rather, de se cognition is constitutive of robust contrastive agency attribution itself.

claims.text: A third-personal proposition identifying God as actualising a world does not itself represent that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.
claims.quote: A third-personal proposition such as “God actualises W1” may identify the correct agent extensionally, yet it does not by itself represent the actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

claims.text: If God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include self-locating content representing God as its source.
claims.quote: If God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, then divine cognition must include self-locating content representing God as the source of that actualisation.

claims.text: Strong non-indexical models of omniscience exclude irreducibly de se content.
claims.quote: Strong non-indexical models of omniscience exclude irreducibly de se content.

claims.text: Strong non-indexical models of omniscience cannot account for robust contrastive divine responsibility.
claims.quote: Therefore, strong non-indexical models of omniscience cannot account for robust contrastive divine responsibility.

claims.text: The argument is conditional on libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: The argument is conditional. Those who reject libertarian agency or robust contrastive responsibility may reject premise (1).

claims.text: On a strong non-indexical interpretation of omniscience, divine cognition contains no irreducible de se structure.
claims.quote: The present argument targets a stronger non-indexical reading according to which divine cognition contains no irreducible de se structure whatsoever.

claims.text: Classical divine simplicity holds that divine omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and being are numerically identical with the divine essence.
claims.quote: On stronger formulations of simplicity, divine omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and being are all numerically identical with the divine essence.

claims.text: Strictly non-indexical divine cognition lacks irreducibly first-personal or self-locating structure.
claims.quote: Since the act, object, and subject of divine knowledge are identical, divine self-knowledge contains no irreducibly first-personal or self-locating structure.

claims.text: A strictly non-indexical divine cognition is difficult to reconcile with robustly contrastive divine agency.
claims.quote: The difficulty, however, is that a strictly non-indexical conception of divine cognition appears difficult to reconcile with robustly contrastive divine agency.

claims.text: If divine will is necessary and identical with divine essence, the contingency of creation is difficult to explain.
claims.quote: If the divine will is necessary and identical with the divine essence, then the contingency of creation becomes difficult to explain.

claims.text: Can strictly non-indexical omniscience account for divine responsibility for actualising one world rather than another?
claims.quote: The central question is whether such a conception of omniscience can account for divine responsibility for actualising one world rather than another.

claims.text: No adequately developed account currently shows how irreducible de se content can occur in a single timeless, simple divine act without metaphysical composition.
claims.quote: The present claim is only that no adequately developed account of this kind is presently available.

claims.text: If such an account is provided, divine simplicity need not be rejected, but divine omniscience cannot remain strictly non-indexical.
claims.quote: If such an account can be provided, then the conclusion is not that simplicity should be rejected, but that divine omniscience cannot remain strictly non-indexical.

claims.text: Indexicals convey information about a subject's cognitive position within a representational context.
claims.quote: Indexical expressions therefore contain information about the cognitive position of a subject within a context of representation.

claims.text: Some self-locating knowledge cannot be reduced to de dicto or de re representation.
claims.quote: Perry (1979) and Lewis (1979) argue that certain forms of self-locating knowledge cannot be reduced to de dicto or de re representation.

claims.text: A complete specification of third-personal facts can fail to determine the cognitive state required for agency.
claims.quote: A complete specification of third-personal facts may therefore fail to determine the cognitive state required for agency.

claims.text: Purely third-personal representation is insufficient to explain agency under robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: Under these conditions, purely third-personal representation appears insufficient for explaining agency.

claims.text: Given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, purely uncentred divine knowledge is insufficient for agency-sensitive explanation.
claims.quote: The remainder of the paper argues that, given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, it is not.

claims.text: Libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility require an explanation of why an agent actualises one possible world rather than relevant alternatives.
claims.quote: If robust contrastive responsibility requires explanation of why this outcome is attributable to this agent rather than relevant alternatives, then de se content appears indispensable.

claims.text: Third-personal truths about God actualising a world do not determine the self-ascriptive content required for robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: Third-personal truths therefore underdetermine the de se content required for robust contrastive responsibility.

claims.text: Knowing that God actualises W1 is not equivalent in action-guiding contexts to representing oneself as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.
claims.quote: Knowing that God actualises W1 is not equivalent, in action-guiding contexts, to representing oneself as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

claims.text: Actualisation creates an explanatory asymmetry between an actualised world and merely possible alternatives, even on timeless models of divine knowledge.
claims.quote: Even on timeless models of divine knowledge, actualisation introduces an explanatory asymmetry between W1 and relevant alternatives.

claims.text: The Self-Location Constraint concerns source attribution by agency rather than God's spatiotemporal location or presence.
claims.quote: The issue is not temporal sequence but source attribution.

claims.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires divine cognition to represent God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.
claims.quote: The relevant question is not merely which world becomes actual, but whether divine cognition represents God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

claims.text: A de se state fixes the agent as the source of an outcome, whereas a third-personal state may remain merely recognitional.
claims.quote: By contrast, the de se state “I actualise W1 rather than W0” fixes the agent as the source of the relevant outcome.

claims.text: Strictly non-indexical omniscience is insufficient to explain libertarian, robustly contrastively responsible divine agency.
claims.quote: The central claim is that non-indexical omniscience, understood as exhaustive knowledge of all true uncentred propositions, is insufficient for explaining libertarian and contrastively responsible divine agency.

claims.text: Extensional equivalence between third-personal and first-personal propositions does not preserve their explanatory role in responsible agency.
claims.quote: Substitution of co-referring expressions may preserve truth while altering explanatory role.

claims.text: The Self-Location Constraint requires cognition to represent both the outcome that obtains and the subject as its source.
claims.quote: A cognitive state satisfies SLC only if it represents both which outcome obtains and the subject as the source of that outcome.

claims.text: The Self-Location Constraint applies only when genuine modal alternatives exist and libertarian agency generates a contrastive explanatory demand.
claims.quote: The Self-Location Constraint therefore applies only where libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility generate an explanatory requirement to account for why one possible world is actualised rather than another.

claims.text: Divine simplicity prohibits metaphysical composition but may permit intentional complexity and irreducible de se content.
The argument does not establish that divine simplicity conflicts with de se cognition; it targets only wholly non-indexical omniscience.
claims.quote: It establishes only that strict non-indexicality is insufficient.

claims.text: Defenders of classical theism may contend that a single timeless, simple divine cognition includes irreducible de se content without metaphysical composition.
claims.quote: Likewise, defenders of classical theism may argue that a single timeless and simple act of cognition can include irreducible de se content without introducing metaphysical composition.

claims.text: Because there is exactly one divine agent, third-personal knowledge that God actualises W1 rather than W0 plus knowledge that I am God suffices for de se knowledge.
claims.quote: Since there is exactly one divine agent, knowledge that “God actualises W1 rather than W0”, together with knowledge of the identity “I = God”, appears sufficient to yield the content “I actualise W1 rather than W0.”

claims.text: Extensional equivalence between third-personal and de se contents does not establish their explanatory equivalence for agency.
claims.quote: This objection, however, conflates extensional equivalence with explanatory equivalence.

claims.text: Self-locating cognition has an action-guiding explanatory role that is not exhausted by third-personal representation.
claims.quote: The central claim of the de se literature is not merely that indexical expressions behave differently in language, but that self-locating cognition performs an explanatory role not exhausted by third-personal representation.

claims.text: Knowledge that God actualises W1 rather than W0 identifies the outcome but does not represent actualisation as issuing from God’s own agency.
claims.quote: Knowledge that “God actualises W1 rather than W0” specifies which contrastive outcome obtains, but does not yet represent divine agency under the aspect required for contrastive explanation.

claims.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that explains why an outcome is attributable to an agent rather than relevant alternatives.
claims.quote: It requires cognition capable of explaining why this outcome is attributable to this agent rather than relevant alternatives.

claims.text: God’s knowledge of the actual world through causing it may seem to supply the cognition required for contrastive agency explanation.
claims.quote: A related objection appeals to divine knowledge-by-causation. God knows the actual world because God causes it.

claims.text: A causal relation between divine agency and actuality does not itself establish self-ascriptive cognition adequate for contrastive agency explanation.
claims.quote: Knowing by causing may establish a metaphysical relation between divine agency and actuality while leaving open whether divine cognition includes the self-ascriptive representation required for contrastive agency explanation.

claims.text: Exhaustive third-personal cognition alone is insufficient for the explanatory demands of robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: It does not show that exhaustive third-personal cognition is sufficient for the explanatory demands imposed by robust contrastive responsibility.

claims.text: Divine simplicity need not preclude internally differentiated explanatory structure, because one timeless cognitive act can have distinct explanatory aspects without metaphysical parts.
claims.quote: A single timeless act of cognition may admit distinct explanatory aspects without thereby consisting of metaphysical parts.

claims.text: A semantically stratified divine cognition could preserve simplicity while including de se representation needed to explain divine agency contrastively.
claims.quote: Divine cognition remains simple and timeless while including the self-ascriptive structure required for representing divine agency as the source of actuality.

claims.text: Necessitarianism avoids the SLC by denying genuine divine alternatives and thus rejecting the conditions for robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: Necessitarianism resolves that tension not by incorporating de se cognition into omniscience, but by denying the modal conditions under which robust contrastive responsibility arises.

claims.text: Strong non-indexical omniscience, libertarian divine agency, and robust contrastive responsibility cannot all be maintained together.
claims.quote:
What cannot be simultaneously maintained, however, is:
 
●
strong non-indexical omniscience;
 
●
libertarian divine agency;
 
●
robust contrastive responsibility.

claims.text: If God is contrastively responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include irreducible de se content.
claims.quote: If God is responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include irreducible de se content representing actuality as issuing from divine agency.

claims.text: Whether a single timeless and simple divine act of cognition can include self-locating content remains the central question.
claims.quote: The central question, therefore, is not whether omniscience is possible, but whether a single timeless and simple act of cognition can include self-locating content.

claims.text: Under classical mereology, something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.
claims.quote: Under classical mereology, the two formulations of DDS are equivalent – something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.

claims.text: On plausible non-antisymmetric mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being part of all its parts without being identical to them.
claims.quote: On some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts, even if it is not identical to all its parts.

claims.text: Divine simplicity can be formulated as God being an improper part of all of God's improper parts.
claims.quote: Thus, it is possible to formulate DDS as a thesis saying that God is simple in the sense of being a part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation of DDS.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation is a viable understanding of divine simplicity, particularly concerning God's relation to God's attributes.
claims.quote: this paper will argue that the symmetry formulation is a viable way of understanding DDS, particularly as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes.

claims.text: Divine simplicity cannot plausibly mean that God lacks improper parts, because reflexivity makes God an improper part of Godself.
claims.quote: DDS cannot plausibly be interpreted as a thesis that God lacks parts in this sense, because the reflexivity of improper parthood implies that God has at least himself as a part.

claims.text: Divine simplicity is most plausibly understood as the claim that God lacks proper parts.
claims.quote: Instead, DDS is more plausibly understood as saying that God lacks proper parts – call this the mereological formulation of DDS.

claims.text: If proper parthood is distinct parthood, the claim that God has no proper parts is equivalent to the identity formulation of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: If proper parthood is distinct parthood, the mereological formulation of DDS is equivalent to the common understanding of DDS as a thesis identifying God with his parts – call this the identity formulation of DDS.

claims.text: If proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, the claim that God has no proper parts yields the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: But if proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood, then explicating proper parthood in the mereological formulation yields the symmetry formulation of DDS.

claims.text: Without antisymmetry, the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is strictly weaker than the identity formulation.
claims.quote: Accordingly, DDS under the symmetric formulation is strictly weaker than under the identity formulation: if God lacks distinct parts, he also lacks non-symmetric parts, but not vice versa.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation is a viable and distinct formal mereological understanding of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: The upshot is that as far as the formal mereological framework goes, the symmetry formulation presents a viable and distinct way of understanding DDS.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation is viable if parthood is antisymmetric or proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric, and distinct from identity when parthood is non-antisymmetric.
claims.quote: The viability of the symmetry formulation is given by the fact that it is equivalent to the mereological formulation if parthood is assumed antisymmetric, or if proper parthood is defined as nonsymmetric parthood, either of which would be independently plausible. The distinctness of the symmetry formulation from the identity formulation is given by the fact that the two are non-equivalent whenever parthood is not antisymmetric, which is also a reasonable possibility.

claims.text: Divine simplicity concerning attributes distinguishes God from other entities more clearly than simplicity concerning other forms of parthood.
claims.quote: One reason for this focus is that simplicity with respect to attributes would set God apart from other entities more distinctly than simplicity with respect to other kinds of parthood, in line with a common motivation for DDS from God’s transcendence.

claims.text: Instantiation can be modelled as parthood because objects may be understood as mereological fusions of their properties.
claims.quote: On the mereological bundle theory suggested by Laurie Paul (2002, 2006, 2012, 2017), for instance, objects are mereological fusions of the properties they bear.

claims.text: When objects are collections of their properties, an object's instantiating a property makes that property a part of the object with respect to similarity.
claims.quote: Whenever an object o has a property p, whatever bears a property more similar to p also thereby becomes more similar to o; hence p is part of o with respect to similarity.

claims.text: Objects can, in principle, be parts of properties with respect to similarity.
claims.quote: It is also possible, at least in principle, for objects to be part of properties with respect to similarity.

claims.text: God and omniscience can be mutual parts with respect to similarity while remaining numerically distinct.
claims.quote: it is also possible, at least in principle, for this symmetric parthood relation to hold while God remains numerically distinct from his omniscience.

claims.text: Similarity-based parthood is not generally antisymmetric if distinct things can be mutual parts.
claims.quote: The possibility of such cases would imply that parthood with respect to similarity is not generally antisymmetric.

claims.text: Defining proper parthood as non-symmetric similarity-based parthood makes proper parthood irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.
claims.quote: If proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood with respect to similarity, it would immediately be irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.

claims.text: Relations between objects and properties can be modelled mereologically so that the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is viable for God and attributes.
claims.quote: The upshot is that the relations between objects and their properties can be modelled mereologically in such a way that DDS on the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about the relation between God and his attributes.

claims.text: Metaphysical dependence is more plausibly entailed by proper parthood than by improper parthood.
claims.quote: Instead, the parthood-dependence relation is more plausibly understood as an entailment from proper parthood (in some sense) to dependence.

claims.text: Dependence should follow from non-symmetric parthood rather than from distinct parthood generally because dependence is usually asymmetric.
claims.quote: it would square better with our usual understanding for dependence to follow from non-symmetric parthood, rather than distinct parthood more generally.

claims.text: If dependence tracks non-symmetric parthood, aseity requires only that God lack non-symmetric parts.
claims.quote: And if dependence tracks non-symmetric parthood, then the doctrine of aseity requires only that God lack non-symmetric parts, as the symmetry formulation posits.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation preserves the transcendence motivation for divine simplicity because ordinary objects are not parts of their properties.
claims.quote: The symmetry formulation maintains this motivation, because ordinary objects are not parts of their properties.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation of divine simplicity makes God unique by holding that God and all divine attributes are mutual parts.
claims.quote: Hence, the symmetry formulation makes God unique by positing that God is part of all his attributes, which are also all parts of each other.

claims.text: Necessary parthood relations between God and the attributes constituting God's intrinsic nature entail that God has those attributes necessarily and unchangingly.
claims.quote: And if God is taken to bear mutual and necessary parthood relations to the properties that constitute his intrinsic nature, God would have these properties necessarily and hence unchangingly, which yields immutability.

claims.text: Things that are mutual parts have the same parts and wholes, and are therefore mereologically indiscernible.
claims.quote: the transitivity of parthood implies that whenever two things are parts of each other, they have all the same parts and are parts of all the same things.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation allows God's nature to lack discernible divisions even if divine attributes are not numerically identical.
claims.quote: Hence, under the symmetry formulation of DDS, God’s nature can be said to admit no discernible divisions, even if his attributes are not numerically identical to each other.

claims.text: The symmetric formulation retains the common motivations for divine simplicity.
claims.quote: the discussion above shows that the symmetric formulation retains the motivations of DDS.

claims.text: If God is identical with omniscience, God is a property or property instance, which may be self-exemplifying and causally inert.
claims.quote: First, if God is his omniscience, then God is a property (or property instance). Besides being unintuitive, this might imply that God’s omniscience is self-exemplifying, and make it difficult to explain how God can interact with the world if properties (or property instances) are causally inert.

claims.text: If God is both omniscience and omnipotence, identity's transitivity implies that omniscience and omnipotence are identical despite appearing distinct.
claims.quote: Second, if God is simultaneously his omniscience and his omnipotence, the transitivity of identity seems to imply that God’s omniscience is his omnipotence; but the two seem intuitively to be distinct.

claims.text: If resemblance consists in shared properties, divine simplicity implies that anyone good like God possesses all God's attributes and perhaps God himself.
claims.quote: if resemblance is understood as property sharing, then DDS seems to imply that someone who resembles God by being good also possesses all of God’s attributes, and perhaps even God himself.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation can address all three difficulties concerning God's distinction from divine attributes.
claims.quote: This section will argue that the symmetry formulation can address all three difficulties.

claims.text: Because God and divine attributes can be numerically distinct under the symmetry formulation, it does not entail that God is a property or that divine attributes are identical.
claims.quote: DDS under the symmetry formulation allows for God and his attributes to be numerically distinct from each other, and hence does not entail that God is a property (instance), or that God’s attributes are all identical.

claims.text: Resemblance can consist in possessing sufficiently similar properties rather than sharing a property, preventing goodness-based resemblance from giving creatures God and all divine attributes as parts.
claims.quote: Then, for someone to resemble God in terms of goodness requires not that they have God’s goodness itself, but only that they have a sufficiently similar property like (say) the property of imperfect goodness.

claims.text: If God necessarily exists and is identical with every divine aspect, divine acts and knowledge become necessary, eliminating free will and contingent truths.
claims.quote: But if all of God’s acts are necessary, then God cannot act differently from how he actually does, which implies that God lacks free will. Moreover, God’s omniscience entails that for any true proposition p, God knows that p.

claims.text: Divine simplicity can allow contingent mutual parthood relations between God and some attributes, while requiring necessity only for attributes constituting God's intrinsic nature.
claims.quote: The account of God’s immutability suggested in section ‘Motivations’ stipulates that some parthood relations between God and his attributes are necessary, but it does not require that this be the case for all of God’s attributes, only those that constitute his intrinsic nature.

claims.text: If God's willingness to create is not intrinsic, contingent parthood with that willingness permits a possible world where necessary God does not create, making God's actual creative act free.
claims.quote: Then, there is a possible world in which God exists (by necessity), but does not have a willingness to create and hence does not, which implies that God’s actual creative act is free.

claims.text: If God’s willingness to create is temporally necessary but metaphysically contingent, God’s actual creative act remains free.
claims.quote: God’s actual creative act hence remains free in this case.

claims.text: God’s omniscience entails God’s knowledge that snow is white in actuality.
claims.quote: Similarly, in actuality, God knows as an implication of omniscience that snow is white

claims.text: God, God’s omniscience, and God’s knowledge that snow is white are mutually parts of each other.
claims.quote: such that God, his omniscience, and his knowledge that snow is white are all parts of each other.

claims.text: God’s parthood relation with omniscience can be necessary, whereas relations involving God’s knowledge that snow is white can be metaphysically contingent.
claims.quote: The parthood relations between God and his omniscience can be taken to be necessary (since omniscience is in God’s intrinsic nature), while those involving God’s knowledge that snow is white are taken to be (metaphysically) contingent.

claims.text: God could lack knowledge that snow is white while remaining omniscient if snow were not white.
claims.quote: Then, there could be a possible world in which God does not have the knowledge that snow is white, but God remains omniscient because snow is not white.

claims.text: That snow is white is contingently true in actuality.
claims.quote: That snow is white is thus a contingent truth in actuality.

claims.text: Divine simplicity can viably be formulated as the thesis that God is part of all God’s parts.
claims.quote: this paper has argued that there is a viable alternative formulation of DDS as a thesis that God is part of all his parts.

claims.text: Plausible mereological theories treat mereological simplicity as lacking non-symmetric parts, and object–property relations can plausibly be understood as parthood.
claims.quote: The viability of this formulation is suggested by the observations that there are plausible mereological theories under which mereological simplicity consists in lacking non-symmetric parts, and that the relation between objects and their properties can plausibly be understood in terms of parthood.

claims.text: The symmetric formulation of divine simplicity preserves the doctrine’s usual motivations and addresses its usual difficulties.
claims.quote: Moreover, this formulation of DDS retains the doctrine’s usual motivations and addresses its usual difficulties.

claims.text: Under perdurantism, the usual formulation of divine simplicity makes it difficult to explain how God interacts with the world.
claims.quote: But DDS on the usual understanding implies that God has no temporal proper parts, and hence cannot exist across extended periods of time, which makes it difficult to explain how God can interact with the world.

claims.text: The symmetric formulation can reconcile divine simplicity with perdurantism by allowing distinct temporal parts of God if God is part of each of them.
claims.quote: The symmetry formulation offers a possible way of reconciling DDS with perdurantism, since it allows that God can have distinct temporal parts, so long as he is a part (in some plausible sense) of all of them.

claims.text: Whether the symmetric formulation provides a viable divine-simplicity model of God’s relation to time requires further investigation.
claims.quote: Whether this is indeed a viable model of God’s relation to time under DDS requires more thorough investigation in future work
