claims.text: If God exists, every nonresistant creature capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God is able to participate in that relationship merely by trying.
claims.quote: Necessarily, if God exists, anyone who is (i) not resisting God and (ii) capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God is also (iii) in a position to participate in such relationship (able to do so just by trying).

claims.text: A person can participate in meaningful conscious relationship with God at a time only if that person believes that God exists at that time.
claims.quote: Necessarily, one is at a time in a position to participate in meaningful conscious relationship with God only if at that time one believes that God exists.

claims.text: If God exists, every nonresistant creature capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God believes that God exists.
claims.quote: Necessarily, if God exists, anyone who is (i) not resisting God and (ii) capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God also (iii) believes that God exists [from (1) and (2)].

claims.text: Some people are nonresistant and capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God but do not believe that God exists.
claims.quote: There are (and often have been) people who are (i) not resisting God and (ii) capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God without also (iii) believing that God exists.

claims.text: God does not exist.
claims.quote: God does not exist [from (3) and (4)].

claims.text: The inference from the claim about nonresistant believers and the existence of nonresistant nonbelievers to God's nonexistence is valid.
claims.quote: The inference from (3) and (4) to (5) is valid, and so one must deny one of these premises in order to maintain that God exists.

claims.text: A perfectly loving God would desire the highest well-being of creatures, which for creatures able to relate personally to God includes a personal relationship with God.
claims.quote: Early on, Schellenberg supported premise (1) by arguing that if a perfectly loving God were to exist, He would desire the highest well-being for His creatures. For all creatures that are capable of personally relating to God, their highest well-being would include a personal relationship with Him.

claims.text: If a person would be better off temporarily not knowing that God exists, an omnibenevolent God would not reveal Godself to that person during that time.
claims.quote: It seems clear that if some person were better off not knowing that God exists (at least for a time), God would not reveal Himself to that person (at that time) even though He desires a personal relationship with that person for its own sake.

claims.text: Greater-goods responses contend that an all-loving God can desire the best for creatures while allowing nonresistant nonbelief for the sake of a greater good.
claims.quote: Greater goods style responses address the support for premise (1) by attempting to demonstrate that an all-loving God could consistently desire the best for His creatures while simultaneously allowing them to be nonresistant nonbelievers.

claims.text: Schellenberg's accommodation strategy holds that a proposed good cannot justify nonresistant nonbelief if God could obtain that good within a personal relationship with God.
claims.quote: If this can be shown, then these goods cannot count as a sufficient reason for God to allow nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: God may reasonably permit nonresistant nonbelief when doing so is no worse than another way of obtaining a significantly greater good.
claims.quote: But Daniel Howard-Snyder (1996) points out, ‘if permitting [nonresistant] nonbelief is no worse than any other means for some significantly greater good to obtain’, then God might reasonably allow for nonresistant nonbelief to obtain in order to acquire that greater good.

claims.text: A good may overcome the accommodation strategy if temporary nonresistant nonbelief makes that good sufficiently more valuable.
claims.quote: I suggest that a proposed good might overcome the accommodation strategy if that good is somehow more valuable given temporary nonresistant nonbelief. If nonresistant nonbelief sufficiently increases the value of some good, then it will constitute a sufficient reason for God to allow for nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: The many-goods response holds that multiple goods jointly produced by nonresistant nonbelief can provide God sufficient reason to allow it, even if no single good can.
claims.quote: Rather than identifying a single good as a proposed reason for why God might allow for nonresistant nonbelief, the ‘many goods’ response [MGR] admits that no single good may be sufficient. Instead, the MGR holds that the multitude of goods brought about by nonresistant nonbelief together provide a sufficient reason for God to allow for nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil.
claims.quote: This is because nonresistant nonbelief is a single evil (if it can be properly called an evil), and multiple goods may arise from a single instance of evil without that evil increasing.

claims.text: If a world containing nonresistant nonbelief has greater total value than a relevantly comparable world without it, God has sufficient reason to create the former.
claims.quote: If W has a total value which is greater than W′, then God has a sufficient reason to bring about W rather than W′.

claims.text: Refuting one proposed good does not refute the many-goods response to divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: Even if a critic is able to demonstrate that some particular good does not qualify as contributing to the overall value brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, she will not have demonstrated that the MGR fails.

claims.text: Goods individually less valuable than a relationship with God can collectively make a world containing nonresistant nonbelief more valuable.
claims.quote: Any good at all that is brought about by nonresistant nonbelief will contribute to the overall value of W. This means that the task of identifying goods might actually be relatively simple.

claims.text: The many-goods response can succeed even when nonresistant nonbelief is not logically necessary for any individual good.
claims.quote: Even if for each good identified for the MGR there is some possible way to attain that good without allowing for nonresistant nonbelief, the MGR may still succeed.

claims.text: The many-goods response succeeds if nonresistant nonbelief is the only way for God to obtain enough goods, or if alternatives cause more evil.
claims.quote: So long as nonresistant nonbelief is the only way for God to acquire a sufficient number of goods, the MGR will succeed. The MGR will also succeed if all of the goods in question might be acquired by some means other than nonresistant nonbelief, but that other means causes a greater amount of evil than nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s accommodation strategy does not defeat the many-goods response merely because an individual good can occur within a relationship with God.
claims.quote: But the accommodation strategy is not so devastating against the MGR. Even if some particular good might be possible to acquire within a relationship with God, it might still count in favour of W, rather than W′.

claims.text: The many-goods response may succeed even if every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God.
claims.quote: Given this, it is possible that the MGR will succeed even if every good identified can also be realized within a relationship with God.

claims.text: If the comparative values of worlds with and without nonresistant nonbelief are too close to determine, the argument from divine hiddenness reaches a stalemate.
claims.quote: If this is the case, then argument from divine hiddenness will result in a stalemate.

claims.text: A relationship with God may be infinitely valuable, or so valuable that no collection of other goods can outweigh its loss.
claims.quote: A proponent of the Problem of Divine Hiddenness might argue that the value of a relationship with God is so great that the total value necessary to outweigh it cannot be achieved even by a great number of other goods.

claims.text: A relationship between God and an imperfect human is reasonably regarded as finitely valuable.
claims.quote: It is reasonable to suppose that a relationship between God and a human would be of finite value on account of the human’s imperfection.

claims.text: Even if a relationship with God is not infinitely valuable, goods arising from nonresistant nonbelief may be unable to outweigh its value.
claims.quote: Even if the value of a relationship with God is not infinite, it might still be so great that there simply aren’t enough goods from nonresistant nonbelief to outweigh the value of a relationship with God.

claims.text: Temporary nonresistant nonbelief can be followed by a person's choice to enter a relationship with God, whereas permanent nonresistant nonbelief cannot.
claims.quote: Temporary nonresistant nonbelief allows for the possibility that the person in question might eventually choose to enter into a relationship with God, while permanent nonresistant nonbelief does not allow for this.

claims.text: Permanent nonresistant nonbelief prevents a person from ever entering a relationship with God.
claims.quote: If some person is a permanent nonresistant nonbeliever, then she can never enter into a relationship with God.

claims.text: For permanent nonresistant nonbelief, the lost value of a relationship with God is plausibly too great for the resulting goods to outweigh.
claims.quote: It is reasonable to think that in this case the value of the relationship lost would be so great that the goods gained from the individual’s nonresistant nonbelief would be insufficient to outweigh that lost value.

claims.text: When nonresistant nonbelief is temporary and followed by a relationship with God, its lost value may be outweighed by many goods.
claims.quote: If she does enter into a relationship with God sometime after she comes to believe, then it seems reasonable that that the total value lost by her temporary nonresistant nonbelief would not be so great that it could not be outweighed by many goods.

claims.text: A world containing temporary nonresistant nonbelief may have greater total value than an alternative world without it.
claims.quote: That is, the total value of W might still be greater than the total value of W′ if the nonresistant nonbelief within W is temporary.

claims.text: It is not evident that permanent nonresistant nonbelief occurs, because people who die as nonbelievers may become believers after death.
claims.quote: But unlike temporary nonresistant nonbelief, it is not obvious that permanent nonresistant nonbelief actually occurs. Even if many nonresistant nonbelievers die without deathbed conversions, they may become postmortem believers.

claims.text: Without evidence that permanent nonresistant nonbelief actually or probably occurs, its incompatibility with God does not threaten theism.
claims.quote: So unless one can demonstrate that permanent nonresistant nonbelief actually occurs, or very likely occurs, the mere fact that it is incompatible with the existence of God does not pose a threat to theism.

claims.text: Permanent nonresistant nonbelief cannot independently support atheism because evidence for or against it depends on whether atheism or theism is probable.
claims.quote: Thus, we should remain agnostic about the existence of permanent nonresistant nonbelievers until we determine whether atheism or theism is very probable. But this means that we cannot use the existence of permanent nonresistant nonbelief in an independent argument for atheism.

claims.text: All possible worlds are comparable in value.
claims.quote: I move forward on the assumption that all worlds are comparable.

claims.text: Human inability to make accurate value judgments does not show that an omniscient being cannot compare possible worlds.
claims.quote: For it may be that any reason to think that they are not comparable proves only that humans are incapable of making accurate judgments of value. But this does not mean that an omniscient being would be incapable of making such judgments.

claims.text: The MGR assumes that God can know all the relevant details and values of possible worlds before creating one.
claims.quote: their values, He must know what those values are prior to creating.

claims.text: Whether God can know every detail of a world containing libertarian free will before creating it is controversial.
claims.quote: But whether God can know all the minute details of the world He creates—especially if that world includes creaturely libertarian free will—is controversial.

claims.text: The MGR would be stronger if it did not depend on a controversial doctrine about divine foreknowledge.
claims.quote: It would be a virtue for the success of the MGR not to depend on the truth of a controversial position like this.

claims.text: Even if open theism is true, God might judge that the potential goods enabled by nonresistant nonbelief outweigh its potential risks.
claims.quote: As long as God knows that there are many goods which can come about only given nonresistant nonbelief, He might be able to determine that the potential reward is greater than the potential risk.

claims.text: If nonresistant nonbelief produces many goods, theism must explain why God permits so many believers rather than universal nonresistant nonbelief.
claims.quote: If there are many goods that are brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, then why is the number of believers so high? Why doesn’t God desire for there to be universal nonresistant nonbelief?

claims.text: God may sacrifice a relationship only when several goods together are sufficiently valuable, and some of those goods may require believers.
claims.quote: First, since no single good is valuable enough on its own for God to sacrifice the good of a relationship, God could only justify sacrificing a relationship with a person if it would allow for a number of goods which together were sufficiently valuable. Second, many of the goods might be possible only if some believers exist.

claims.text: Nonresistant nonbelief may enable morally significant free choices because awareness of God can make choosing rightly easier.
claims.quote: God would make Himself hidden so that humans could have a real opportunity to exercise their will.

claims.text: Some morally significant choices are more valuable and require greater strength of will when made by nonresistant nonbelievers than by believers.
claims.quote: It seems plausible that there are at least some cases in which a morally significant free choice is more valuable, and in which choosing the good demonstrates a greater strength of will, when it is chosen by a person who does not even have evidence sufficient for belief in the existence of God.

claims.text: Allowing nonresistant nonbelief lets some humans bear the responsibility of telling others that God exists.
claims.quote: A second benefit of allowing for nonresistant nonbelief is that it makes it possible for some humans to have the responsibility of telling other humans about God’s existence.

claims.text: God may temporarily remain hidden until a person is prepared to seek a relationship with God for the right reasons.
claims.quote: God might remain hidden from someone until she is ready to respond in the right way.

claims.text: Nonresistant nonbelief can make genuine self-sacrifice possible because a person who believes no God exists can give up life without hope of an afterlife.
claims.quote: But unless she sacrifices her life knowing that she is truly giving everything up, her sacrifice cannot be genuine.

claims.text: World W permits a greater variety of personal testimonies about entering a relationship with God than world W′.
claims.quote: In W, there can be a greater variety of personal testimony about entering into a relationship with God.

claims.text: Personal testimonies can be good for both the person giving the testimony and the community that receives it.
claims.quote: It is plausible that an individual’s personal testimony can be good for both the individual and for the community to which an individual shares her testimony.

claims.text: A person's story of entering a relationship with God may be the best story for that individual.
claims.quote: It may be that each person’s story of how she entered into a relationship with God is the best story for that individual.

claims.text: If God eternally knew each person's best story of coming to know God, God would create a world in which each person lives that story.
claims.quote: If God knew this from eternity, then He would do what he could to create a world where each person lives the story of coming to know God that is best for her.

claims.text: Sharing personal testimonies can strengthen and help a religious community flourish by enabling deeper mutual understanding and encouragement.
claims.quote: The community itself is then strengthened as people are able to understand each other in deeper ways. These testimonies may also encourage the members of the community.

claims.text: A testimony that includes nonresistant nonbelief may be especially valuable to its subject and to the subject's religious community.
claims.quote: A testimony which includes a period of nonresistant nonbelief may be particularly valuable.

claims.text: Fictional stories of nonresistant nonbelievers might provide believers with the communal benefits attributed to actual nonresistant nonbelievers.
claims.quote: If W′ contains fictional stories of nonresistant nonbelievers, then the believers in that world might have the communal benefits of those stories;

claims.text: Testimonies from former resistant nonbelievers may be sufficient to secure the testimonial benefits, making nonresistant nonbelief unnecessary.
claims.quote: A second objection is that the stories of resistant nonbelievers would be enough to gain these benefits, so nonresistant nonbelief would not be necessary.

claims.text: The value of former resistant nonbelievers' testimonies does not eliminate the added value of former nonresistant nonbelievers' testimonies.
claims.quote: It does not mean that the testimony of a former nonresistant nonbeliever would not be valuable. That added value is all that is needed to contribute to the MGR.

claims.text: Nonresistant nonbelief may be preferable to resistant nonbelief because nonresistant nonbelievers do not sin through their nonbelief.
claims.quote: Furthermore, nonresistant nonbelief might be a more desirable state of affairs than resistant nonbelief, since nonresistant nonbelievers do not sin in their nonbelief.

claims.text: Testimonies of nonresistant nonbelievers help people appreciate union with God without every person having experienced nonresistant nonbelief.
claims.quote: The personal testimonies of nonresistant nonbelievers allow many people to gain this new appreciation without all of them having been nonresistant nonbelievers themselves.

claims.text: If nobody had been a nonresistant nonbeliever, sharing personal testimonies would plausibly be less common.
claims.quote: Second, if there were never any nonresistant nonbelievers, it’s plausible that the practice of sharing personal testimonies would itself be less common.

claims.text: If nonresistant nonbelief brings about enough goods, a world containing it may be more valuable overall than a world without it.
claims.quote: If there are enough goods brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, then the value of a world containing nonresistant nonbelief might be greater, all else being equal, than the value of a world without nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: Any good caused by nonresistant nonbelief contributes to the total value of a world containing nonresistant nonbelief, regardless of how valuable that good is.
claims.quote: A response of this kind simplifies the task of identifying goods because any good brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, no matter how valuable it is, contributes to the value of that world on the whole.

claims.text: Proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, and the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is the thesis that God is part of all God's parts.
God's contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another is robust responsibility, and representing God as the source of that actualisation requires irreducible de se content.
The hiddenness argument holds that a perfectly loving God would preclude non-resistant nonbelief.
claims.quote: the existence of a perfectly loving God entails (or, at the very least, strongly suggests) the absence of non-resistant nonbelief

claims.text: Non-resistant nonbelief exists in the world.
claims.quote: the fairly uncontroversial fact that there is non-resistant nonbelief in our world

claims.text: The existence of non-resistant nonbelief supports the non-existence of a perfectly loving God.
claims.quote: one can infer the non-existence of a perfectly loving God.

claims.text: God might permit non-resistant nonbelief so that humans can freely choose a loving relationship with God.
claims.quote: God might permit the existence of non-resistant nonbelief in our world to procure the good of humans freely choosing to enter into a loving relationship with God.

claims.text: Any reason for divine withdrawal must be one whose dominant concern cannot be met through divine-human interaction.
claims.quote: any reason God finds appealing as a reason for remaining withdrawn from human beings must be one whose dominant concern cannot be met within the framework of divine-human interaction

claims.text: Schellenberg regards a world of basic divine self-revelation, with withdrawal that preserves possible relationship, as intellectually preferable.
claims.quote: Given what we know about God’s love and nature, Schellenberg maintains that (1) is the “more intellectually attractive picture”.

claims.text: Schellenberg's two categories of criticism do not exhaust candidate defeaters of the hiddenness argument.
claims.quote: they do not exhaust the list of candidate defeaters to the argument.

claims.text: A relevant objection to the hiddenness argument need not supply a plausible reason for God's hiddenness.
claims.quote: a theistic respondent to the hiddenness argument need not think that a relevant objection against it has to provide a plausible reason for God’s hiddenness.

claims.text: Providing a reason for divine hiddenness is sufficient but unnecessary for questioning the alleged entailment between perfect love and absent non-resistant nonbelief.
claims.quote: providing a reason for hiddenness is sufficient to question the entailment, but it is not necessary.

claims.text: Schellenberg claims that perfect divine love places every non-resistant relationship-capable creature in a position to participate in a meaningful relationship with God.
claims.quote: if there is a perfectly loving God, all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who haven’t freely shut themselves off from Him are in a position to participate in such a relationship.

claims.text: Schellenberg claims that belief in God's existence is necessary to be positioned to exercise one's capacity for relationship with God.
claims.quote: the belief that God exists is a necessary condition for being in a position to exercise one’s capacity for relationship with God

claims.text: The authors argue that belief in God's existence is not necessary for being positioned to exercise one's capacity for relationship with God.
claims.quote: We shall argue that Schellenberg’s claim here is false. Belief is not a necessary condition to be in a position to exercise one’s capacity for relationship with God.

claims.text: The authors conclude that Schellenberg's hiddenness argument is unsuccessful because its two core expectation claims can be challenged or rejected.
claims.quote: Given that we have reason to question the first (in the form of an undercutting defeater) and to plainly reject the second (in the form of a rebutting defeater), Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument is therefore unsuccessful.

claims.text: If a perfectly loving God exists, every creature capable of an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with God and not freely closed to God can enter that relationship merely by trying.
claims.quote: P1. If there is a perfectly loving God, all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who have not freely shut themselves off from God are in a position to participate in such a relationship – i.e. able to do so just by trying.

claims.text: Believing that God exists is necessary for being able to participate in an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with God.
claims.quote: P2. No one can be in a position to participate in such a relationship without believing that God exists.

claims.text: If a perfectly loving God exists, every relationship-capable creature not freely closed to God believes that God exists.
claims.quote: C1. If there is a perfectly loving God, all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who have not freely shut themselves off from God believe that God exists (from P1 and P2).

claims.text: Some creatures capable of relationship with God have not freely shut themselves off from God but do not believe that God exists.
claims.quote: P3. It is not the case that all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who have not freely shut themselves off from God believe that God exists: there is non-resistant nonbelief; ‘God is hidden’.

claims.text: No perfectly loving God exists.
claims.quote: C2. It is not the case that there is a perfectly loving God (from C1 and P3).

claims.text: If God exists, God is perfectly loving.
claims.quote: P4. If God exists, God is perfectly loving.

claims.text: God does not exist.
claims.quote: C3. It is not the case that God exists (from C2 and P4).

claims.text: A perfectly loving God would seek an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with every creature capable of it that has not freely shut itself off from God.
claims.quote: P1′. A perfectly loving God would seek explicit and positively meaningful relationship with all creatures who are capable of it and who have not freely shut themselves off from God.

claims.text: God is capable of seeking an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with all creatures capable of it who have not freely shut themselves off from God.
claims.quote: by making a further assumption—one which we may grant for now—that God is capable of doing so

claims.text: The plausibility of P1′ must be argued for before its rational acceptability can support P1.
claims.quote: Hence, one would need to argue for the plausibility of P1′, so that the rational acceptability of P1′ would then ‘transfer’ over to P1.

claims.text: Schellenberg maintains that P1 and P1′ are logically equivalent.
claims.quote: Schellenberg thinks that this is not required because he maintains that P1 and P1′ “are in fact logically equivalent”.

claims.text: Schellenberg holds that P1 expresses a conceptual truth about divine love, is necessarily true, and is justified a priori.
claims.quote: Not only is P1 conceptually true, but, secondly, it is also necessarily true, according to Schellenberg. Thirdly, we are rationally entitled in holding P1 to be true based on a priori considerations.

claims.text: A conceptually true proposition is known a priori and necessarily true.
claims.quote: It would appear that Schellenberg is suggesting that a conceptually true proposition is known a priori and is also necessarily true.

claims.text: Schellenberg provides very little support for the claim that P1 is a conceptual truth, and his conceptual analysis appears to collapse into an analogy from human love.
claims.quote: there is very little in Schellenberg’s work in support of the claim that the initial conditional premise in the argument, P1, is a conceptual truth. As a matter of fact, it appears that Schellenberg’s ‘conceptual analysis’ of divine love collapses into another, distinct strategy he uses to support P1—using human love as an analogue for divine love

claims.text: The fact that a proposition is not obviously necessary does not show that it is not necessarily true.
claims.quote: The mere fact that a certain proposition doesn’t strike us as a necessary truth in any obvious way does not mean that it is not necessarily true.

claims.text: A person claiming that a proposition is necessarily true has greater reason to explain its necessity when that necessity is not obvious.
claims.quote: But a person who claims that a certain proposition is necessarily true has all the more reason to explain why the proposition in question is necessarily true if the proposition’s (alleged) necessity doesn’t seem obvious to us!

claims.text: Schellenberg forms the conception of divine love by extrapolating from human love.
claims.quote: So, according to Schellenberg, we form our conception of divine love with reference to human love, by extrapolating from the concept of human love.

claims.text: Human understanding of love is formed through observations in the actual world.
claims.quote: But it is obvious that we form our understanding of human love through our observations in the actual world.

claims.text: P1 cannot confidently be called necessarily true because there is no reason to think considerations about human love hold in every possible world containing humans.
claims.quote: It is too bold for the simple reason that we have no reason to suppose that our considerations over human love will hold in every possible world containing human beings.

claims.text: Schellenberg replies that understanding human love grasps conceptual and necessary truths, and that the best human love introduces similarly necessary normative considerations.
claims.quote: He argues that (1) a proper understanding of human love means that we are talking about something that is conceptual and necessarily true, and so holds in all (relevant) possible worlds. And, in any case says Schellenberg, (2) it is our understanding of not just any human love but rather the best human love that is pertinent and so brings in normative considerations that are likewise conceptual and necessarily true.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s second response requires the first because understanding human love must grasp its essence to yield a conceptual and necessary truth.
claims.quote: It should be clear that (1) is a necessary condition for (2) once we see that, for Schellenberg, to ‘understand’ something is to grasp the essence of it.

claims.text: If human love’s essence is uncertain, then what is judged best in human love cannot be known to be a necessarily true conceptual truth.
claims.quote: Now, if it turns out that we cannot be sure what the essence of human love is, or, in other words, if we cannot be sure whether our insight into human love is complete, then we cannot be sure whether what we take to be the best of human love is a conceptual truth that is necessarily true.

claims.text: Understanding something can differ logically from grasping its essence, and only grasping an essence supports an inference to conceptual necessity.
claims.quote: These examples illustrate that there can be a logical gap between understanding something and having an insight into its essence; only the latter can allow us to infer a conclusion that is conceptually and necessarily true.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s argument that human love holds across possible worlds because its essence is understood begs the question.
claims.quote: But this argument is hardly rationally persuasive, for it rests on a (synonymous) begging of the question—the premise is simply a reworded expression of the conclusion.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s response provides no substantive reason to regard P1 of the hiddenness argument as a conceptual truth.
claims.quote: Thus, Schellenberg’s response still gives us no substantive reason to think that P1 of the hiddenness argument is a conceptual truth.

claims.text: It is conceivable that a person can love someone without seeking a personal relationship with that person.
claims.quote: And, surely, if it is conceivable how, in this world, certain human beings might be loving even though they do not seek personal relationships, it is certainly conceivable that there are other possible worlds in which this is also the case.

claims.text: The claim that seeking a personal relationship is essential to human love is unsupported and extravagant.
claims.quote: Thus, the claim that the seeking of a personal relationship is an essential part of human love (i.e. that it obtains in every possible world containing human beings) is extravagant and unsupported.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s attempt to establish P1 as an a priori, necessary conceptual truth fails.
claims.quote: For this reason, we think that Schellenberg’s attempt to support P1 as a conceptual truth, one which is also necessarily true and known a priori, is a failure.

claims.text: Vanstone’s position does not fit either version of Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument and can be turned against both.
claims.quote: Upon scrutiny, Vanstone’s position fits neither version of the hiddenness argument. What is more, not only does the view propounded in Love’s Endeavor, Love’s Expense not lend itself to be enlisted for Schellenberg’s early as well as later groundwork for his atheistic conclusion, it can effectively be turned against both deliveries of the hiddenness argument.

claims.text: Vanstone’s view supplies undercutting defeaters against Schellenberg’s analogical argument for P1.
claims.quote: we argue that Vanstone’s position provides several powerful undercutting defeaters against Schellenberg’s analogical argument in support of P1.

claims.text: Vanstone’s phenomenological method infers authentic love from the distortions and failures of love.
claims.quote: Vanstone’s phenomenological method works ex negativo. Even if we could never experience directly the positive side of authentic love, still we could get at its meaning through a phenomenological detour.

claims.text: Humans can identify authentic love through distorted instances because they possess practical discriminatory power.
claims.quote: For humans, as Vanstone says, are equipped with what he calls a “practical power of discrimination” (p. 42), which allows them to recognise the positive through the negative.

claims.text: Vanstone understands divine love as total self-giving, namely total self-emptying, in God’s relation to creation.
claims.quote: Vanstone’s notion of self-giving is embedded in a particular theory of kenosis, which interprets total self-giving as total self-emptying.

claims.text: For Vanstone, God gives himself entirely to creation, so creation necessarily makes God vulnerable.
claims.quote: God unreservedly gives Himself over to His creation, without holding anything back. Hence, for Vanstone, ‘love’s expense’ or cost (as announced in the title of his book) is epitomised by God’s vulnerability as inevitably engendered by the activity of creation.

claims.text: Vanstone’s account abandons traditional divine omnipotence because God has forfeited control over future earthly affairs.
claims.quote: Out of self-giving love for His creation-to-be, He has forfeited control over earthly future affairs, in that “triumph or . . . tragedy has passed from His hands”. This directly gainsays God’s attribute of omnipotence.

claims.text: Vanstone’s account may undermine traditional divine omniscience because God cannot predict whether creation ends in tragedy or triumph.
claims.quote: At the same time, the future trajectory of tragedy or triumph is not predictable by God either, which might undercut the attribute of omniscience.

claims.text: Vanstone distinguishes authentic love from benevolence, treating benevolence presented as love as an affront.
claims.quote: “kindness or benevolence . . . under its own name is usually welcome: but it becomes an affront when it masquerades as love” (p. 42).

claims.text: Schellenberg’s use of traditional theistic attributes cannot accommodate Vanstone’s rejection of traditional omnipotence and omniscience.
claims.quote: Schellenberg’s overarching strategy of turning traditional claims of theism against the theist position itself, can hardly accommodate for Vanstone’s express abandonment of the traditional conceptions of God’s omnipotence and omniscience.

claims.text: Vanstone’s divine-love analogy emphasizes God as an artist and God’s waiting for creatures’ response in an open-ended creation.
claims.quote: Two of the basic constituents of Vanstone’s understanding of Divine self-giving love are thus completely absent from Schellenberg’s truncated, borrowed version thereof: a detailed exploration of the idea of God as artist and the suggestion that upon His precarious endeavour in the course of an on-going and open-ended process of creation, it is in fact God who is waiting for a response by His creatures.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s abandoned-child story represents a sincere divine seeker who lacks confirmation sufficient for meaningful relationship with God.
claims.quote: This kind of mindset is genuinely open to an encounter with the Divine but not graced with any confirmation that would sustain the minimum of belief necessary for entering into an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.

claims.text: Schellenberg infers that God does not exist because a loving mother would not remain hidden from her child in such life-threatening circumstances.
claims.quote: Thus Schellenberg infers that there is no God, for “[a] loving mother would not be hidden from her child in circumstances like those mentioned if

claims.text: Vanstone holds that God as Creator cannot always predict, respond to, or prevent human tragedies.
claims.quote: he insists not only on the possibility but on the inevitability of the fact that God as Creator cannot at all times predict, respond to, and prevent the tragedies in our lives.

claims.text: God’s creative limitations arise from concrete creative activity rather than from the concept of God.
claims.quote: such limitations cannot be derived from the concept of God, but can only be ascertained a posteriori from the perspective of the sincere seeker and possible theist

claims.text: Schellenberg’s jungle analogy assumes unlimited divine intervention and ignores that God may vulnerably await a response from creation.
claims.quote: Because of his robust notion of omnipotence, Schellenberg, in his jungle story, never entertains the more cooperative possibility that God might be the vulnerable one who is waiting for a response from His creation.

claims.text: A mature seeker can form an explicitly meaningful relationship through cooperative survival without recognizing God.
claims.quote: This joint effort of survival and the personal bonds that may grow out of it, surely makes for an ‘explicit and positively meaningful’ relationship

claims.text: Vanstone rejects divine supremacy as an illegitimate implication of creation and as a threat to religious integrity.
claims.quote: That God should be superior, in every or any respect [!], to an inferior universe is a quite illegitimate deduction from the doctrine of creation. It is also a deduction which endangers the integrity of religion.

claims.text: Schellenberg maintains that divine love values a relationship with creatures intrinsically, not merely for its benefits to them.
claims.quote: his conception of divine love implies a God who would not value the relationship to His creatures only in terms of the benefits that His children might reap from it, but also for the relationship’s own sake, i.e., its intrinsic value.

claims.text: Within Vanstone’s framework, humans know God’s vulnerability and loving power only mediately through concrete creative activity.
claims.quote: it is not only God’s vulnerability that can be known only mediately, namely through the concrete manifestations of His creative activity, the same applies to His general power of loving His creatures as well.

claims.text: God’s love cannot be recognized in a single momentary revelation because God is immersed in an ongoing creation.
claims.quote: But this implies that actual recognition of God’s love is never ‘momentary’, i.e., it can never be encapsulated within a single revelatory timeslice of divine presence.

claims.text: Schellenberg relies on a basic revelatory encounter with personal divinity, whereas Vanstone holds that encounter is indirectly mediated by concrete expressions of love.
claims.quote: Schellenberg relies on the possibility of a basic, revelatory encounter between the personal human and the personal divine, whereas Vanstone, overtly indebted to Paul Tillich’s Cultural Protestantism, holds that any such encounter can be only indirect, namely, mediated through concrete (artistic, symbolic) expressions of love.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s analogical argument for P1 is unsuccessful because it distorts Vanstone’s vulnerable conception of divine love.
claims.quote: we consider Schellenberg’s analogical argument in support of P1 as unsuccessful. Independent of whether or not one agrees with Vanstone’s conception of God on its own terms, Schellenberg’s reliance on a Vanstone-inspired notion of divine love has proven distorted in character.

claims.text: Vanstone’s analogy gives strong reason to reject Schellenberg’s notion of recognition as a basic revelatory encounter.
claims.quote: Vanstone’s own argument from analogy, when properly considered within its context of Tillich-style Christology, provides powerful reasons to reject Schellenberg’s notion of recognition

claims.text: Schellenberg has not shown that basic revelatory encounters display the care and guidance constitutive of divine love.
claims.quote: Schellenberg has not shown how they could be properly construed as displaying the love-defining quality of care and guidance

claims.text: Revelation as a temporally patterned process better explains divine care and guidance than a basic revelatory encounter.
claims.quote: which, it seems to us, is much better explained in terms of revelation as a patterned process.

claims.text: Schellenberg's second premise states that belief that God exists is necessary for explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.
claims.quote: The second premise of the expectations sub-argument (and of the overall hiddenness argument), P2, states that the belief that God exists is a necessary condition to be in a position to participate in an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.

claims.text: Schellenberg holds that loving, thanking, contemplating, praising, or praying to God logically requires belief that God exists.
claims.quote: Such attitudes and actions are not just contingently difﬁcult but logically impossible for one who does not believe that God exists.

claims.text: Weak belief that God exists can support gratitude, love, trust, contemplation, praise, and prayer.
claims.quote: Even a weak belief that God exists is compatible with gratefulness, love toward God, trust, contemplation, and the like, for even a weak belief involves a disposition to feel it true that God exists.

claims.text: A nonbeliever who responds to goodness may be responding to God himself.

claims.quote: Wainwright has substituted his own notion of relationship between God and human beings for Schellenberg’s conception of it which involves “explicit, reciprocal interaction”.

claims.text: An atheist could clearly hear God through conscience and committedly act on that guidance without believing God exists.
claims.quote: Suppose I am an atheist, and God speaks to me clearly through my conscience so that, when faced with a moral decision, I have no hesitations about the proper course of action; I then ‘respond’ to the voice of God in a ﬁrm and committed way, e.g. in ending up doing the right thing, even though I do not believe that God exists.

claims.text: It is coherent that a person can engage in an explicit and reciprocal relationship with God without believing God exists.
claims.quote: So in the scenarios described by Wainwright and Moser, it appears coherent to suppose that one can engage in both an explicit and reciprocal relationship with God without believing that God exists.

claims.text: For argument's sake, a positively meaningful relationship with God requires reciprocity based on regarding God's existence as true.

claims.text: Under that interpretation, Moser's and Wainwright's objections do not show that an explicit positively meaningful relationship is possible without belief.

claims.quote: Even with this clariﬁcation, which renders Schellenberg’s claim impervious to the criticisms of Moser and Wainwright, we maintain that Schellenberg’s claim is false.

claims.text: Acceptance that a proposition is true involves a more positive attitude toward it than merely acting on the proposition's assumption.

claims.text: A person can have an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God while accepting, rather than believing, that God exists.

claims.text: The second premise of the expectations sub-argument is false because belief that God exists is unnecessary for a positively meaningful relationship with God.
claims.quote: For this, we do not need the belief that God exists. We conclude, therefore, that the second premise of the expectations sub-argument, P2, is false.

claims.text: Schellenberg's hiddenness argument is unsuccessful because both its conditional premise and its belief requirement are independently vulnerable.
claims.quote: Each of these two (independent) criticisms suffices to render the hiddenness argument unsuccessful.

claims.text: A reasonable non-believer cannot form belief in God because the available evidence is insufficient, and belief formation normally depends on evidence.

claims.text: The charge that reasonable non-believers are unfairly abandoned dissipates because they can voluntarily accept God's existence and enter a relationship with God without belief.

claims.text: Pre-evangelical people who have never encountered the concept of God cannot use belief, hope, or acceptance to enter a relationship with God.

claims.text: The exclusion of pre-evangelical people concerns divine justice more directly than divine love.

claims.text: Possible unknown greater goods may explain why propositional attitudes toward God are not universally available.
claims.quote: For all we know, it might be that the non-universality of propositional attitudes towards God is related to the existence of some unknown (greater) goods.

claims.text: If justification for Schellenberg's conditional premise is undermined, possible goods of mystery remain a viable theistic option.

claims.text: An explicit personal relationship with God would provide moral and experiential benefits that promote human flourishing.
claims.quote: Well, first, there would be broadly moral benefits. We would be able to draw on the resources of that relationship to overcome seemingly ever present flaws in our character.

claims.text: Phenomenology is necessary when the phenomenon in question is hidden.

claims.text: Rea’s response to divine hiddenness does not rely on God allowing hiddenness to secure human goods.
claims.quote: Importantly, Rea claims that his response does not depend on the commonly held theistic view that God allows hiddenness to secure human goods.

claims.text: Rea’s account of what justifies God in allowing divine hiddenness is unsuccessful.
claims.quote: In this paper I offer a detailed criticism of Rea’s account of what justifies God in allowing divine hiddenness, arguing that Rea’s response to the argument from divine hiddenness is unsuccessful.

claims.text: Appeals to alleged biblical precursors of contemporary philosophical-theological problems require caution.
claims.quote: By way of pointing out a number of similarities and differences between concepts of divine hiddenness in the theologies of the Hebrew Bible and in a specific formulation thereof in analytic philosophy of religion, this article not only reveals some neglected specifics of the historical variability of an important theological idea but also suggests taking caution when appealing to alleged biblical precursors to contemporary philosophical-theological problems.

claims.text: Abraham’s faith is a lived movement irreducible to ontology or epistemology.
claims.quote: Abraham's faith is a lived movement irreducible to either ontology or epistemology.

claims.text: Faith is an action that awaits what it alone could never accomplish.
claims.quote: Faith is an action that waits upon what it alone could never accomplish.

claims.text: The dynamics of faith reveal God as hidden precisely in God’s intimate nearness.
claims.quote: It is these dynamics of faith that show God to be hidden, precisely within the intimate drawing near of God.

claims.text: Freud's claim that belief in God is immature reflects an earlier undermining of public theology's justification.
claims.quote: This article traces the intellectual history behind Clifford's claim, and argues that, by the time that Freud offers his claim that belief in God is immature, the justification for public theology has been undermined.

claims.text: Defending public theology requires responding to Kant's critique of reason and Hume's skepticism.
claims.quote: If public theology is to be defended, this response is both necessary and timely.

claims.text: Desire depends on an interval between concealment and anticipated disclosure.
claims.quote: Pornography, by striking contrast, is not only revolting but boring: by revealing exactly everything, it short-circuits the interval between hiddenness and anticipated disclosure that makes desire possible.

claims.text: The Eucharist's veiling of Christ provokes desire for his full revelation.
claims.quote: desire subsists in the interval between concealment and disclosure, and indeed it is precisely because the Eucharist "veils" Christ's presence under the species of bread and wine that it also provokes the poet's "desire" for the full "revelation" of that presence in the Kingdom of God.

claims.text: Appeals to alleged biblical precursors of contemporary divine-hiddenness problems require caution because relevant concepts vary historically.
claims.quote: this article not only reveals some neglected specifics of the historical variability of an important theological idea but also suggests taking caution when appealing to alleged biblical precursors to contemporary philosophical-theological problems.

claims.text: If God existed, he would provide sufficient evidence to seekers, but such evidence is absent.
claims.quote: این برهان مدعی است که اگر خداوند وجود داشت باید شواهد و دلایل کافی برای این باور را حداقل برای انسان‌هایی که در جست‌وجوی او هستند فراهم می‌کرد، اما اکنون این‌گونه نیست، پس خداوند وجود ندارد.

claims.text: Therefore, God does not exist.
claims.quote: این برهان مدعی است که اگر خداوند وجود داشت باید شواهد و دلایل کافی برای این باور را حداقل برای انسان‌هایی که در جست‌وجوی او هستند فراهم می‌کرد، اما اکنون این‌گونه نیست، پس خداوند وجود ندارد.

claims.text: Nonresistant nonbelief caused solely by insufficient evidence is evidence against God's existence.
claims.quote: That there are people who do not believe God exists due only to a lack of evidence is therefore a reason for thinking that God does not exist.

claims.text: Greater-goods responses hold that God withholds evidence to bring about some greater good.
claims.quote: One of the most prominent ways to respond to this kind of argument from divine hiddenness is to maintain that God withholds evidence of Himself in order to bring about some greater good or another.

claims.text: Greater-goods responses are puzzling if conscious personal relationship with God exceeds every other good.
claims.quote: Third, if a conscious personal relationship with God is greater than all other goods we might wonder how there could be goods for the sake of which God would be willing to withhold such relationship from some people.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness supports atheism when sincere seekers cannot find God, while agnosticism sees equal evidence on both sides.
claims.quote: From an atheistic perspective the existence of people who are sincerely looking for God but cannot reach Him is a supportive point for atheism. On the other side, same problem supports agnosticism since there are equal evidence from both side for the existence of God from an agnostic perspective.

claims.text: The divine-hiddenness problem should be postponed because its premises are not verifiable by everyone.
claims.quote: I have tried to show the problem has nothing new since premises of the divine hiddenness problem are not verifiable by everyone. As a conclusion I have offered postponing the divine hiddenness problem and discussing existence of God on a rational ground by presenting a counterargument.

claims.text: An Augustinian account of original sin can provide an empirically grounded response to divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: I show that a classically Augustinian notion of original sin can provide a sufficient response to those objections, and that appeal to original sin can form an empirically grounded response to the divine hiddenness problem, beyond a simple defense.

claims.text: Apparently nonresistant nonbelief may indicate that humanity lost capacities for relationship with God through a Fall-like event.
claims.quote: If the possibility of original sin-type scenarios is compatible with God’s perfect love, then the phenomenon of apparently nonresistant nonbelievers would push us toward considering the possibility that humans have lost those capacities for relationship with God by a Fall-like event in the past.

claims.text: The requirement that goods permitting divine hiddenness benefit the hidden person has numerous exceptions, especially in cases of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: I will argue that this principle has a number of exceptions, even in the context of evil, but particularly in the context of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: If God wants relationships with humans, widespread blameless nonbelief appears problematic because belief is needed for such relationships.
claims.quote: if God wants relationships with us, then why does God allow so many people to fail to believe in him through no apparent fault of their own, since not believing in him seems to be an impediment to having a relationship with him?

claims.text: Perfect divine love combined with widespread blameless nonbelief provides an argument against theism.
claims.quote: If we add that God, being perfectly loving, would want relationships with us, this provides grounds for an argument against theism.

claims.text: God reveals himself primarily through the Church, whose liturgy, sacraments, and members explain or reduce divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: God is operating through the Church to reveal himself to the world

claims.text: Schellenberg holds that inculpable failures to find sufficient evidence for God constitute evidence for atheism.
claims.quote: In other words, that many people inculpably fail to find sufficient evidence for the existence of God constitutes evidence for atheism.

claims.text: Schellenberg's defenses of divine love's incompatibility with doubt and of agnostics' inculpable nonbelief are unsuccessful.
claims.quote: This paper argues that his defense of two controversial premises of his argument is unsuccessful: one is that God’s love is incompatible with His allowing some to remain in doubt about His existence, and the other is: the nonbelief of some agnostics is inculpable.

claims.text: Theistic religions have plausible unrebutted reasons for holding that every instance of nonbelief is culpable.
claims.quote: Theistic Religions have plausible reasons, which Schellenberg has not succeeded in refuting, for thinking that every nonbelief is culpable

claims.text: Maimonides and Kierkegaard are fictionalists whose views are grounded in their respective conceptions of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: I show that both are fictionalists, that their fictionalism is grounded in their respective conceptions of divine hiddenness, and that these give rise to their construals of “truth as subjectivity”.

claims.text: Their accounts challenge assumed religious distinctions and enable fellowships that cross some denominational boundaries.
claims.quote: I argue that their construals challenge the very nature of the religious distinctions that we tend to assume; they give rise to different types of “religious fellowship” that may cross denominational distinctions, dissolving some religious boundaries while creating others.

claims.text: Such fictionalism deserves serious consideration in interreligious dialogue because it can embrace some religious others in fellowship.
claims.quote: Since some religious others are not merely tolerated but embraced in fellowship, I maintain that such forms of fictionalism deserve serious consideration in discussions of interreligious dialogue.

claims.text: Christian doctrines imply that nonresistant nonbelief is unsurprising and that purely nonresistant nonbelief does not exist.
claims.quote: The doctrine of the Church shows it as an end in itself, and in order for the Church to have meaning and to exist there has to be nonbelief in the world. Finally, the dogma of the Original Sin shows that there is no category of purely nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: The ontological chasm between God and humans may obstruct interpersonal relationships more seriously than nonbelief does.
claims.quote: The first one indicates that there could be greater than nonbelief obstacle in forming interpersonal bonds with God, namely the ontological chasm between him and human persons.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness should not be equated with divine absence, since Psalm 88 depicts a God who is hidden yet hostilely present.
claims.quote: This article challenges this influential account in light of Psalm 88—where the hidden God is hostilely present, not absent—and reevaluates divine hiddenness. Divine hiddenness is not conterminous with divine absence.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is a refusal of audience with YHWH and concerns petitionary, rather than merely experiential, inaccessibility.
claims.quote: Rather, with its roots in the ancient Near Eastern idea of the royal and cultic audience, the meaning of “hide the face” (סתר + פנים) may be construed as a refusal of an audience with the divine king YHWH.

claims.text: An absent or hostilely present God is not thereby hidden.
claims.quote: I probe the relationships between divine hiddenness, divine absence, and hostile divine presence, concluding that the absent or hostilely present God is not ipso facto hidden.

claims.text: Accepting the argument from divine hiddenness rules out all de jure objections to theism.
claims.quote: In this article I will show that accepting the argument from divine hiddenness carries a high cost: it eliminates all de jure objections to theism.

claims.text: Atheists must choose between de jure objections to theism and the divine-hiddenness objection.
claims.quote: So atheists can either have de jure objections to theism or the objection from divine hiddenness, but they cannot have both.

claims.text: The common sharp distinction between problems of evil and problems of divine hiddenness is doubtful.
claims.quote: Such a sharp distinction is not so obvious to me.

claims.text: The ambiguity of religious phenomena can be a benefit of divine hiddenness when it grounds interreligious solidarity.
claims.quote: In my paper, I pose the thesis that the ambiguity of religious phenomena can be counted among the “benefits of divine hiddenness”. This will be possible when the ambiguity of religious phenomena becomes the basis for the formation of interreligious solidarity.

claims.text: The central issue raised by divine hiddenness is how to respond to ambiguous religious phenomena rather than why they are ambiguous.
claims.quote: I also argue that in the context of divine hiddenness, the most important question is not the one concerning the genesis of this problem (“why are religious phenomena not more unambiguous?”), but the question concerning the meaning of this problem (“what to do with the ambiguity of religious phenomena?”).

claims.text: Honest unbelievers challenge the claim that God is caring or exists because a well-ordered divine reality would make God conspicuously evident.
claims.quote: Those who criticize complain that if all things are being done well, he would be conspicuously displayed; the existence of these honest unbelievers indicates a lack of care or no such thing at all.

claims.text: Theists maintain that divine hiddenness serves purposes including protecting free will, eliciting genuine faith, and enabling moral and spiritual growth.
claims.quote: To this, theists reply that divine hiddenness has needful purposes, e.g., keeping free will, provoking true faith, and facilitating moral and spiritual perfection growth.

claims.text: Purim should count as a holiday of Redemption because its narrative and practices respectively depict and anticipate divine redemption.
claims.quote: I argue that Purim should be considered a holiday of Redemption, whose narrative depicts the hidden hand of God in redeeming the world, and whose commandments and customs give us a foretaste of the redeemed world itself.

claims.text: Contrary to Rosenzweig, Purim is the genuine redemptive climax of the Jewish liturgical year.
claims.quote: Ultimately, pace Rosenzweig, I suggest that Purim ought to be regarded as the genuine redemptive climax of the liturgical year.

claims.text: A loving God would make God's existence or love sufficiently clear to show sufferers that their suffering has some good, though inscrutable, reason.
claims.quote: But if we assume, as seems most plausible, that God's reasons for permitting evil will (in many, if not most, instances) be impossible for us to comprehend, would we not expect a loving God to at least make his existence or love sufficiently clear to us so that we would know that there is some good, albeit inscrutable, reason why we (or others) are permitted to suffer?

claims.text: Hick's epistemic-distance response fails because the freedom to enter a personal relationship with God does not require God to remain epistemically distant.
claims.quote: But this kind of freedom, I go on to argue, does not necessitate an epistemically distant God, and so the problem of divine hiddenness remains unsolved.

claims.text: Kant offers a compelling solution to divine hiddenness by explaining why an all-loving God need not make divine existence evident.
claims.quote: I argue that Kant provides a compelling solution to this problem in an often overlooked passage located near the end of the secondCritique.

claims.text: God's self-revelation would impede virtue by removing the conflict between self-interest and the moral law.
claims.quote: Kant’s suggestion is that God’s revealing himself would preclude the development of virtue because we would lose the experience of conflict between self-interest and the moral law.

claims.text: Rea's claim that relationships with God are widely available leaves some nonbelievers unaccounted for.
claims.quote: However, I will suggest that it invites a response from proponents of the hiddenness argument because it leaves some nonbelievers unaccounted for.

claims.text: Panentheism can allow every person, including nonbelievers, to have a relationship with God because God is embodied in the cosmos.
claims.quote: I will rectify this by suggesting that a model of panentheism in which God is embodied in the cosmos allows all, including all nonbelievers, to have a relationship with God.

claims.text: Unrecognized relationships with God can satisfy Schellenberg's personal-relationship motivations and challenge the hiddenness argument.
claims.quote: I will then challenge the hiddenness argument by suggesting that these relationships can accommodate the key motivations behind Schellenberg's insistence on personal relationships without requiring subjects to recognize that they are in a relationship with God.

claims.text: Our universe exists because it realizes unique goods, and making it better would instead produce another universe God has also created.
claims.quote: God has created our particular universe because it contains unique goods. While God could have made our universe better, that would in fact have turned our universe into another universe, which God has also created.

claims.text: Vague revelation is defensible because an independent universe with it realizes unique goods and purposes.
claims.quote: Since our kind of independent universe with vague revelation actualizes unique goods, God has created our universe where the vague revelation serves specific purposes.

claims.text: Moser's Divine Hiddenness Response exacerbates rather than resolves the problem of evil and is therefore strongly undesirable.
claims.quote: I will argue that, far from helping the situation, this approach exacerbates it and is therefore strongly undesirable.

claims.text: Moser's assumption that no adequate theodicy exists is undermined by the demonstrated merits of process theodicy.
claims.quote: In addition, Moser’s assumption of the absence of an adequate theodicy is unjustified in light of the demonstrable merits of process theodicy in accomplishing what omnipotence-preserving approaches cannot do—defusing the defeaters to Christianity’s Four Noble Truths effectively.

claims.text: God's omnipotence should be replaced by a coherent, evidence-based conception of perfect power.
claims.quote: Thusy it is desirable andy in the absence of better optionsy epistemically obligatory that omnipotence be modified and replaced with a version of God’s perfect power that is more coherent and evidence-based, and is also in line with a significant strand within the Bible.

claims.text: Plantinga’s Reformed Epistemology maintains that belief in God can be rational without support from valid philosophical arguments.
claims.quote: Against the common objection that belief in God is only rational if supported by valid philosophical arguments, the main assertion of Plantinga's Reformed Epistemology is that belief in God is in fact prope

claims.text: Baker-Hytch’s epistemic-interdependence theodicy is incomplete or depends on a faulty modal judgment.
claims.quote: In this article I argue that Baker-Hytch's response is at best incomplete and at worst relies on a faulty modal judgement.

claims.text: Maitzen’s demographics-based argument from divine hiddenness succeeds despite attempted salvages of Baker-Hytch’s theodicy.
claims.quote: After exploring some ways Baker-Hytch might salvage his theodicy and maintaining their failure, I conclude with the success of Maitzen's argument.

claims.text: Avicenna’s ontological foundations support the possibility of relational experiences with the divine.
claims.quote: Avicenna’s ontological foundations not only support the possibility of relational experiences with the divine

claims.text: Avicenna’s ontological and epistemological foundations refute the divine-hiddenness argument and atheism.
claims.quote: Consequently, the argument from divine hiddenness—and by extension, atheism—is effectively refuted.

claims.text: Common arguments that infer nonhuman intelligences are absent from unexpected behavior are unsound.
claims.quote: I argue that common variations of this line of reasoning are unsound.

claims.text: A standard philosophical rebuttal to divine hiddenness applies at least as well to Fermi-paradox and White-House-lawn arguments.
claims.quote: In section 6, I demonstrate how this rebuttal applies at least as well to both of the other arguments.

claims.text: A common reason scientists dismiss UAP studies rests on a bad argument.
claims.quote: The primary upshot is that a common reason for serious scientists not to take UAP studies seriously rests on a bad argument.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s divine hiddenness argument is unsound because he is mistaken about its burden of proof.
claims.quote: This paper demonstrates that Schellenberg is mistaken about the burden of proof concerning his Divine Hiddenness Argument against the existence of God and that his argument is unsound.

claims.text: Schellenberg has not ruled out that God delays relationship initiation for unknown good reasons or to achieve a deeper free relationship.
claims.quote: I also explain that Schellenberg has failed to refute the possibility that God delays the starting of the relationship for the purpose of achieving a deeper relationship for the good of the creature in a way that respects the creaturely free will.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s development of the divine hiddenness argument is inconsistent with his concepts of an omnipotent, morally perfect, and ontologically perfect God.
claims.quote: I argue that the way he develops his argument is simply inconsistent with each of these concepts.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s version of the divine hiddenness argument is implausible.
claims.quote: As a result, Schellenberg’s version of the divine hiddenness argument proves to be implausible.

claims.text: Anselmian Christian narratives of lapses from knowledge-infused grace provide a neglected approach to divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: Moreover, he provides the ingredients for an interesting and heretofore neglected approach to the PDH, one rooted in multiple Christian narratives about lapses from knowledge-infused states of grace, both angelic and human.

claims.text: At least two of Lewis's responses resemble modern responses to divine hiddenness despite predating Schellenberg's argument.
claims.quote: I argue that at least two of Lewis's responses in Till We Have Faces are similar to those found in this literature, despite predating Schellenberg's argument by almost fifty years

claims.text: Lewis's third, distinct response is an important but often neglected contemporary response to divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: and that a third response, though different, is an important though often neglected response today.

claims.text: The existence of non-resistant nonbelievers is allegedly incompatible with a perfectly loving God.
claims.quote: This is incompatible with the existence of a perfectly loving God.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is the only strategy consistent with a loving God because humans weaponize ideas of superiority.
claims.quote: I instead argue that divine hiddenness, instead of being special pleading is the only strategy consistent with a loving God, and the observation that humans weaponize the ideas of superiority.

claims.text: Schellenberg holds that rational nonbelief gives reason to believe God does not exist.
claims.quote: According to philosopher John Schellenberg, the existence of rational nonbelief poses a problem for divine hiddenness which provides a reason to believe that God does not exist.

claims.text: Middle knowledge permits a loving Anselmian God to coexist with reasonable nonbelief because God knows each person's evidential threshold and who would remain unbelieving regardless.
claims.quote: We first offers a defense for the doctrine of middle knowledge, including a brief biblical defense, before arguing that a loving Anselmian God can coexist with a world where he permits reasonable nonbelief given his knowledge of how much evidence is necessary to bring a person to faith, and those for whom no amount of evidence would suffice.

claims.text: Schellenberg argues that logical unbelievers show divine hiddenness contradicts absolute divine love and thus supports God's nonexistence.
claims.quote: Therefore, through a deductive argument, one can consider Divine hiddenness as a contradiction to Divine absolute love and ultimately, as proof of the inexistence of God.

claims.text: If divine absolute love is not absolute in its actions, Schellenberg's argument cannot reach its conclusion.
claims.quote: If one is able to challenge this foundation of his argument in terms of the extent of absoluteness and that Divine absolute love is not absolute in the action aspect, his argument, in order to reach his sought conclusion, would fail.

claims.text: For distressed God-seekers considering hiddenness arguments, their distress is evidence that God is not hidden because God instigated their desire.
claims.quote: for any person who is distressed about not finding God, and who (for this reason) seriously considers the Argument from Hiddenness, the PCH would show that their own distress constitutes evidence that God is in fact not hidden to them (because this desire for God has been instigated in them by God himself).

claims.text: The Pascalian Conditional of Hiddenness offers a plausible response to the first-person problem and should form part of a complete account of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: I argue that the PCH strategy offers a plausibly actual story to respond to the first-person problem. As a result, even if we need to complement the PCH strategy with other more traditional strategies (in order to respond to other versions of the problem), the PCH strategy should plausibly be part of the complete true story about Divine Hiddenness.

claims.text: Luther uses divine hiddenness inconsistently, covering Christ's crucifixion, ordinary sustaining means, sinners' suffering, and naked divine majesty.
claims.quote: Landrum notes that Luther offers no consistent approach to the use of the word "hiddenness," since it encompasses matters as different as God's counterintuitive presence in Christ's crucifixion, God's sustaining life through ordinary means, and the suffering that sinners experience as a result of God's wrath.

claims.text: Only proclamation of Christ as God's mercy and future vindication can comfort people bewildered by terror or loss.
claims.quote: In this case, only the proclamation of Christ, as both God's mercy and future vindication, can comfort those bewildered due to terror or loss.

claims.text: Vanhoozer’s authorial analogy appears to intensify divine hiddenness and neglect by portraying God as absent without good reason.
claims.quote: The Author is absent from those characters who are open to relationship with Him and is likewise absent in situations wherein we would expect Him to lovingly intervene in His story, and furthermore, there doesn’t seem to be any good reason for His absence.

claims.text: Vanhoozer’s model offers orthodox answers to hiddenness and neglect that vindicate and support further use of the authorial analogy.
claims.quote: ultimately Vanhoozer’s particular model can provide unique and orthodox answers to these problems which not only exculpate the analogy but commends its further use in theology and philosophy of religion.

claims.text: Moser’s epistemic response to evil worsens rather than resolves the problem.
claims.quote: I will argue that, far from helping the situation, this approach exacerbates it and is therefore strongly undesirable.

claims.text: God’s omnipotence should be replaced by a more coherent, evidence-based conception of perfect power.
claims.quote: Thus, it is desirable and, in the absence of better options, epistemically obligatory that omnipotence be modified and replaced with a version of God’s perfect power that is more coherent and evidence-based, and is also in line with a significant strand within the Bible.

claims.text: Holmes misunderstands Jüngel’s trinitarian account and nearly collapses his doctrine of the Trinity.
claims.quote: Holmes's critique fails to grasp the trinitarian nuance of Jüngel's position and, in doing so, Holmes actually comes perilously close to collapsing Jüngel's entire doctrine of the Trinity.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is theologically salutary when understood as the Father-Son distance bridged by eternal self-interpretation.
claims.quote: Accordingly, divine hiddenness is a salutary theological category if it is understood as the distance between the Father and the Son bridged by God's eternal self-interpretation in terms commensurate with creation's possibilities.

claims.text: God does not remain hidden for the sake of any human goods that divine hiddenness might promote.
claims.quote: it rules out the idea that whatever human goods may be promoted by divine hiddenness are the goods for the sake of which God remains hidden.

claims.text: Several objections to the hiddenness argument are irrelevant and therefore fail to address it.
claims.quote: I focus on objections sharing the defect – sometimes well-hidden – of irrelevance, using their shortcomings to highlight important features of the argument that are commonly overlooked.

claims.text: The hiddenness argument against God’s existence depends on unjustified assumptions about divine love and goodness.
claims.quote: The central argument of the book is that the hiddenness problem, construed as an argument against the existence of God, rests on unwarranted assumptions and expectations about God’s love and goodness.

claims.text: Why accept traditional positive accounts of God’s love rather than negative accounts suggested by hiddenness?
claims.quote: the book also raises the question of why we should accept traditional positive characterizations of God’s love (God as perfect heavenly parent, for example) rather than the negative ones suggested by the phenomena of divine hiddenness (God as absent or neglectful parent, for example).

claims.text: The problem of divine hiddenness differs from the problem of evil.
claims.quote: I think, however, that the problem of Divine hiddenness (whatever exactly it may be) is not the same problem as the problem of evil, for we can imagine a world in which the problem of divine hiddenness pretty clearly does not arise and in which the problem of evil is no less a problem than it is in the actual world.

claims.text: Kant’s central reply holds that knowledge of God would prevent viewing moral obedience as a genuine sacrifice of self-interest.
claims.quote: Kant's central claim is not that knowledge of God would preclude the possibility of transgression, but rather that it would preclude one's viewing adherence to the moral law as a genuine sacrifice of self-interest.

claims.text: Kantian insights about hiddenness ground a new theodicy worthy of serious attention.
claims.quote: I argue that, despite Kant's general skepticism about theodicy, his insights pertaining to hiddenness also provide the foundation for a new theodicy that merits serious attention.

claims.text: Maitzen claims that uneven theistic-belief distribution poses an atheological challenge unlikely to be overcome.
claims.quote: His claim is that an uneven distribution of theistic belief (and not just the mere existence of non-belief) provides an atheological challenge that cannot likely be overcome.

claims.text: A hidden premise makes Maitzen overlook a Molinist solution, softening the demographic data’s atheological import.
claims.quote: I argue that a hidden premise causes Maitzen to overlook a Molinist solution. The upshot is a softening of the atheological import of the demographic data.
