claims.text: Prabhupāda’s account resolves divine hiddenness by treating knowledge of God and divine attributes as an educational process of yoga.
claims.quote: Prabhupāda’s identifying Kṛṣṇa as the perfect teacher, particularly in his role as Arjuna’s teacher in the Bhagavad-Gītā , enables consideration of how the divine hiddenness issue is resolvable, particularly by framing awareness of God’s existence and understanding of divine attributes as an educational process encapsulated by the word “ yoga ”.

claims.text: Bhakti-yoga inverts divine hiddenness from a philosophical problem into a theological solution.
claims.quote: This approach further enables appreciation of the bhakti-yoga perspective—in its celebration of divine absence—as an inversion of divine hiddenness as a philosophical problem into a theological solution to the adept’s acute sense of divine absence, even while perceiving evidence of God’s existence at every turn.

claims.text: Hidden Mickey identifications and experiences of God’s presence and love are often ambiguous.
claims.quote: it is often ambiguous whether some constellation of shapes is a Hidden Mickey, and similarly, it is often ambiguous whether some experience is an experience of God's presence and love.

claims.text: Reflection on Hidden Mickeys can partially advance a solution to divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: This chapter shows that reflecting on Hidden Mickeys can take people at least part of the way to a solution to the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: God may be unable to make divine existence as apparent as Disney can make intentional agency apparent.
claims.quote: God simply cannot make his existence as apparent to people as the Disney corporation can make it apparent that it is run by agents acting intentionally.

claims.text: God the creator must be hidden from creatures in order to be God the creator.
claims.quote: Phenomenologically speaking, God the creator, in order to be God the creator, must be hidden to creatures.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is natural and need not impugn the moral status of God or humans.
claims.quote: Divine hiddenness is, therefore, natural and does not necessarily call into question the moral status of God or of humans.

claims.text: The absence of strong evidence for theism may itself strongly support atheism.
claims.quote: One might argue that the absence of strong evidence in support of theism is itself strong evidence in support of atheism.

claims.text: Pascalian resources can refute the divine-hiddenness argument and its strict evidentialist basis.
claims.quote: A Pascalian has adequate resources to refute this argument and the strict Evidentialism on which it is erected.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is distinct from the problem of evil and merits separate treatment.
claims.quote: divine hiddenness constitutes a distinct problem from that presented by the problem of evil and thus deserves individual treatment.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness makes a distinct contribution that merits its own treatment.
claims.quote: The chapter then motivates the idea that divine hiddenness makes a distinct contribution that merits its own treatment.

claims.text: The hiddenness problem may seriously challenge theism independently of conclusions about the problem of evil.
claims.quote: What we will find is that when certain knots threatening to hamper intellectual movement are unravelled, the hiddenness problem emerges as a contender in its own rightone that may generate serious difficulties for theism regardless of conclusions drawn concerning the force of the problem of evil.

claims.text: Nonresistant nonbelief strongly supports the proposition that God does not exist.
claims.quote: overlooked facts about the nature of love and about the connection between loving relationship with God and belief in God reveal that the existence in many times and places of a certain sort of nonbelief -I call it nonresistant nonbelief -counts strongly in favor of there being no God.

claims.text: Contemporary philosophy holds that divine hiddenness counts against God's existence.
claims.quote: In chapter 1, he contrasts the contemporary notion that "divine hiddenness counts against the existence of God" with earlier Hebrew and Christian traditions which integrate God's presence and hiddenness in such a way that "God's love and existence remain unchallenged" (5).

claims.text: A theory of divine attributes and love can portray hiddenness as a natural consequence of God's nature.
claims.quote: He explains that his "aim in this book" is to develop "a theory about the attributes of God, and particularly about the love of God, and the way in which it is manifested to humans, that makes room for divine hiddenness in its various forms as a natural outgrowth of who and what God is rather than of what God is doing to serve human needs and desires" (7).

claims.text: A hidden theistic world contains both theistic goods and the experience of atheistic goods.
claims.quote: This is because in a hidden theistic world all of the theistic goods obtain in addition to the experience of atheistic goods.

claims.text: Theistic goods can obtain in a world where God is hidden.
claims.quote: I complete this line of argument by showing that theistic goods do (or could) indeed obtain in a world where God hides.

claims.text: The correct axiological answer solves the problem of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: The correct answer to the axiological question turns out to be a solution to the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: God is hidden to creation because God is its creator.
claims.quote: As a basic phenomenological constraint, God is hidden to creation in virtue of being the creator.

claims.text: If God is the hidden creator, people are always implicitly related to God even when unaware of it.
claims.quote: Against the atheist who holds than an all-loving God would always want to be in a relation with us, the conclusion argues that if God is in fact the hidden creator, our ultimate source, he would be uniquely the sort of thing we were implicitly always in relation to even if we were unaware of it.

claims.text: A seeker's resistance can only be detected retrospectively through faith, making it theological rather than philosophical.
claims.quote: Against the theist who wants to explain divine hiddenness in terms of a moral defect of the one seeking, the conclusion argues that such resistance would only be detectable after the fact, in light of faith, and so would be an issue for theological, not philosophical explication.

claims.text: The Schellenberg problem attacks a straw conception of God rather than the God of traditional Christian theology.
claims.quote: This chapter argues that the Schellenberg problem is an attack on a straw deity.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s argument relies on theological claims rejected by traditional Christian theology and influential Christian theologians.
claims.quote: More specifically, it proposes that Schellenberg’s argument against the existence of God depends on certain theological claims that are not commitments of traditional Christian theology and that would, furthermore, be repudiated by many of the most important and influential theologians in the Christian tradition.

claims.text: The evidence for God is unexpectedly weak if a God with the Judeo-Christian character exists.
claims.quote: It has long seemed to me that however strong our evidence that God exists is, it is not what I would have expected it to be—and, more specifically, it is not as strong as I would have expected given the existence of a God with the character that the Judeo-Christian tradition affirms.

claims.text: The overall evidence concerning God is mixed, even if it ultimately favors God’s existence.
claims.quote: However we evaluate the total package, the evidence is mixed. Even for those who take the overall evidence to favor God, as I do, there is ample room for wonder that we find ourselves in this type of evidential situation.

claims.text: Naturalism is the dominant hypothesis in the realistic average Bayesian scenario, despite theistic support from fine-tuning and consciousness.
claims.quote: The results indicate that while Theism receives significant support from fine-tuning and consciousness, the cumulative weight of existential and logical defeaters—specifically the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and modal collapse—renders Naturalism the dominant hypothesis with a probability exceeding 89% in the realistic average scenario.

claims.text: If two prominent views about evil and divine hiddenness are accepted, theism entails pointless atheism.
claims.quote: Furthermore, not only is theism compatible with pointless atheism, it entails pointless atheism.

claims.text: Objections to divine hiddenness often claim that every instance of non-resistant atheism is needed for a greater good.
claims.quote: This is significant because many objections to the argument from divine hiddenness have tried to show that all instances of non-resistant atheism are required for a greater good.

claims.text: Given theism, non-resistant atheism need not serve a purpose and should be expected sometimes to be pointless.
claims.quote: But if I’m right, given theism, there need not be a point to non-resistant atheism. Indeed, we should expect there to be pointless atheism.

claims.text: Evidential arguments about God depend on whether evidence is more likely given theism than given its denial.
claims.quote: The central issue for any evidential argument for or against God is whether the evidence is more likely on theism or the denial of theism.

claims.text: Using non-tendentious descriptions of hiddenness evidence permits more progress than tendentious descriptions.
claims.quote: Although there is some precedence for describing the evidence in a way that is tendentious, this chapter argues that reliance on non-tendentious statements of the evidence allows for more progress.

claims.text: Assessing hiddenness requires comparing its likelihood under both God’s existence and God’s nonexistence.
claims.quote: The second moving part depends on judgments concerning how likely the hiddenness evidence is given God exists and how likely the evidence is given God does not exist. Current discussion tends to leave out this last piece, which is crucial to assessing the evidential impact.

claims.text: God can be understood as hidden in laws of nature, history, and human relationships.
claims.quote: According to my proposal God can be understood as hidden in three ways: in the laws of nature, in history, and in relationships with humans.

claims.text: Seeking the threefold Hidden God is a promising route toward deeper Trinitarian renewal of the analytic tradition.
claims.quote: The search for “threefold hidden God” seems to be more appropriate for our times and seems to be a promising proposal for an even deeper Trinitarian renewal of the analytic tradition.

claims.text: The Church’s liturgy is a way of knowing God and bears on the Problem of Divine Hiddenness.
claims.quote: I argue that the liturgy of the Church is a way we know God and is relevant to the Problem of Divine Hiddenness.

claims.text: In evidential hiddenness arguments, theodicies most often contribute through credence realignment.
claims.quote: The chapter considers various options for ways one’s evidential situation can unfold when a theodicy is introduced and suggest that, most often, the contribution a theodicy makes is via realignment.

claims.text: Realignment adjusts credences to better reflect evidential probabilities.
claims.quote: Realignment involves adjusting our credences to better reflect the evidential probabilities.

claims.text: Theodicies contribute less straightforwardly to evidential arguments than they historically did to deductive arguments.
claims.quote: the contribution is not as straightforward as that which theodicies have historically made in response to deductive arguments.

claims.text: Divine transcendence should have a more central role in theorizing about divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: This chapter argues that the attribute of divine transcendence ought to figure more centrally in our theorizing about divine hiddenness.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness means that God can seem distant, absent, or nonexistent even if God exists.
claims.quote: The hiddenness of God is the fact that, even if God exists, sometimes God seems distant, absent, or even nonexistent.

claims.text: The hiddenness problem concerns doubt about God’s existence rather than only God’s intentional activity in particular situations.
claims.quote: The hiddenness problem leaves us doubting the very existence of God, not just whether some situation in the world is the result of God's intentional activity.

claims.text: Hidden Mickeys do not fully solve the problem of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: Hidden Mickeys, therefore, don't take us all the way to a solution to the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: Marsh’s Molinist explanation does not undermine the conclusion that theistic explanations of theistic-belief demographics are implausible and less plausible than naturalistic explanations.
claims.quote: For several reasons, Marsh's inventive Molinist explanation of the lopsided worldwide distribution of theistic believers does not threaten the conclusion I argued for originally: theistic explanations of that distribution are implausible on even their own terms and in any case less plausible than naturalistic ones.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness must be reframed through trauma theory and the secular age’s sociocultural conditions.
claims.quote: This article argues that the contemporary existential and intellectual problem of divine hiddenness ( Deus absconditus ) must be reframed through the intersecting lenses of trauma theory and the sociocultural conditions of a secular age.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness can be understood as kenotic solidarity requiring an ethical, narrative, and communal response.
claims.quote: This model reconceives divine hiddenness not primarily as an epistemological puzzle or a mystical ascent, but as a potential mode of kenotic solidarity – a divine participation in godforsakenness that calls for an ethical, narrative, and communal theological response.

claims.text: Theological possibility should be regrounded in responsibility to traumatized others and humble openness to silence.
claims.quote: This approach seeks to reground theological possibility in a responsibility to the traumatised other and in a humble, reflective practice that holds open the space of silence without premature resolution.

claims.text: Dumsday’s three replies become more formidable when synthesized around a Christian mystical conception of God.
claims.quote: These three responses, while each insufficient on their own, become a far more formidable reply to the problem of hiddenness when combined and synthesized around a more mystic conception of God imported from the Christian mystic tradition.

claims.text: God remains hidden to preserve nonbelievers’ well-being and reveals himself only to morally virtuous, diligent seekers.
claims.quote: I argue that the great mystery that we call God remains hidden in order to preserve the well-being of nonbelievers, and that He does indeed reveal Himself, but only to those who cultivate the requisite level of moral virtue and seek Him diligently.

claims.text: The spiritual turn in epistemology occurs when doing good includes and shapes the search for truth.
claims.quote: The author first argues that the spiritual turn in epistemology occurs when the act of doing good includes and shapes the search for truth.

claims.text: Schellenberg's argument requires reasonable nonbelief to exist in order to succeed.
claims.quote: I present Schellenberg's argument and argue that the kind of reasonable nonbelief Schellenberg needs for his argument to succeed is unlikely to exist.

claims.text: The empirical improbability of reasonable nonbelief makes the conclusions of Schellenberg's argument empirically improbable.
claims.quote: Since Schellenberg's argument is an inductive-style version of the problem of evil, the empirical improbability of the premise Ichallenge renders the conclusions derived fron1 it empirically improbable as well.

claims.text: An accommodationist strategy can defuse objections by accommodating reasons for divine withdrawal within the hiddenness argument's divine-human relationship framework.
claims.quote: This strategy involves showing that the dominant concern of reasons for divine withdrawal can be met or accommodated within the framework of divine–human relationship envisaged by the hiddenness argument.

claims.text: Critical discussion has strengthened rather than defeated the hiddenness argument.
claims.quote: I conclude that critical discussion leaves the argument very much alive and kicking, and indeed strengthened as it moves into its second decade of life.

claims.text: The overlap challenge holds that divine hiddenness adds no evidence against God beyond the existing problem of evil.
claims.quote: Instead, it asserts that the highlighted issue surrounding non-belief is merely one of the alleged evils or imperfections in the world, and thus, the argument, whether sound or not, fails to offer evidence against God beyond what is already addressed by the existing problem of evil.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is not merely a disguised problem of evil, but constructing a sufficiently independent hiddenness argument remains difficult.
claims.quote: The general lesson is that, while the divine hiddenness problem should not be regarded as merely a problem of evil in disguise, it remains difficult to formulate a hiddenness argument that is sufficiently independent of the problem of evil.

claims.text: Evidence of divine reality should be purposively available to humans, only in ways suitable to divine self-revelatory purposes.
claims.quote: The central thesis is that we should expect evidence of divine reality to be purposively available to humans, that is, available only in a manner suitable to divine purposes in self-revelation.

claims.text: This account reorients religious epistemology around the character and purposes of an authoritative, perfectly loving God.
claims.quote: The result is a much-needed reorienting of religious epistemology to accommodate the character and purposes of an authoritative, perfectly loving God.

claims.text: A perfectly loving God would ensure that everyone wanting a personal relationship with God could have one.
claims.quote: For, if there is such a God, it seems as though he would make sure that everyone who wanted that relationship would be in a position to have it.

claims.text: Belief in God's existence appears necessary for a personal relationship with God, so clear evidence should be available to all.
claims.quote: However, one thing which seems required for a personal relationship with God is that the individual in question believe that God exists in the first place. So it is natural to expect God to make evidence of his existence sufficiently clear to all.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness positively supports nonbelief in the traditional theistic God.
claims.quote: This divine hiddenness therefore seems to give positive support for nonbelief in the God of traditional theism.

claims.text: An infinite regress of existentially dependent realities does not adequately account for existence.
claims.quote: It argues that an infinite regress of existentially dependent realities does not adequately account for existence

claims.text: A necessary ground of being is a more coherent explanatory terminus than a brute contingent universe.
claims.quote: a necessary ground of being offers a more coherent explanatory terminus than a brute contingent universe.

claims.text: A Jewish approach to divine love holds that God seeks meaningful relationships with communities as well as individuals.
claims.quote: A Jewish approach to divine love includes the thought that God desires meaningful relationship not only with individual persons, but also with communities of persons.

claims.text: An individual's nonbelief may result from culpability of their larger community rather than an individual failing.
claims.quote: In combination with John Schellenberg’s account of divine love, the admission of God’s desire for such relationships makes possible that a person may fail to believe that God exists not because of any individual failing, but because the individual is a member of a larger community that itself is culpable.

claims.text: Owen’s Spirit Christology is deficient in several important respects.
claims.quote: Although there is much to commend in Owen’s approach, it is deficient in several important respects.

claims.text: An Owenite pneumatologically sensitive Christology succeeds where Owen’s account is wanting.
claims.quote: This succeeds in precisely the areas where Owen’s account is wanting.

claims.text: An infinite regress of existentially dependent realities does not adequately account for existence.
claims.quote: It argues that an infinite regress of existentially dependent realities does not adequately account for existence

claims.text: A necessary ground of being is a more coherent explanatory terminus than a brute contingent universe.
claims.quote: a necessary ground of being offers a more coherent explanatory terminus than a brute contingent universe.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness challenges belief in God by rendering the supposition that God exists absurd.
claims.quote: This latter problem starts from the supposition that God exists-after all, God is hidden only if God existsand then reduces that supposition to absurdity by pointing out that if God exists, then the following mutually inconsistent claims are true:

claims.text: God has remained hidden from many people.
claims.quote: P1. God has allowed himself to remain hidden from many people.

claims.text: Openness to relationship with God is compatible with initial divine concealment.
claims.quote: First, it shows how Schellenberg’s understanding of openness is deficient by arguing that openness to relationship is consistent with initial concealment.

claims.text: Other persons can make a relationship between God and a nonbeliever more likely.
claims.quote: Then, the paper develops the dianthropic strategy, which focuses on the role of other persons in making a relationship between God and the nonbeliever more likely.

claims.text: If a perfectly loving God exists, there is no non-resistant nonbelief.
claims.quote: J.L. Schellenberg’s Argument from Divine Hiddenness maintains that if a perfectly loving God exists, then there is no non-resistant non-belief.

claims.text: The existence of non-resistant nonbelief entails that no perfectly loving God exists.
claims.quote: Given that such nonbelief exists, however, it follows that there is no perfectly loving God.

claims.text: The required revisions to hiddenness arguments leave them substantially less forceful.
claims.quote: Finally, we turn to possible variants of Schellenberg’s case, and argue that the modifications necessary to accommodate our criticismas leave those variants with much less of a sting than originally suggested by his provocative formulation.

claims.text: Religious pluralism requires a theological response.
claims.quote: The fact of religious pluralism demands a theological response.

claims.text: Recent pluralism models inadequately address sin and divine hiddenness and cannot coherently relate dialogue to proclamation.
claims.quote: However, they inadequately address the categories of sin and divine hiddenness, while struggling to articulate a coherent relationship between dialogue and proclamation.

claims.text: Classic Lutheran resources can engage religious pluralism while balancing dialogue and gospel proclamation.
claims.quote: The classic Lutheran tradition offers three fruitful resources (the gospel as promise, the law/gospel distinction, and the hiddenness of God) for engaging religious pluralism and balancing interreligious dialogue and gospel proclamation.

claims.text: A correct understanding of divine transcendence avoids both extremes of the transcendence continuum.
claims.quote: this chapter makes a case for avoiding both poles, thus locating the correct understanding of transcendence somewhere in between.

claims.text: The consequences of a theologically adequate divine transcendence undermine the hiddenness argument against God’s existence.
claims.quote: the chapter aims to identify several consequences of a theologically adequate understanding of divine transcendence, followed by an explanation of how these consequences undercut the argument from divine hiddenness against the existence of God.

claims.text: Textual variants in New Testament manuscripts pose a problem for religious belief.
claims.quote: I argue that textual variants pose a problem for religious belief.

claims.text: Numerous, sometimes ideologically motivated New Testament textual variants should reduce confidence in the Bible as an information source.
claims.quote: Specifically, the existence of hundreds of thousands of textual variants in the New Testament's manuscript tradition, many of them large and ideologically motivated, should reduce a believer's confidence in the Bible as a source of information.

claims.text: The textual-variants problem is epistemic rather than a direct entailment that a religious claim is false.
claims.quote: This problem is different from the problems of evil and divine hiddenness because, whereas those problems entail the falsity of a religious claim, such as theism, this problem poses an epistemic challenge instead.

claims.text: The Cosmic Conflict Theodicy, together with several other theodicies and arguments, can address the problem of horrendous evil.
claims.quote: The author defends the Cosmic Conflict Theodicy against philosophical and theological objections, and uses it together with the Connection Building Theodicy, Adamic Fall Theodicy, arguments for divine hiddenness, and Afterlife Theodicy to address the vexing problem of horrendous evil.

claims.text: A purely secular explanation of religious beliefs across human cultures is vastly superior to religious explanations.
claims.quote: Finally, it is argued that a purely secular explanation of all religious beliefs in human cultures is vastly superior to religious accounts.

claims.text: Jewish theodicies developed for historical catastrophes are equally suited to address mass extinctions in natural history.
claims.quote: One significant reason for the disparity is that the theodicies created by Jews to contend with the catastrophes which punctuated Jewish history are equally suited to address the massive extinctions which characterize natural history.

claims.text: God's silence amid profound suffering can produce despair that undermines agency directed toward a person's good.
claims.quote: The silence of God either by itself or in circumstances of profound suffering can induce hopelessness and despair, eroding a person’s ability to act in ways conducive to her own good.

claims.text: Standard responses to divine hiddenness may fail to address existential crises caused by God's silence.
claims.quote: And the standard responses to the problem of divine hiddenness may not address the existential crises occasioned by God’s silence.

claims.text: Jüngel holds that describing divine action as God's right and left hands can replace Luther's Deus absconditus and avoid a terrible hidden God.
claims.quote: Jünegel believes that it is possible to replace Luther's idea of Deus absconditus with a description of divine action as the action of the "right" and "left" hands, which will allow avoiding the presence of the "terrible" Deus absconditus in theology.

claims.text: Jüngel's account of divine hiddenness is less tragic than Luther's because it eliminates divine temptation.
claims.quote: Compared with Luther, Jünegel's idea of the hiddenness of God should be assessed as less tragic, it eliminates the possibility of divine temptation, which for Luther was one of the important moments of God's attitude to sinful man.

claims.text: Barth's theology of revelation both affirms a form of divine hiddenness and denies the Deus absconditus.
claims.quote: As I shall argue, Barth’s complex theology of revelation exhibits a tension, both affirming a certain notion of God’s “hiddenness” and denying the Deus absconditus.

claims.text: Many accounts of Ecclesiastes's God-talk exaggerate its hiddenness and overlook Qohelet's wider theological perspective.
claims.quote: I will argue that many descriptions of the God-talk of Ecclesiastes are exaggerated and insensitive to Qohelet’s larger theological perspective.

claims.text: The Exemplarist Theodicy resolves Schellenberg’s objection by distinguishing goods of primary hiddenness from goods achievable within belief.
claims.quote: Beginning with J.L. Schellenberg&s;s argument from non-resistant non-belief, which contends that a perfectly loving God would ensure no one capable of relationship with him would fail to believe, the chapter shows how the Exemplarist Theodicy resolves this challenge by articulating a richer conception of divine love and demonstrating that the goods achievable under primary hiddenness differ in kind from those achievable within belief, blocking Schellenberg&s;s objection that any good associated with hiddenness could be achieved through relationship-compatible means.

claims.text: The current distribution of belief is justified because it optimally enables exemplar formation, which overrides God’s desire for universal belief.
claims.quote: Next, it examines Theodore Drange&s;s argument focusing on the non-belief in the gospel message, demonstrating how the Exemplarist Theodicy explains why the current distribution of belief creates optimal conditions for exemplar formation by identifying exemplar transformation as the specific divine desire that overrides God&s;s desire for universal belief, directly meeting Drange&s;s challenge to opponents and demonstrating consistency with the biblical evidence he cites.

claims.text: Geographic clustering of belief enables distinctive exemplar types across cultures and is predicted more specifically by exemplarism than naturalism.
claims.quote: Next, it examines Stephen Maitzen&s;s formulation centred on the geographic distribution of belief, showing how this distribution enables distinctive exemplar types to develop across different cultural contexts, with the exemplarist framework predicting the geographic clustering with greater specificity than naturalism&s;s explanatorily shallow account of cultural transmission.

claims.text: Theism may be incoherent because omnipotence and omniscience make no sense.
claims.quote: The first couple of arguments attack the coherence of theism with the suggestion that omnipotence and omniscience make no sense.

claims.text: The problem of evil challenges how an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good being could permit extensive pain and suffering.
claims.quote: The chapter then explores the problem of evil and the argument from divine hiddenness which raise the following two questions: how could an all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good being allow for the proliferation of pain and suffering; and why doesn’t God make it easier for us to believe in Him?

claims.text: Religion is accused of obstructing scientific advancement.
claims.quote: The chapter closes with a discussion of the accusation that religion is an obstacle to the advance of science.

claims.text: Any solution to experiential or intellectual divine hiddenness requires an account of personal knowledge of God.
claims.quote: Despite differences, a solution to either would require some account of how God is personally known.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness should be reformulated Christologically because Christianity holds that God is known in Jesus Christ.
claims.quote: Yet for the Christian tradition, God is known in the man Jesus Christ. I suggest, then, a Christological reformulation of the hiddenness argument.

claims.text: Knowing Christ in the church offers a response to the problems of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: With special attention to the ecclesiology of Gregory of Nyssa, I offer an account of knowing Christ in the church. I then explore this as a response to the problems of divine hiddenness, and anticipate a considerable objection to my response.

claims.text: Jordan’s case against equal maximal divine love consists of two conceptually distinct arguments.
claims.quote: In this paper I argue that Jordan's case can be better understood as two conceptually distinct arguments, only one of which depends on his proffered principles of perfect being theology.

claims.text: Both of Jordan’s arguments against the thesis that perfect divine love is maximally extended and equally intense are unsuccessful.
claims.quote: I then critically evaluate each of these arguments, arguing that both are unsuccessful.

claims.text: The thesis that divine perfection requires maximally extended, equally intense love is central to contemporary arguments from evil and divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: Jordan notes that this thesis is widely accepted by theistic and nontheistic philosophers, and that it plays a prominent role in contemporary presentations of the evidential argument from evil and the argument from divine hiddenness.

claims.text: Given divine hiddenness, depictions of God are literary constructs whose reification troubles religious people.
claims.quote: Given divine hiddenness, every depiction of God is a literary construct, and when reified, becomes a source of consternation to religious people.

claims.text: Spiritual allegiance does not depend on external circumstances because true devotion serves God without expectation of reward or punishment.
claims.quote: Spiritual allegiance does not depend on external circumstances, for a truly devout person will serve God without thought of reward and punishment.

claims.text: God owes humanity nothing because the creator has already granted life, humankind’s highest gift.
claims.quote: Reflecting on the book of Job, Saadia Gaon grounds all worship in nature itself, noting that the creator has already bestowed life, the highest gift, on humankind and therefore owes us nothing.

claims.text: Experiences of God’s presence are much more widely available than divine-hiddenness literature typically acknowledges.
claims.quote: This chapter, together with Chapter 6, presents a theory about encounters with God according to which experience of God’s presence is much more widely available than is typically credited in the literature on divine hiddenness.

claims.text: The proposed account of divine encounters is the most plausible explanation of how material creatures might experience divine presence.
claims.quote: The chapter concludes with some reasons for thinking that the view of divine encounters sketched here is the most plausible account of how creatures like us might experience divine presence in a material world.

claims.text: Contemporary epistemology of religion assumes an overly individualistic account of knowledge and justification.
claims.quote: More generally, the chapter argues, contemporary epistemology of religion assumes an overly individualistic account of knowledge and justification, including reductionist accounts of testimonial knowledge and evidence.

claims.text: A social religious epistemology can enrich and expand the field by adopting advances in testimony and social epistemology.
claims.quote: By adopting recent advances in the epistemology of testimony and in social epistemology more generally, a social religious epistemology promises to enrich and expand the field.

claims.text: Skeptical theists claim humans are cognitively ill-equipped to know God's reasons for permitting suffering or hiding from us.
claims.quote: One of the most influential and frequently addressed responses to the evidential argument from Evil and divine hiddenness is advocated by so called skeptical theists, who claim that we are cognitively ill-equipped to know Gods reasons for permitting suffering or for hiding from us.

claims.text: Skeptical theism is alleged to entail skepticism about moral decision-making and most or all theistic beliefs.
claims.quote: In this article I evaluate Skeptical theism with regard to two common arguments, namely the argument that Skeptical theism entails skepticism concerning our moral decision making and that it entails skepticism concerning most if not all theistic beliefs.

claims.text: Skeptical theism faces no serious trouble from these two skeptical implications.
claims.quote: It is concluded that Skeptical theism isn’t in any serious trouble with regard to these arguments.

claims.text: Evidence for God is morally and existentially challenging because humans willingly become evidence by receiving and reflecting God's moral character.
claims.quote: Rather, it is morally and existentially challenging to humans, as they themselves responsively and willingly become evidence of God's reality in receiving and reflecting God's moral character for others.

claims.text: Personifying evidence of God requires evidence to be personified in an intentional agent and inherent evidence of an intentional agent.
claims.quote: Moser calls this 'personifying evidence of God,' because it requires the evidence to be personified in an intentional agent - such as a human - and thereby to be inherent evidence of an intentional agent.

claims.text: Natural nonbelief parallels and corroborates well-known worries about natural evil.
claims.quote: Problem one introduces something I call natural nonbelief, which is significant because it parallels and corroborates well-known worries about natural evil.

claims.text: The two problems support naturalism over theism and intensify the problem of divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: Problems one and two, especially when combined, support naturalism over theism, intensify the problem of divine hiddenness, challenge Alvin Plantinga's views about the naturalness of theism, and advance the discussion about whether the conflict between science and religion is genuine or superficial.

claims.text: Abū al-Barakāt's formulation anticipates atheistic challenges from the evidential argument from evil and divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: I argue that Abū al-Barakāt’s formulation, distinct from customary articulations of the problem in his intellectual milieu, anticipates atheistic challenges posed by the evidential argument and divine hiddenness.

claims.text: Complementary responses can be developed through taqlīd and divine Decree and Predestination.
claims.quote: Finally, I propose that potential complementary responses to these challenges can be developed by analyzing (1) Abū al-Barakāt’s conception of taqlīd (conformism) in light of Alvin Plantinga’s concept of the basicality of belief, and (2) his use of the Islamic doctrine of al-Qaḍāʾ wa al-Qadar (divine Decree and Predestination), which allows for a skeptical response.

claims.text: Schellenberg argues that a perfectly loving God would not create inculpable nonbelief by hiding from willing seekers.
claims.quote: He maintains that a perfectly loving God, if he exists, would not create “inculpable nonbelief” by hiding his existence and love from seekers who are willing to believe if they are offered sufficient evidence.

claims.text: Schellenberg concludes that a perfectly loving God does not exist because such seekers still exist.
claims.quote: Schellenberg concludes that there still exist such seekers and thus a perfectly loving God does not exist.

claims.text: Schellenberg's analogy argument is unreasonable because it ignores the infinite disanalogy between a human mother and God.
claims.quote: It is my thesis that this transfer is not reasonable because it does not do justice to the infinite disanalogy between a human mother and God.

claims.text: Religious Zionists in Palestine offered multiple, sometimes contradictory theological explanations for the Holocaust.
claims.quote: This article identifies a number of their prevailing, often coexisting, and sometimes contradictory theological explanations for the Holocaust: punishment for sins (such as assimilation, lack of a homeland, or reduced childbirth), common early in the war; the “birth pangs of the messianic age,” which gained credence as the war continued; and “divine hiddenness,” a notion that emerged late in the war.

claims.text: Repentance was believed capable of hastening redemption and ending persecution.
claims.quote: These ideas also found expression in the belief that repentance had the ability to hasten redemption and to bring persecution to an end.

claims.text: Religious Zionists in Palestine advanced several coexisting and sometimes contradictory theological explanations for the Holocaust.
claims.quote: This article identifies a number of their prevailing, often coexisting, and sometimes contradictory theological explanations for the Holocaust: punishment for sins (such as assimilation, lack of a homeland, or reduced childbirth), common early in the war; the “birth pangs of the messianic age,” which gained credence as the war continued; and “divine hiddenness,” a notion that emerged late in the war.

claims.text: Repentance was believed capable of hastening redemption and ending persecution.
claims.quote: These ideas also found expression in the belief that repentance had the ability to hasten redemption and to bring persecution to an end.

claims.text: Cognitive-science explanations of religious belief are less supportive of atheism than some proponents claim.
claims.quote: The chapter argues that the purported explanations of religious belief found in this literature are not nearly as atheist-friendly as some practitioners suggest.

claims.text: The Holistic Evaluation Framework offers a novel method for assessing the moral and theoretical merits of theodicies.
claims.quote: Theodicies on Trial presents and defends the Holistic Evaluation Framework, a novel way to assess the moral and theoretical merits of theodicies.

claims.text: Assessing theodicies should attend to the social and psychological effects of explanations for suffering.
claims.quote: It provides one of the most thorough interdisciplinary assessment of these topics in the literature, while focusing attention on the social and psychological impacts of explanations for why suffering exists.

claims.text: Schellenberg argues that God's existence is incompatible with the existence of nonresistant non-believers.
claims.quote: God’s existence entails that there would never be any nonresistant non-believers; however, there are some non-resistant non-believers; therefore, God does not exist.

claims.text: Molinism undermines the claim that God would necessarily prevent all nonresistant non-belief.
claims.quote: Finally, we argue that Molinism undercuts the view that God would necessarily ensure there will never be any nonresistant non-believers.

claims.text: Interpersonal knowledge can illuminate religious epistemology, including divine hiddenness, divine love, liturgy, and epistemic injustice.
claims.quote: Section 3 examines how interpersonal knowledge may figure in liturgical practice, in diffusing the problem of divine hiddenness, and in motivating a novel understanding of divine love. Finally, section 4 explores the possibility of epistemic injustice arising from dismissal or neglect of our religious testimony to one another, or of divine testimony to humanity, focusing specifically on the import of interpersonal knowledge.

claims.text: Mystical theology is central to Gregory of Tatev's thought and spiritual practice despite his strongly logical and analytical theology.
claims.quote: However, it can be shown that mystical theology is at the heart of his thinking and his own spiritual practice.

claims.text: For Gregory, divine hiddenness and incomprehensibility ground the epistemology and hermeneutics of cataphatic theology.
claims.quote: This paper shows that the divine hiddenness and incomprehensibility shape Gregory’s cataphatic theology in that they underlie its epistemology and hermeneutics.

claims.text: God's ultimate ineffability makes unknowing the highest form of knowing God.
claims.quote: Both are developed from the spiritual experience that God is ultimately ineffable and that ‘unknowing’ is the highest form of knowing him.

claims.text: Religious trauma can profoundly impair a person's relationship with God and spiritual practice.
claims.quote: When religion is the site of abuse and trauma, it can deeply impact a person's ability to relate to God and engage in spiritual practice.

claims.text: Survivors' insights may help religious communities prevent abuse by addressing failures of knowledge.
claims.quote: Section 3 explores the social epistemology of religious trauma, focusing on how failures of knowledge create space for religious abuse and the insights of survivors may help communities guard against it.

claims.text: The current divine-hiddenness argument has the structure of the logical problem of evil, which philosophers regard as dead.
claims.quote: This chapter argues that the current framing of the argument from divine hiddenness bears the same structure as an argument from evil which philosophers have deemed ‘dead’—namely, the so-called logical problem of evil.

claims.text: Some attempts to convert a deductive argument into an evidential argument make it invalid.
claims.quote: Some strategies for turning a deductive argument into an evidential argument result in the argument becoming invalid.

claims.text: Bayesian methods are the best tools for this type of probabilistic reasoning.
claims.quote: The chapter suggests the best tools for undertaking this type of reasoning are Bayesian.

claims.text: Al-Ghazali argues that religious belief can properly rest on neither theology, esotericism, nor philosophy.
claims.quote: Third, the chapter considers al-Ghazali’s arguments that religious belief can properly rest on neither theology, esotericism, nor philosophy.

claims.text: Arguments from divine hiddenness typically rely on robust but relatively undefended empirical commitments about the distribution of belief in God.
claims.quote: These arguments and responses to them typically rely on robust but relatively undefended empirical commitments as to the distribution of belief in God.

claims.text: The distribution of belief in God is messier and more philosophically interesting than currently appreciated.
claims.quote: This article synthesizes results from psychology, anthropology, and the cognitive science of religion to show that the distribution of belief in God is much more messy and much more philosophically interesting than is currently appreciated.

claims.text: Trozzo argues for an intra-historical and intra-worldly account of divine possibility oriented around a contemporary theology of the cross.
claims.quote: Trozzo argues for an intra-historical and intra-worldly account of divine possibility oriented around a contemporary theology of the cross marked by reclamation of the biblical and mystical practice of silence as the space that creates hope.

claims.text: The project seeks to overcome a tendency toward extrinsic notions of divine glory and transformation.
claims.quote: Seeking to overcome a tendency toward extrinsic notions of divine glory and transformation, the author explores Luther’s early construction of the theology of the cross and divine hiddenness in concert with the work of the Lutheran mystical tradition and modern Lutheran theology.

claims.text: God might be justified in allowing fundamentally natural-appearing universes to exist if God can make many distinct universes.
claims.quote: If God is capable of making a vast number of distinct universes, then God might be justified in allowing universes to exist that are fundamentally natural in how they can appear to a great many sentient beings in those universes.

claims.text: The moral principle prohibiting ambiguous universes implies either that God's existence cannot be known or that sentient life must be prevented by ethical means.
claims.quote: Adopting such a principle implies that one must either contradictorily assert that we cannot know God's existence, or that we have a moral obligation to prevent the continuation of sentient life in this universe by any ethical means available.

claims.text: God's presence and certain kinds of divine communication are experientially available much more widely than divine-hiddenness literature typically credits.
claims.quote: God’s presence, as well as certain kinds of divine communication are, and always have been, experientially available to a much greater degree than is typically credited in the literature on divine hiddenness.

claims.text: The wide availability of experiences of God undermines reasons for treating negative analogies of divine love as more apt than traditional positive analogies.
claims.quote: Insofar as it implies that experiences of God’s presence and of communication from God are widely available, it undermines the reasons we might have for thinking that certain negatively valenced analogies—God as distant or neglectful lover, for example—are more apt than traditional positive analogies for characterizing divine love.

claims.text: Intellectualism is inadequate for determining whether God exists.
claims.quote: The article argues against intellectualism, and offers a better alternative involving a kind of volitional evidentialism.

claims.text: If God seeks divine-human reconciliation, evidence for God should be redemptive.
claims.quote: If God is redemptive in virtue of seeking divine -human reconciliation, we should expect the evidence for God to be likewise redemptive.

claims.text: Evidence for God depends on a person's volitional stance toward its source.
claims.quote: Accordingly, the available evidence for God would be volitionally sensitive in that one’s coming to possess it would depend on one’s volitional stance toward its source.

claims.text: The atheistic hiddenness argument depends on a consciousness constraint for divine-human love.
claims.quote: The success of the atheistic hiddenness argument depends on the “consciousness constraint” it imposes on the divine-human loving relationship: namely, that this relationship requires human conscious awareness of being in the relationship with God.

claims.text: A physical relationship with God can exist without conscious awareness of it.
claims.quote: I challenge the truth of this proposition by introducing the concept of a physical relationship with God that is not subject to this constraint.

claims.text: A perfectly loving God would prefer physical relationships because they protect freedom and include people with varying cognitive capacities.
claims.quote: I argue, first, that a physical relationship with God is metaphysically possible; second, that its plausibility is supported by natural theology; and third, that a perfectly loving God would prefer physical relationships with human beings over consciousness-constrained relationships, because a perfectly loving God would prefer to preserve the integrity of human freedom of participation and allow inclusion of all people regardless of their natural cognitive capabilities.

claims.text: Divine absence can be a generative theological space rather than a failure of faith.
claims.quote: Through close examination of selected prooftexts, this study illuminates how the experience of divine absence functions not merely as a failure of faith but as a generative theological space.

claims.text: Doubt is inherent to religious experience rather than opposed to it.
claims.quote: The analysis demonstrates how these scholarly perspectives contribute to a nuanced understanding of doubt as an inherent component of religious experience rather than its antithesis.

claims.text: The Stoics interpreted Heraclitus's fire doctrine as recurring cosmic conflagration.
claims.quote: The ancient Stoics took Heraclitus’ account of fire to mean that the world constantly underwent cycles of conflagration.

claims.text: Most people fail to recognize the hidden rational order because they hold private conceptions of things.
claims.quote: Just as the meaning of Heraclitus’ own words (logoi) this divine, hidden rational order is not obvious to most people, who believe in their own ‘private’ conceptions of things, without realizing that they exemplify the logos on a small scale and are part of the logos on the ‘macrocosmic’ scale.

claims.text: William Alston's externalist epistemic model is unsatisfactory.
claims.quote: I argue that one influential externalist model—that of William Alston—is unsatisfactory, and advance in its place an internalist, phenomenal conservative approach bolstered by considerations from responsibilist virtue epistemology.

claims.text: An internalist phenomenal conservative approach better accommodates contemplative experiences and supports Coakley's response to divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: I argue that such an approach can much more satisfactorily accommodate contemplative experiences than can that of Alston and thus can buttress Coakley’s response to the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: Exaltation views that kenotically define humility cannot justify divine concurrence with evil.
claims.quote: This article rejects exaltation views of humility which define humility kenotically, justify their arguments from a divine hiddenness perspective, and which conclude that divine concurrence with evil is justified as long as all humble believers eventually are exalted and blessed.

claims.text: Exaltation views misunderstand humility and exaltation even by their own Christian standards.
claims.quote: Rather, I will contend that exaltation views misunderstand the meaning of both ‘humility’ and ‘exaltation,’ even from their own Christian standpoint.

claims.text: An existential conception of humility redirects responses to atrocity from individual kenosis toward community.
claims.quote: I ultimately offer an alternate response to the problem of evil based on an existentially grounded conception of ‘humility’ (a recognition of our need for others), which provides for a transmuted turn away from individual kenotic acts and toward community to transform those who suffer from atrocities.

claims.text: The problem of divine hiddenness supports the divine presence model and exposes weaknesses in rival views.
claims.quote: The author argues that the problem of divine hiddenness is intertwined with the problem of hell, and reflection on the problem lends support to the divine presence model even as it reveals critical weaknesses in its competitors.

claims.text: The divine presence model rejects retribution as hell's purpose while preserving punishment as inflicted on the damned.
claims.quote: In closing, the author considers the way that the model rejects the claim that the purpose of hell is retribution, yet still manages to accommodate the traditional idea that the punishment of hell is inflicted upon the damned, rather than being a simple function of the choices of those who are finally lost.

claims.text: God's theophany in Job offers a tender response that takes Job's grievances seriously and begins repairing their relationship.
claims.quote: that the theophany at the end of the biblical book of Job presents God as providing a tender loving response to Job that takes his grievances seriously and puts him on a path toward a repaired relationship with God;

claims.text: God's authorization of lament and protest forms part of a broader biblical pattern in God's relationship with Israel.
claims.quote: that those very signs of God’s love for Job and concern for his grievances—in particular, God’s authorization of lament and protest—are part of a broader pattern in the biblical portrayal of God’s relationship with Israel;

claims.text: Biblical portrayals of God provide positive evidence that God generally cares about human grievances against God.
claims.quote: that the fact that God is portrayed in these ways constitutes a positive sign—available to anyone who has access to these portrayals—that God is generally concerned with human grievances against God.

claims.text: Genuine loving relationships can exist without conscious reciprocity from one party.
claims.quote: I show that genuine loving relationships can exist without conscious reciprocity from one party

claims.text: Classical Christian perfect love does not require conscious reciprocal God-creature relationship.
claims.quote: Ultimately, I demonstrate that a Christian account of perfect love in the tradition of classical theism does not necessitate the kind of conscious reciprocal relationship that Schellenberg, among others, demands from the God-creature relationship.

claims.text: Detachability resolves the disagreement between the two drafts across their three registers.
claims.quote: the third paper resolves all three by supplying a mechanism: detachability.

claims.text: If God exists, God may have reasons for acting that humans cannot know.
claims.quote: According to skeptical theism, if there were a God, it is likely that he would have reasons for acting that are beyond our ken

claims.text: Not seeing a good reason for X does not justify concluding that no good reason for X exists.
claims.quote: In particular, the fact that we don’t see a good reason for X does not justify the conclusion that there is no good reason for X.

claims.text: Skeptical theism undercuts most a posteriori arguments against God’s existence.
claims.quote: Thus, skeptical theism purports to undercut most a posteriori arguments against the existence of God.

claims.text: Belief in an all-powerful God leaves the problems of evil without adequate answers.
claims.quote: Keller argues that as long as God is believed to be all-powerful, there are no adequate answers to these problems

claims.text: Appealing to human ignorance does not adequately solve these problems.
claims.quote: nor is it enough for theists simply to claim that human ignorance makes these problems insoluble.

claims.text: Process theism provides a religiously adequate concept of God and an adequate solution to the problems of evil.
claims.quote: Keller instead defends the understanding of God and God's power found in process theism and shows how it makes possible an adequate solution to the problems of evil while providing a concept of God that is religiously adequate.

claims.text: Believers and non-believers should stop blaming one another on the basis of mere evidence.
claims.quote: both believers and non-believers should stop blaming each other based on mere evidence.

claims.text: Spiritual progress may be promoted by setting aside evidential primacy and committing to God and the good.
claims.quote: Ultimately, believers and non-believers alike might promote spiritual progress by setting aside the primacy of evidence and committing themselves to God and the good.

claims.text: Sterba's and Tooley's atheistic arguments from animal suffering are self-undermining.
claims.quote: This article examines the arguments of Sterba and Tooley and contends that both are self-undermining.

claims.text: Each argument includes premises that give reason to regard other premises in that argument as false.
claims.quote: Each of the arguments employs premises that provide reason for thinking that other premises found in their arguments are false.

claims.text: Penal substitution emerged from doctrines of extrinsic divine action and a discourse of punishment in Lutheran and Reformed theology.
claims.quote: Penal substitution emerged out of two streams in Lutheran and Reformed theology: doctrines of extrinsic divine action in forensic justification and predestination, and a discourse of punishment underlying the persecution of heretics and discipline of believers.

claims.text: The Puritans made believers interiorize Christ's substitutionary punishment through affective exercises of undergoing divine wrath.
claims.quote: Christ dies on the cross as a substitutionary punishment of divine wrath, but the Puritans also develop affective exercises of undergoing divine wrath for sin in the believer.

claims.text: Greater punishment of Christ for human sin led believers to take that punishment into their own interiority.
claims.quote: The more Christ is punished for human sin, the more believers take that punishment into their own interiority.

claims.text: A morally perfect God necessarily desires that all rational agents behave morally.
claims.quote: A morally perfect God necessarily desires that all rational agents behave morally.

claims.text: Blameless moral agents have lacked sufficient moral knowledge to behave morally.
claims.quote: However, there has been a wide range of moral agents who, without blame, have lacked the moral knowledge to behave morally.

claims.text: God does not exist.
claims.quote: Therefore, God does not exist.

claims.text: If belief in God is essential to ultimate human fulfillment, God would be expected to provide unambiguous evidence of his existence.
claims.quote: If, as most theists claim, belief in God is essential to ultimate human fulfillment, one would expect that God would provide us with unambiguous evidence for His existence.

claims.text: Unambiguous evidence for God's existence is not forthcoming.
claims.quote: However, such evidence is not forthcoming.

claims.text: It is unlikely that the theist's God exists.
claims.quote: Therefore, it is unlikely that the theist’s God exists.

claims.text: Reasons for accepting nonresistant nonbelief also support evidentially compelling religious experiences.
claims.quote: Yet some reasons for accepting nonresistant nonbelief are also reasons for accepting theistic-supporting and naturalism-falsifying evidentially compelling religious experiences (ECREs).

claims.text: The existence of evidentially compelling religious experiences contradicts the divine hiddenness argument's conclusion.
claims.quote: Yet the existence of ECREs contradicts the ADH’s conclusion.

claims.text: The argument from divine hiddenness is self-defeating.
claims.quote: So the ADH is self-defeating.

claims.text: Non-resistant non-belief is relatively common.
claims.quote: I take up the question of whether such non-belief is pervasive and argue that it is, in fact, relatively common.

claims.text: To be resistant in Schellenberg's sense, a non-believer must be acquisition-responsible for their non-belief in God.
claims.quote: I argue that, for a non-believer to count as resistant in Schellenberg’s sense, they must be acquisition-responsible for their non-belief in God.

claims.text: Many non-believers lack acquisition responsibility and thus qualify as non-resistant.
claims.quote: I further contend that many non-believers lack such responsibility and therefore qualify as non-resistant.

claims.text: Divine silence in Lamentations is a theological space for questioning, protest, and hope in God’s hidden presence.
claims.quote: It argues that the silence of God in the text is not mere absence but a theological space that invites existential questioning, protest, and ultimately, the hope of the hidden presence of God.

claims.text: Divine silence intensifies rather than suppresses the tension between trust and human questioning.
claims.quote: The analysis demonstrates that rather than silencing human lament, divine silence intensifies the tension between trust and human questioning.

claims.text: The premise that non-resistant non-belief exists is problematic because its purported instances are resistant or permissible to a loving God.
claims.quote: The putative categories of non-resistant non-belief are really instances of resistance, or non-resistant non-belief of the sort that is not incongruent with what a good and loving God would allow (or could prevent).

claims.text: Schellenberg’s critique of religious experience undermines the hiddenness argument’s assumption that God would provide conscious apprehension.
claims.quote: But if religious experience is as epistemically tenuous as he argues it is (as against the veridicality of religious experience) then God would not be interested in bequeathing it.

claims.text: Non-belief is either resistant or compatible with what a loving God would allow.
claims.quote: Non-belief is either resistant or non-resistant, but not of the sort incompatible with what a loving God would allow.

claims.text: A formal procedure can determine the probability that God would perform a specified action from moral knowledge and perfect-being theology.
claims.quote: This article sets out a formal procedure for determining the probability that God would do a specified action, using our moral knowledge and understanding God as a perfect being.

claims.text: The procedure offers an attractive alternative to skeptical theism for structuring natural theology and a-theology debates.
claims.quote: Then I show the usefulness of the procedure by describing how it can help structure discussions in natural theology and a-theology, and how it offers an attractive alternative to 'skeptical theism'.

claims.text: Process theism provides a more satisfactory response to suffering and wickedness than traditional Christian theism.
claims.quote: The chapter examines why process theists claim to have a more satisfactory response to the first problem of evil suffering and wickedness than do traditional Christian theists.

claims.text: Traditional theists hold that natural evils occur only with God’s permission, whereas process theists hold that God cannot stop them.
claims.quote: Traditional theists have to admit that natural disasters and other natural evils occur only with God&s;s permission, while process theists would insist that God cannot stop them.

claims.text: Theists should be more open to divine hiddenness as evidence against God.
claims.quote: The author has suggested that theists should be more open to the idea that hiddenness can be evidence against God.

claims.text: Hiddenness does not make theism irrational because rational belief depends on one’s total evidence.
claims.quote: As always, it is our total evidence that determines what is rational to believe—and theism can be reasonable on our total evidence even in light of hiddenness.

claims.text: Theistic religious commitments have imposed philosophical pressures on contemporary theories of moral responsibility.
claims.quote: It identifies and explains five common features of theistic religious commitment that can be seen to have imposed philosophical pressures on contemporary accounts of moral responsibility.

claims.text: These pressures include divine likeness, divine purposes, eternal expectations, divine foreknowledge, evil, and divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: These features are (1) an emphasis on human likeness to God (Imago Dei), (2) a disposition to see human agency as having divine purposes, (3) an assumption of eternal expectations (Heaven and Hell) for human agents, (4) the need to respond to internal philosophical tensions like the problem of divine foreknowledge, and (5) the need to respond to external philosophical challenges like the problem of evil and the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: A perfectly loving God must manifest himself to every person at all times.
claims.quote: Dios –al ser perfectamente amoroso– debe manifestarse a cualquier persona y en cualquier tiempo

claims.text: There are nonresistant agnostics and atheists who are not culpable for their unbelief.
claims.quote: existen agnósticos y ateos sin resistencia que no tienen culpa de su increencia.

claims.text: Finite epistemic agents must economize cognitive resources and seek substantive rather than trivial epistemic goods.
claims.quote: The argument begins from the fact that finite epistemic agents must economize their cognitive resources, and thus should seek sources of substantive, rather than trivial, epistemic goods.

claims.text: If God exists, his omniscience and moral perfection uniquely position him to provide personally fitting and valuable epistemic goods.
claims.quote: If God exists, He would be uniquely well-positioned—given His omniscience and moral perfection—to deliver epistemic goods that are personally fitting and epistemically valuable.

claims.text: For many agents, theistic hope remains epistemically appropriate even under skeptical-theist constraints.
claims.quote: concluding that even under skeptical theist constraints, theistic hope remains epistemically appropriate for many.

claims.text: Suffering is logically necessary for transforming individuals into exemplars of moral goodness through a four-stage process.
claims.quote: The chapter introduces the Exemplarist Theodicy as a comprehensive alternative that demonstrates how suffering functions as a logical necessity for transforming individuals into exemplars of moral goodness through a four-stage process: participation in basic goods, exercise of self-formation, acquisition of virtues, and undergoing transformative experiences.

claims.text: The Exemplarist Theodicy provides a unified explanation of human and animal suffering, uneven adversity, and anti-theodicy critiques.
claims.quote: This theodicy provides a unified explanation for both human and animal suffering, addresses the uneven distribution of adversity, and responds to anti-theodicy critiques.

claims.text: If God is perfectly loving, every person capable of a personal relationship with him could reasonably believe that God exists.
claims.quote: According to the problem of divine hiddenness, if God is perfectly loving, he would make it so that anyone capable of having a personal relationship with him would be able to reasonably believe that God exists.

claims.text: The existence of faultless nonbelief entails that a perfectly loving God does not exist.
claims.quote: Given that some people do not believe in the existence of God – and after careful, sincere investigation and due to no fault of their own – then such a perfectly loving God does not exist.

claims.text: Rejecting either the perfectly loving or no-fault assumption can avoid the divine-hiddenness conclusion, though doing so is challenging.
claims.quote: In §2, we will consider how both assumptions can be rejected so as to avoid the problem of divine hiddenness’s conclusion; however, I’ll also note that doing so comes with challenges.

claims.text: The Marapu death prayer is not a conflict of faith but a religious expression that enables analogical theological dialogue.
claims.quote: These findings affirm that the practice does not represent a conflict of faith, but rather a religious expression that opens an analogical space for theological dialogue.

claims.text: The Marapu death prayer can serve as a locus theologicus that enriches contextual theology and supports dialogical pastoral practice.
claims.quote: Consequently, the Marapu death prayer may be understood as a locus theologicus that enriches contextual theology and encourages a more dialogical, contextual, and non-reductionist pastoral approach within the Church.

claims.text: Because creation relates God intimately to limited beings, the holiness framework gives God reasons not to create.
claims.quote: Because creation is an intimate relationship between God and other things, and all such other things are limited in goodness, the holiness framework entails that God has standing reasons not to create at all.

claims.text: God has reason to remain hidden because being known by limited, imperfect persons is an intimate relationship.
claims.quote: And as being known by is an intimate relationship, God would have reason to remain hidden rather than known by us limited, imperfect persons.

claims.text: God's intimate relation to the world is explained only by the loving reasons he graciously and contingently acts upon.
claims.quote: God’s willingness to be intimately related to this world is against the reasons given by divine holiness, and is accounted for only through the reasons of love for us that God graciously, contingently acts upon.

claims.text: Contemporary problems of evil miss the mark when applied to classical theism.
claims.quote: Keltz discusses Aquinas’s thought on God, evil, and what kind of world God would make, then turns to contemporary problems of evil and shows how they miss the mark when it comes to classical theism.

claims.text: Contemporary formulations of the problem of evil miss the mark against classical theism.
claims.quote: Keltz discusses Aquinas’s thought on God, evil, and what kind of world God would make, then turns to contemporary problems of evil and shows how they miss the mark when it comes to classical theism.

claims.text: The problem of horrendous and apparently pointless evil can be explained by several theodicies taken together.
claims.quote: I address the problem of horrendous evil and apparently pointless evil and cognitive biases (Park 2018) by arguing that it can be accounted for by the reasons for divine hiddenness and moral testing ( Chapter 7 ), the Connection Building Theodicy and Cosmic Conflict Theodicy, the Adamic Fall Theodicy, and the Afterlife Theodicy, taken together.

claims.text: God's permission of suffering rests primarily on love and free will, not consequentialist compensation.
claims.quote: I reply by clarifying that, on my view, God’s justification for allowing suffering is not based solely on the benefits that the sufferer would receive but on values of love and the prerogatives based on love, which involve allowing humans to exercise their free will in morally significant ways.

claims.text: Sterba's ideal-political-state analogy for divine action is false.
claims.quote: I argue that God has the prerogative to create a world in which the duty to prevent and eliminate evil is temporarily given to humans, and that Sterba’s analogy of an ideal political state for how God should act is a false analogy.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness is neither unjust nor anomalous, but results naturally from God living God's own life.
claims.quote: In contrast, throughout the book, Rea contends that such hiddenness is neither an injustice nor an anomaly but instead a natural result of God living out God's own life (6).

claims.text: Personalistic analogies of parental and divine love have limits and can create unwarranted expectations of God.
claims.quote: Rea believes that an investment in such personalistic imagery can lead to unwarranted expectations about God's love.

claims.text: The Bible's continuum between personalistic depictions of God and divine transcendence should be honored.
claims.quote: We too should honor that continuum instead of largely singling out the personal side in divine-human relations.

claims.text: The received YHWH figure is a synthetic composite of attributions from multiple structural layers.
claims.quote: The study demonstrates that the received YHWH figure is a synthetic composite, containing attributions from multiple structural layers: L₄ DL (Sophis), IL₄ IDL (Nyxea), L₀ substrate language, and cultural elevation to L₅ / L₀.

claims.text: Christian and Gnostic traditions err by treating their partial readings of the composite YHWH figure as monovalent.
claims.quote: Christian and Gnostic traditions each correctly perceive real material within the composite but err by treating their partial reading as monovalent.

claims.text: The New Testament separates what the Old Testament conflated, displacing some attributions while fulfilling others.
claims.quote: The NT is shown to separate what the OT conflated, displacing IL₄ IDL attributions while fulfilling L₄ DL architectural material.

claims.text: Public conversion explains conversion's rationality and helps solve divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: The article offers a defense of public conversion, arguing it explains the rationality of conversion and offers a solution to the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: Knowledge of God is obtained through loving one another within the institutional Church.
claims.quote: Sullivan suggests that we obtain knowledge of God by loving one another, which takes place in the framework of the institutional Church.

claims.text: The paper denies that Ryan MacLean is God the Father despite evidence portrayed as strongly suggestive.
claims.quote: This work is a hybrid academic–satirical theological paper that rigorously examines — and ultimately denies — the possibility that Ryan MacLean is God the Father, despite a vast preponderance of empirical, symbolic, numeric, typological, liturgical, and psycho-spiritual evidence that suspiciously aligns with Catholic tradition.

claims.text: Schellenberg's work was regarded as a new, well-argued challenge to the theistic conception of God.
claims.quote: 1993 metais pasirodęs Johno L. Schellenbergo veikalas „Dievo paslėptis ir žmogaus protas“ („Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason“), anot apžvalgininkų, tarp kai kurių religijos filosofų bei filosofinės teologijos atstovų sukėlė geroką sumaištį – jis buvo įvertintas kaip naujas, gerai argumentuotas iššūkis teistinei Dievo sampratai.

claims.text: Schellenberg's atheism addresses God's possible existence through epistemology rather than purely theological revision.
claims.quote: Schellenbergo pozicija yra originali dėl to, kad jis šiuo principu operuoja ne siekdamas naujai persvarstyti kurią nors grynai teologinę temą, bet filosofinį Dievo buvimo galimybės klausimą, tiksliau – epistemologinį klausimą religijos filosofijos kontekste.

claims.text: The received YHWH figure is a synthetic composite of attributions from multiple structural layers.
claims.quote: The study demonstrates that the received YHWH figure is a synthetic composite, containing attributions from multiple structural layers: L₄ DL (Sophis), IL₄ IDL (Nyxea), L₀ substrate language, and cultural elevation to L₅ / L₀.

claims.text: Christian and Gnostic traditions err by treating their partial readings of the composite YHWH figure as monovalent.
claims.quote: Christian and Gnostic traditions each correctly perceive real material within the composite but err by treating their partial reading as monovalent.

claims.text: The New Testament separates what the Old Testament conflated, displacing some attributions while fulfilling others.
claims.quote: The NT is shown to separate what the OT conflated, displacing IL₄ IDL attributions while fulfilling L₄ DL architectural material.

claims.text: Ryan MacLean is not God the Father, even if the evidence all but insists otherwise.
claims.quote: Ryan MacLean is not God the Father… even if he is.

claims.text: Empirical, symbolic, numeric, typological, liturgical, and psycho-spiritual evidence suspiciously aligns Ryan MacLean with Catholic tradition.
claims.quote: a vast preponderance of empirical, symbolic, numeric, typological, liturgical, and psycho-spiritual evidence that suspiciously aligns with Catholic tradition.

claims.text: A morally challenging version of theism is cognitively tenable.
claims.quote: In the end, a morally challenging version of theism emerges as cognitively tenable.

claims.text: Evidence of God becomes salient when inquirers willingly receive and reflect God’s moral character for others.
claims.quote: This evidence becomes salient to inquirers as they themselves responsively and willingly become evidence of God's reality in receiving and reflecting God's moral character for others.
