claims.text: Hedonic adaptation constrains theodicy because even improved conditions cannot secure lasting experiential relief.
claims.quote: The framework shows why even benevolently calibrated trajectories can at best reduce cumulative burden rather than secure lasting experiential relief.

claims.text: Relief loses experiential force as evaluative baselines reset and perceived suffering reasserts itself.
claims.quote: Even when objective conditions improve, relief tends to lose experiential force as evaluative baselines reset and perceived suffering reasserts itself.

claims.text: Adaptation reframes what divine benevolence can accomplish within affective life.
claims.quote: These dynamics have differential implications for soul-making, free-will, providential-restraint, and interventionist theodicies, reframing what divine benevolence can be taken to accomplish within affective life.

claims.text: Hell is how a sinful creature necessarily experiences God’s unmitigated holy presence, not suffering intentionally inflicted by God.

claims.quote: It motivates the idea that APR should expand its focus to address topics more central to lived religion "on the ground", and it shows through its own careful explorations of liturgical practice how such philosophy can be done (and be done well).

claims.text: Some finite persons are or have been nonresistant nonbelievers regarding God's existence.
claims.quote: Some finite persons are or have been nonresistantly in a state of nonbelief in relation to the proposition that God exists.

claims.text: No perfectly loving God exists.
claims.quote: No perfectly loving God exists.

claims.text: We should reject the claim that unsurpassable divine love necessarily requires openness to reciprocal conscious relationship with every capable creature at every time.
claims.quote: I argue that we should resist the temptation.

claims.text: Schellenberg's premise of nonresistant nonbelief relies on the assumption that resistance would probably be detectable if it existed.
claims.quote: This assumption is that, regarding putative nonresistant nonbelievers, more likely than not we’d detect these nonbelievers’ resistance toward God if there were any.

claims.text: It is no more reasonable to affirm than refrain from affirming Schellenberg's Noseeum Assumption.
claims.quote: I give reasons for thinking that it is not more reasonable to affirm than to refrain from affirming Schellenberg’s Noseeum Assumption, and so reason to think that the hiddenness argument is not a good argument for atheism.

claims.text: The hiddenness argument is not a good argument for atheism.
claims.quote: I give reasons for thinking that it is not more reasonable to affirm than to refrain from affirming Schellenberg’s Noseeum Assumption, and so reason to think that the hiddenness argument is not a good argument for atheism.

claims.text: God would value and therefore create properly valuable persons, including people who undergo nonresistant nonbelief.
claims.quote: Building on this distinction, I argue that God would value and therefore create persons such as those who exist in our actual world, including nonresistant nonbelievers (i.e., persons who exist in a state of nonresistant nonbelief at some point during the course of their lives).

claims.text: Most actual persons are properly valuable, and God would value them before their existence.
claims.quote: My reasoning is based on the notion that most persons who exist in our actual world are properly valuable; we may discover their value by way of human experience, but God would value such persons even prior to their existence.

claims.text: Divine loving concerns actual persons and presupposes their existence, whereas divine valuing concerns possible persons and chooses their existence.
claims.quote: Loving is properly directed toward actual persons as such and presupposes the existence of the beloved, but valuing is properly directed toward possible persons as such and chooses the existence of the beloved.

claims.text: The article defends the author's earlier claim that nonresistant nonbelievers' reasons for unbelief essentially originate in moral errors.
claims.quote: Artykuł jest obroną przed zarzutami postawionymi wobec mojego poprzedniego tekstu, w którym wskazywałem, że powody do niewiary u nonresistant nonbelievers mają w swej istocie źródła błędów moralnych.

claims.text: The article addresses objections concerning noncognitive religious belief, doxastic voluntarism, natural knowledge of God, anonymous Christians, and social sin.
claims.quote: W kolejności staram się odpowiedzieć na następujące zarzuty: 1) że postrzegam przekonania religijne w sposób niekognitywny, co jest niezgodne z tradycyjnym podejściem chrześcijańskim; 2) że, głoszę z jednej strony woluntaryzm przekonaniowy, a z drugiej strony obwiniam niewierzących za ich decyzje; 3) że odwołując się do naturalnego poznania Boga, nie wyjaśniam satysfakcjonująco przyczyn niewiary; 4) że w błędny sposób wykluczam z grupy anonimowych chrześcijan osoby niewierzące, żyjące we współczesnym świecie; 5) że w sposób niejasny wpisuję ideę grzechu społecznego w osobistą winę, jaką ponoszą osoby niewierzące za swoją niewiarę.

claims.text: Divine love would motivate God to actualize nonresistant nonbelief when it is necessary for persons God could love to exist.
claims.quote: Yet if particular persons can only come into existence under particular circumstances, then given Schellenberg’s own conception of divine love, God would be motivated by his love to actualize nonresistant nonbelief in order to bring about (and form relationships with) persons who can only come into existence under circumstances that include other capable persons being in a state of nonresistant nonbelief.

claims.text: Natural nonbelief in early humans provides weakened support for naturalism over theism.
claims.quote: Second, since theism entails Axiarchism, and it is far from clear on our total available evidence that eliminating the possibility of natural nonbelief would have led to a choiceworthy degree of moral, intellectual, and aesthetic value being realized for early humans, the degree to which natural nonbelief supports naturalism over theism is softened.

claims.text: God could have a morally sufficient reason to permit natural nonbelief in early humans.
claims.quote: However, I will argue that it is epistemically possible that God has a morallysufficient reason for permitting natural nonbelief in early humans.

claims.text: According to Axiarchism, God aims to structure physical reality to realize a choiceworthy degree of moral, intellectual, and aesthetic value.
claims.quote: First, according to Axiarchism, God’s goal for physical reality is to intentionally structure it so that a choiceworthy degree of moral, intellectual, and aesthetic value will be realized.

claims.text: Theists lack grounds to claim with certainty that nonresistant nonbelievers do not exist.
claims.quote: Dążę do wykazania, że teiści nie mają podstaw, by twierdzić, że z pewnością nie istnieją nonresistant nonbelievers.

claims.text: If average Christians are epistemically reliable, epistemically reliable contemporary atheists in secular Western societies cannot be excluded.
claims.quote: Twierdzę między innymi, że jeśli uznamy, że przeciętny chrześcijanin jest rzetelny poznawczo, to nie możemy wykluczyć, że współczesny ateista, żyjący w zlaicyzowanym społeczeństwie Zachodu, również jest rzetelny poznawczo.

claims.text: Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument relies on an uncritically assumed account of love that can be challenged.
claims.quote: I offer objections to the account of love that Schellenberg uncritically assumes and applies to divine-human relationships.

claims.text: Alternative plausible accounts of divine love allow Christian theists to avoid the hiddenness argument’s conclusion.
claims.quote: Christian theists have several plausible ways of avoiding the conclusion of the hiddenness argument by adopting a different account of divine love.

claims.text: Reconstructing the hiddenness argument using other contemporary accounts of love makes it unsuccessful.
claims.quote: In each case, the hiddenness argument is rendered unsuccessful.

claims.text: The evidence gives reflective inquirers substantial reason to reduce confidence in strong Christian disclosure claims and suspend allegiance.
claims.quote: It does give reflective inquirers substantial reason to reduce confidence in strong Christian disclosure claims and to suspend allegiance when the alleged source cannot be distinguished from ordinary religious formation.

claims.text: Religious diversity and the lack of a shared corrective are more expected under ordinary cultural religious formation than universally available divine revelation.
claims.quote: This pattern is more expected if religions develop through ordinary human cognition and cultural transmission than if a perfectly capable communicator is providing universally available, source-identifying revelation.

claims.text: Merely naming a possible good does not answer the challenge posed by religious ambiguity.
claims.quote: Freedom, soul-making, social dependence, private experience, transcendence, sin, and mystery may explain some ambiguity, but none answers the challenge merely by naming a possible good.

claims.text: Theological silence provides a framework for knowing God and for human ennoblement with God’s character.
claims.quote: Theological silence, whether human or divine, creates the framework for knowing God. Silent concealment of God provides the framework for human ennoblement with God’s character.

claims.text: Silence is complementary to speech and has greater potential for meaning than speech.
claims.quote: Subordinate to the field of communication, silence is not an epiphenomenon of speech, but complementary to it. Finding its limits between ambiguity and paradox, silence proves to have a greater potential for meaning than speech.

claims.text: Only the lack of divine response in Lamentations bears on whether God is present or absent in the Megilloth.
claims.quote: It is determined that only the lack of divine response in Lamentations informs whether God is present or absent in the Megilloth.

claims.text: Divine silence is not abandonment but an invitation to faith through action and spiritual growth.
claims.quote: This paradoxical silence functions not as abandonment but as an invitation to faith expressed through action and spiritual growth.

claims.text: The Genesis acquisition of knowledge of good and evil initiates shame, fear, exile, and God’s silence.
claims.quote: Beginning with the Genesis narrative, the acquisition of the �knowledge of good and evil� triggers shame, fear, and exile from Paradise, marking the onset of God�s silence.

claims.text: The divine Voice’s iconographic descent as a hand suggests a shift from verbal communication to divine action.
claims.quote: Additionally, it explores the theological and iconographic significance of the divine Voice symbolized as a descending hand from heaven, suggesting a shift from verbal communication to divine action embodied in deeds.

claims.text: Genesis 12 is best interpreted as five speech-response pairs whose central silence makes testing the episode's central theme.
claims.quote: This article aims to demonstrate that the text is best viewed as a series of five speech-response pairs, with the central ‘pair’ emphatically omitting any speech. The absence of speech in v.10 is an interpretive key, identifying the theme of testing as central to this episode.

claims.text: God's gifts and blessings matter less than a properly ordered relationship with God.
claims.quote: the gifts and blessings of God are ultimately less important than being in properly ordered relationship with the Giver.

claims.text: Divine silence may result from anger, when prophecy and other means of discerning God's will are absent or scarce.
claims.quote: Korpel and De Moor indicate that in certain situations prophecy and other means to learn the will of God were absent or scarce, especially when God was angry.

claims.text: The Bible explicitly and implicitly warns against speaking imprudently in God's name.
claims.quote: The Bible contains many explicit and implicit warnings against imprudent speaking in the name of God.

claims.text: In Qohelet, God acts without speaking, and those acts are incomprehensible.
claims.quote: In Qohelet God acts, but he does not speak and his acts are incomprehensible.

claims.text: Human libertarian freedom and divine middle knowledge support meticulous providence without making God responsible for evil.
claims.quote: It then argues that accepting the truth of human libertarian freedom and divine middle knowledge provides a powerful basis for thinking that God has meticulous providential control over the world without implicating God in evil

claims.text: This Molinist account can help believers trust God amid trials, divine silence, and apparent unanswered prayer.
claims.quote: and this can help believers to trust God when they face trials and wrestle with His silence and apparent unresponsiveness to prayer.

claims.text: An absent deity cannot speak because it is not present, whereas a silent deity may listen attentively or have reasons for silence.
claims.quote: Korpel and de Moor draw a distinction between divine silence and divine absence, noting absent deity does not speak because he is not there to enter into a dialogue, whereas a silent deity can be attentively listening or may have reason to keep silent.

claims.text: Family religion's concern to preserve favorable divine-human relations becomes concern about divine absence or silence across life and death.
claims.quote: This chapter demonstrates the family religion's concern for maintaining favorable divine-human relationships translated into a concern over divine absence or silence in connection with birth, daily life, and death.

claims.text: Islamic theodicy locates suffering within divine moral order, while existential absurdity treats it as evidence of an indifferent universe.
claims.quote: Islamic theodicy, which highlights suffering within a divine moral order, and existential absurdity that views suffering as primary evidence of an indifferent universe.

claims.text: Modern literature allows theological and modern frameworks to intersect and reimagine divine justice and existential absurdity.
claims.quote: The study further argues that modern literature is a discursive space where modern and theological frameworks intersect, presenting a mutually inclusive space for characters that reimagined divine justice and existential absurdity.

claims.text: Divine silence expresses human fragmentation but does not prove divine absence.
claims.quote: Divine Silence is an expression of the uncomprehended and incomprehensible laceration and fragmentation of the human existence. It is no proof of divine absence.

claims.text: All language about God is metaphorical, and silence must be understood in the context of speaking.
claims.quote: The author agrees with Korpel and De Moor, when they state that all language about God has a metaphorical character. Korpel and De Moor correctly locate 'silence' in the context of 'speaking'.

claims.text: Divine silence as communication has deep ancient roots and voices what cannot otherwise be communicated.
claims.quote: Korpel and De Moor make more than clear that the concept of divine silence as means of communication is not to be seen as only an idea from contemporary culture, but has deep roots in antiquity and beyond. Silence gives voice to something otherwise incommunicable.

claims.text: Divine silence can be explained as an answer to diverse circumstances and requires appropriate human conduct in response.
claims.quote: In their view, divine silence can be explained as an answer to a variety of circumstances. Additionally, they opt for the view that divine silence needs to be answered by appropriate human conduct.

claims.text: Some contributors suggest that divine silence should instead be understood as evidence of divine absence.
claims.quote: Some authors hint at the view that divine silence should be construed as an indication of divine absence.

claims.text: Korpel and De Moor respond to their critics.
claims.quote: Korpel and De Moor give a learned response to their critics.

claims.text: Divine silence can be explained as an answer to diverse circumstances and requires appropriate human conduct in response.
claims.quote: In their view, divine silence can be explained as an answer to a variety of circumstances. Additionally, they opt for the view that divine silence needs to be answered by appropriate human conduct.

claims.text: Some contributors suggest that divine silence should instead be understood as evidence of divine absence.
claims.quote: Some authors hint at the view that divine silence should be construed as an indication of divine absence.

claims.text: Korpel and De Moor respond to their critics.
claims.quote: Korpel and De Moor give a learned response to their critics.

claims.text: Divine silence in Zephaniah 3:17 should be interpreted positively as divine mercy rather than cruel absence.
claims.quote: This article examines the divine silence in Zephaniah 3,17, which demonstrates the positive interpretation of silence as divine mercy.

claims.text: Korpel and De Moor's examples do not convincingly establish divine silence.
claims.quote: The examples that Korpel and De Moor present of divine silence are not really convincing.

claims.text: Divine silence and abandonment indicate divine anger in the prophetic books.
claims.quote: Divine silence and abandonment are symptomatic of divine anger.

claims.text: God's speaking and silence both follow a divine plan that humans cannot fully understand.
claims.quote: Both in his speaking and in his silence, God acts according to his own divine plan, which is a mystery to humans.

claims.text: Discrepancy is a fundamental condition of human existence, not itself a pathology.
claims.quote: This project develops the General Theory of Discrepancy (GTD), a conceptual framework proposing that discrepancy is a fundamental condition of human existence rather than pathology itself.

claims.text: Endō's Silence supplies a corrective to pragmatist deliberative philosophy.
claims.quote: The following essay argues that Shūsaku Endō’s 1966 novel Silence, elucidates a corrective to pragmatist deliberative philosophy.

claims.text: The narrative directs readers toward practical concern for their form of life rather than explaining its characters' suffering.
claims.quote: Instead, it draws its readers into a practical concern for what Ludwig Wittgenstein referred to as their form of life.

claims.text: When suffering is inevitable, embodied silence may be the only way to speak.
claims.quote: In sum, the essay contends that when immanent suffering is inevitable, practices of embodied silence can be the only way to speak.

claims.text: Awareness of God's silence may be essential for shaping individual choices and collective histories.
claims.quote: But in an age in which the power of words has been systematically eroded and the orthodoxy of language has been questioned, it may be that our awareness of God’s silence is essential in shaping our individual choices and defining our collective histories.

claims.text: Early German Romanticism rebelled against modern European philosophy by restoring Nature's neglected role.
claims.quote: The early German Romantics,inspired by the divine silence and melancholy in Nature and the longing for the salvation of human beings through the forces in Nature,have in fact launched a rebellion against the mainstream European modern philosophy which largely ignores the role of Nature.

claims.text: For early German Romantics, revelation and interpretation are dialogue between humanity and Nature, ideally uniting truth and Nature.
claims.quote: For the early German Romantics,the so-called revelation and interpretation are in essence the dialogue between Man and Nature,the ideal state of which consists in the perfect unity of truth and Nature.

claims.text: The Byzantine altar's Mystery has a liminal character manifested through concealing-revealing devices that structure liturgical participation.
claims.quote: The main focus is to investigate the liminal nature of the Mystery, manifested through concealing-revealing devices, which are thresholds in the liturgical participation of the Byzantine subject.

claims.text: Analysis of Lamentations 3:55–57 suggests that the q strophe interrupts divine silence by recognizing God as speaking.
claims.quote: Analysis of Lam 3,55-57, the crux interpretum for the divine silence, suggests the q strophe may break this oppressive silence. The strophe reflects an awareness of God who speaks.

claims.text: Lamentations' account of God's oblique emergence resembles postmodernism's ambiguous and indeterminate approach to reality.
claims.quote: This perspective is similar to the ambiguous, indeterminate approach to reality in postmodernism.

claims.text: Ecstasy explains the unity of divine love in both the inner and outer Trinity.
claims.quote: In order to understand the love by which the Father loves both the Son and the world, the concept of ecstasy is proposed and fleshed out as the one concept explaining the divine love on both sides of the Trinity.

claims.text: The Father's inner-trinitarian love is self-giving of his essence to the Son.
claims.quote: the inner-trinitarian ecstasy is worked out formally as the oscillation between activity and passivity, and materially as the quintessence of love: the Father's self-giving of his essence to the Son.

claims.text: Christ's loving self-giving, taking on, and transforming human incapacity to love manifests the ecstatic structure of his person.
claims.quote: The address of love represents the ecstatic structure of his person to give himself, and the flipside, to take upon himself and to transform the human in tis incapacity to love in its longing to be loved.

claims.text: God remains silent while Job debates his friends and approaches blaming God for his suffering.
claims.quote: As Job debates with his friends and teeters on the brink of blaming God for his suffering, God, though present, remains silent.

claims.text: God speaks because Job and his friends wrongly presume to know God's intentions.
claims.quote: At the last, however, God bursts forth in speech, provoked because Job and his friends have presumed to know God's intentions.

claims.text: God's creative presence provides consolation amid grief and tragedy even when events are not righted as Job wishes.
claims.quote: In his speeches, God assures Job that although things may not be righted to his liking, God will nevertheless, through the gifi of God's creative presence, provide sources of consolation amid grief and tragedy.

claims.text: The Megilloth share apparent divine absence, yet also contain traces of God's presence.
claims.quote: Their juxtaposition in the Hebrew Bible highlights their shared theme of apparent divine absence, but, paradoxically, traces of God's presence are unearthed as well.

claims.text: The Megilloth's ambiguity about divine presence and absence challenges prevailing Hebrew Bible conceptions of both.
claims.quote: By examining various aspects of this theme, including the literary absence of God, divine abandonment, God-talk, allusive language, God's providence, and divine silence, it becomes clear that the ambiguity of divine presence and absence in the Megilloth presents a significant challenge to current conceptualizations of divine presence and absence in the Hebrew Bible.

claims.text: Rose advances a theology of dialogue grounded in negotiation and law-making, whereas Weil advances a negative theology of counterbalance from divine silence.
claims.quote: While Rose draws us towards a theology of dialogue rooted in the creative necessity of negotiation and law-making, Weil draws us towards a negative theology ofcounterbalance, carved not from divine speech but from divine silence.

claims.text: Germain rejects easy theodical consolations and solutions to the problem of evil.
claims.quote: While Germain rejects easy theodical consolations and “solutions” to the problem of evil, her Pleurante posits remembering and attentive listening as a viable ethical response, spiritual posture, and literary practice to move forward while honoring the past.

claims.text: Remembering and attentive listening offer a viable ethical, spiritual, and literary response that honors the past while moving forward.
claims.quote: While Germain rejects easy theodical consolations and “solutions” to the problem of evil, her Pleurante posits remembering and attentive listening as a viable ethical response, spiritual posture, and literary practice to move forward while honoring the past.

claims.text: AI-generated responses are immediate and coherent but non-intentional and lack ethical and ontological responsibility.
claims.quote: While AI systems generate immediate and linguistically coherent outputs, such responses remain non‐intentional and lack ethical and ontological responsibility.

claims.text: Speech act theory distinguishes simulated AI responsiveness from divine address.
claims.quote: Drawing on speech act theory, the study clarifies the distinction between simulated responsiveness and divine address.

claims.text: Prayer involves waiting, vulnerability, and openness to transformation, while divine silence is a mode of temporality rather than absence.
claims.quote: Prayer is interpreted as a performative practice marked by waiting, vulnerability, and openness to transformation, while divine silence is understood not as absence but as a mode of temporality.

claims.text: The Megilloth’s ambiguity about divine presence and absence challenges prevailing conceptions of these categories in the Hebrew Bible.

claims.text: Divine silence prevents dialogue in Psalm 88.
claims.quote: Because of the divine silence, dialogue does not take place.

claims.text: Psalm 88 progressively descends from an exclamation to a powerless whispered conclusion foregrounding darkness.
claims.quote: Viewed as a whole, there is a progressive descent from the opening exclamation to the dismayed and powerlessly whispered conclusion in which 'a dark place' occupies the foreground.

claims.text: If God created humanity for a purpose, God would have clarified that purpose and humanity’s role by now.
claims.quote: If God created humanity to fulfill a purpose, then God would have clarified his purpose and our role by now, as I will argue.

claims.text: Failing to clarify humanity’s role would undermine God’s achievement of the purpose God conceived.
claims.quote: Thus, by failing to clarify our role, God would be undermining himself in achieving the purpose he conceived, which would not make sense.

claims.text: Humanity was likely not created by God to fulfill a purpose.
claims.quote: Because God, if he exists, would not engage in this self-defeating behavior, this suggests that humanity was not created by God to fulfill a purpose.

claims.text: Skeptical theism is purportedly unacceptable because it undermines trust in God.
claims.quote: Undermining our trust in God is one of the purported unacceptable consequences of the truth of skeptical theism.

claims.text: Divine silence justifies distrust only if God provides no accessible experience of divine presence.
claims.quote: Silence would only justify a lack of trust in God if God did not provide an accessible way of experiencing His presence despite His silence.

claims.text: Liturgical practices can sustain trust in God without providing propositional knowledge of God’s justification for evil.
claims.quote: This chapter argues that liturgical practices can provide a basis of maintaining one’s trust in God even if those practices do not result in propositional knowledge regarding His justification for evil.

claims.text: Job’s suffering is an essential crucible through which authentic faith is refined.
claims.quote: This paper argues that Job’s suffering is not incidental but essential mandatory crucible through which authentic faith is refined.

claims.text: Prosperity theology offers a superficial understanding of suffering.
claims.quote: It challenges superficial understandings of prosperity theology, proposing instead a spiritual maturity rooted in the tension between lament and trust.

claims.text: God is most present to believers not in explanations, but in enduring presence.
claims.quote: In living “between ashes and hope,” the believer learns that God is most present not in explanations, but in enduring presence.

claims.text: Job’s deepest cry seeks intimacy with an apparently distant and indifferent God, rather than justice or reward.
claims.quote: Drawing on ontology, philosophical existentialism, and theology, the paper proposes that Job’s deepest cry is directed not toward justice or reward, but toward intimacy with a God who appears distant and indifferent.

claims.text: Job’s suffering becomes a site of relational hope rather than punishment.
claims.quote: The article explores how Job, stripped of all worldly meaning, confronts not merely divine silence but the trauma of „metaphysical“ abandonment, thereby opening a theological space in which suffering is no longer punishment but a site of relational hope.

claims.text: Rejecting moral rationalizations, Job anticipates a grace theology that defines righteousness as reciprocal desire between God and humans.
claims.quote: In rejecting moral rationalizations, Job anticipates a theology of grace that redefines righteousness as the capacity to desire a God who desires us back.

claims.text: Esther presents the Hebrew Bible’s most consistently silent God.
claims.quote: Of all the books of the Hebrew Bible, the book of Esther presents the most consistently silent God.

claims.text: God’s silence in Esther does not entail the complete absence of God or faith.
claims.quote: Silent though God may be in the book of Esther, it does not necessarily imply a complete absence of the divine person or of faith.

claims.text: Esther’s extensive intertextual links to texts portraying God acting and speaking support its portrayal of eloquent divine silence.
claims.quote: The wealth of intertextual links between the book on the one hand and texts that explicitly speak of God as both acting and speaking on the other is vast.

claims.text: Divine silence frustrates or terrifies faithful people who perceive divine indifference amid adversity and cruelty.
claims.quote: Divine silence has frequently frustrated or even terrified the faithful, who continue to pray notwithstanding what appears to be divine indifference in the face of adversity and cruelty.

claims.text: Divine silence confirms atheists’ belief that no God exists.
claims.quote: At the same time, that very silence confirms for atheists their belief in the absence of any God.

claims.text: Biblical silence is an experiential reality, especially evident in the Gospels.
claims.quote: Silence is an experiential reality rather than an abstract concept in the Bible, and this reality is no more obvious than in the four gospels that tell the story of Jesus Christ.

claims.text: Lavant’s poetry artistically expresses an inner self confronting divine silence and existential uncertainty.
claims.quote: Lavant’s poetry is interpreted as an artistic expression of the inner self confronting both divine silence and existential uncertainty.

claims.text: Isaiah 40–66 conveys its message primarily through poetic images, juxtapositions, and emotional encounters rather than conceptual argument.
claims.quote: As poems, the texts of Isaiah 40–66 convey their message more through vivid word pictures, juxtapositions, and emotional encounters than through an argument about ideas.

claims.text: The prologue of Job alludes to Leviticus 8–10 through a shared sequence and identical lexemes.
claims.quote: Although it is not impossible that these features could have resulted unintentionally from a shared scribal culture, the textual evidence is strong enough to indicate that the scribe of Job’s prologue alludes to the priestly inauguration story of Leviticus 8–10.

claims.text: Job rejects a mechanistic understanding of both traditional wisdom and Priestly cultic tradition.
claims.quote: This study clarifies how the story of Job rejects a mechanistic understanding not only of traditional wisdom, but of the Priestly cultic tradition of ancient Israel and Judah.

claims.text: Carlyle’s imperial reannouncement ignores Britain’s long colonial history and recasts it as eternal beginning.
claims.quote: The long history of British colonisation, announced by Hakluyt’s clarion call almost three hundred years previously 1 , plays no part in Carlyle’s reannouncement of imperial destiny, unless it be included as just another instant of that inspiring, if slightly confused, ‘incessant’, ‘present’, ‘eternal’ beginning.

claims.text: Imperial rhetoric continues to portray inhabited continents as available for European scientific exploitation.
claims.quote: Despite three hundred years of colonisation, there are still potentially fertile continents — conveniently inhabited only by wild beasts (about whom we shall hear much more) — expectantly and hopefully awaiting the productive thrust of European science.

claims.text: A Liberal Quaker Literary Aesthetic is a distinctive expression of Liberal Quakerism.
claims.quote: I demonstrate that this QLA is a distinctive expression of Liberal Quakerism.

claims.text: The QLA is fully demonstrated by Gross and Ruth through Quaker values and an apophatic approach transferred into literary writing.
claims.quote: I argue that this QLA, whilst partially displayed by other writers of faith or none, is fully demonstrated by these writers, as a development in this context of particular values and the silent, apophatic approach found amongst British Liberal Quakers, brought over into literary writing.

claims.text: For Eckhart, unknowing is divine Silence that discloses God in creation and self-presence.
claims.quote: This “unknowing”, for Eckhart, is the divine Silence that discloses God through the experience of creation and through the experience of self-presence.

claims.text: Eckhart revises analogy to preserve God’s distinction from creation while enabling the creature’s return to its source.
claims.quote: Like Aquinas, Eckhart modifies the conventional understanding of analogy to preserve the creator’s distinction from creation while creating a linguistic space for the human creature’s return to its source.

claims.text: Esther purposefully constructs a theology of divine absence through its allusive relationship to Joseph.
claims.quote: While previous scholarship has seen Esther’s divine silence indicating God’s hidden hand, the characters’ or readers’ quiet faiths, or the secular concerns of an ancient Jewish nationalism, key aspects of Esther’s allusive character illustrate how the book purposefully constructs a theology of divine absence.

claims.text: The Joseph pattern extends into Persia even though the divine remains unseen.
claims.quote: As good-looking Israelites continue to rise in foreign courts to deliver themselves and their people from imminent dangers, the patterns God initiated in the Egyptian past are shown to extend into the Persian present even when the divine remains out of sight.

claims.text: MT Esther’s redactors altered an earlier version to place the Hebrew Megillah alongside Joseph’s backdrop.
claims.quote: Since this diachronically-oriented analysis suggests this theological interest was developed by Esther’s authors, it engages with Esther’s ancient Greek witnesses to demonstrate that the MT redactors altered an earlier version of the Scroll to position the Hebrew Megillah alongside Joseph’s instructive backdrop.

claims.text: Job’s deepest cry seeks intimacy with a distant God rather than justice or reward.
claims.quote: Drawing on comparative theology, Pauline typology, and philosophical existentialism, the paper proposes that Job’s deepest cry is not for justice or reward, but for intimacy with a God who seems distant, indifferent, or even cruel.

claims.text: Job rejects passive surrender by seeking a Redeemer who stands with him in the flesh.
claims.quote: While Islamic conceptions of submission (islām) frame suffering as a path to metaphysical alignment, Job rebels against the logic of passive surrender, seeking instead a Redeemer who will stand with him in the flesh.

claims.text: Job anticipates grace by redefining righteousness as desiring reciprocal divine desire.
claims.quote: In refusing to be consoled by moral rationalizations, Job anticipates a theology of grace that transcends submission and redefines righteousness as the capacity to desire a God who desires us back.

claims.text: La Nuit functions as memoir, anti-biblical narrative, and hypertext, especially as an anti-Exodus marked by divine absence.
claims.quote: Drawing on Gérard Genette’s theory of transtextuality, the paper argues that La Nuit functions simultaneously as memoir, anti-biblical narrative, and hypertext, especially as an “anti-Exodus” marked by divine absence.

claims.text: Memory ethically preserves humanity against radical evil and divine silence.
claims.quote: Central to this reading is the role of memory as an ethical act that preserves humanity in the face of radical evil and divine silence (hester panim).

claims.text: La Nuit denies redemption while affirming testimony as moral responsibility to victims and the future.
claims.quote: Ultimately, the paper positions La Nuit as an “anti-Tanakh” that denies redemption while affirming testimony as a moral responsibility toward the victims and the future.

claims.text: Perplexed affirmation partly derives from Thomas’s reckoning with David Hume.
claims.quote: In this essay, I explore how this affect derives partly from Thomas’s reckoning with David Hume.

claims.text: Hume complicates theology but empowers experience for Thomas.
claims.quote: But if Hume complicates thought, including theology, he empowers experience.

claims.text: Thomas surpasses Hume’s modern limits through faith or sacred experiences he cannot fully conceptualize.
claims.quote: For Thomas, this means that Hume demarcates modern limits the poet implicitly surpasses through faith, or through experiences of the sacred he can no longer fully conceptualize.

claims.text: God seems silent and indifferent to the suffering of the weakest people, despite the faithful's invocations.
claims.quote: God seems not to hear the invocations of the faithful; it looks as though He doesn’t care about the problem of suffering (especially of the weakest persons) that remains apparently unrelieved by divine intervention.

claims.text: Ezra and Nehemiah do not support interpreting temple vessels as iconic representations of Yhwh's return.
claims.quote: This seems to undermine the speculation of an iconic representation of Y hwh ’s return, and probably insinuates they were regarded more as relics.

claims.text: The temple vessels are not personified as implying divine presence in Ezra or Nehemiah.
claims.quote: Moreover, the vessels are never personified to imply presence in either book, as in the sparse and unconvincing ancient Near Eastern examples provided.

claims.text: Grief should be understood as a theological, social, and political practice rather than merely a psychological reaction to death.
claims.quote: Instead, as a practice, it sees grief as theological, social and political.

claims.text: Ritualized Biblical and Shia mourning resists dominant power and preserves victims' dignity through ethical and political engagement with death and suffering.
claims.quote: Ritualized mourning practices in both traditions, therefore, are counter-discursive responses against the dominant power.

claims.text: Transmission and ritualization of mourning form a shared ethical grammar across historical contexts and sectarian differences.
claims.quote: The article further argues that the transmission and ritualization of mourning contribute to the formation of a shared ethical grammar across historical contexts and sectarian differences.

claims.text: Orthodox liturgical music shaped the spiritual transformations and Eastern Christian mental-ideological constructs of ancient Kyivan Rus.
claims.quote: It has been scientifically proven and substantiated that the musical art of the Kyivan Rus became the personification of spiritual transformations, formed the mental and ideological constructs of Eastern Christianity in its ancient Old Rus form thanks to Orthodox liturgical music.

claims.text: The adoption of Eastern Christianity was foundational to Kyivan Rus musical culture, which patristic and hesychast spirituality significantly influenced.
claims.quote: According to the results of scientific analysis, it appears that the adoption of Eastern Christianity in Kyivan Rus became a fundamental milestone in the development of its musical culture, which was significantly influenced by the patristic doctrine and spirituality, in particular hesychast views and customs that came to Rus from Athos.

claims.text: Silence is the best praise of God because multiplying words in praise is futile.
claims.quote: Rashi explains the verse in two ways: firstly, the futility of multiplying words in praise of God, so that the best praise is silence.

claims.text: Remaining silent in suffering conflicts with the moral imperative to speak out against evil.
claims.quote: This derives from a passage in Midrash Tehillim which culminates with the Psalmist's own commitment to stay silent in the face of suffering, a stance which is in tension with the moral imperative of speaking out in the face of evil.

claims.text: There is a proper time for silence before mysteries beyond human understanding.
claims.quote: In conclusion, there is 'a time to be silent' in the face of mysteries beyond our grasp,

claims.text: Chekhov's theatre functions as a metaphysical space staging philosophical and theological themes of mortality, transcendence, and human agency.
claims.quote: This research contributes to the broader discourse on religious philosophy and dramatic arts, arguing that Chekhov’s theatre functions as a metaphysical space where philosophical and theological themes—such as the confrontation with mortality, the longing for transcendence, and the ethical dilemmas of human agency—are staged and explored.

claims.text: Habakkuk questions faith because God appears silent about injustice in Judah.
claims.quote: In general, we can see that in the first part of Habakkuk (1:1-2:4) the prophet questions the validity of his faith in God, because of the apparent long divine silence about injustice in Judah (1:2-4).

claims.text: Faith is the proper response while awaiting God’s solution to crisis.
claims.quote: After the prophet’s complaint (1:7-2:1), God advises him and his people to trust His solution in overcoming the crisis (2:2-4).

claims.text: The volume presents three kinds of intertextual readings of Lamentations.
claims.quote: Over against more bifurcated models of intertextual approaches—for example, "diachronic" versus "synchronic" studies or a "traditional" versus "postmodern" binary—T. and M. highlight three kinds of intertextual readings represented in the volume: (1) analyses of the historical relationship between texts (how Lamentations uses or is used by other traditions), (2) readerly responses to Lamentations (how pertinent intertexts selected by the reader uncover new meanings), and (3) canonical approaches (how Lamentations illumines and is illumined by the "sea of intertexts" constituted by the Jewish and Christian Scriptures).

claims.text: Justification by faith entails resisting anthropocentrism and nihilism, solidarity supporting justice, and humble but responsible political action.
claims.quote: He began with three brief comments on the significance and implications of the doctrine of justification by faith in the contemporary context of the globalizing world: specifically a) a source of moral obligation to resist anthropocentrism and nihilism; b) a sense of solidarity with all things that will support social and environmental justice; and c) an attitude toward good works that is both humble and responsible enough to commit itself to political action.

claims.text: Confucian doctrines of Heaven, sympathetic unity, and humble responsible good works provide resources for a contemporary theology of good works.
claims.quote: He continues with a turn to functional equivalents in Confucianism for insights in the construction of a theology of good works for today by examining the following: a) the doctrine of Heaven and its Dao and Li: b) the doctrine of the sympathetic unity of all things that brings together all things by ties of ren and shu; and c) a spirituality of good works that is humble but also responsible enough to do what the Dao of Heaven requires.

claims.text: Old Testament theology remains disputed regarding whether it exists and what form it should take.
claims.quote: There is an ongoing debate about whether something called "Old Testament theology" exists and, if it does, what it should look like.

claims.text: Kessler’s work follows the focused approach that examines how the Hebrew Bible presents divine character.
claims.quote: The work of K. is closer to this second conception of the field, and a large part of this latest volume examines when and why that character goes silent.

claims.text: Silence is not total and should be understood as changes in the biblical text’s soundscape, not merely sound’s presence or absence.
claims.quote: Silence is rarely, if ever, total, and K. understands it broadly. He is concerned with more than the presence or absence of sound; the book's primary interest is changes in the "soundscape" of the biblical text and what these changes signal.

claims.text: Pentecostals are often criticized for giving inadequate attention to Jesus’ life.
claims.quote: Though Pentecostals generally welcome the label "people of the Spirit," they often receive ridicule for inadequate attention to the life of Jesus.

claims.text: Pentecostals return to Jesus’ life as the exemplary Spirit-filled life to imitate and extend in the present world.
claims.quote: Yet they also return to the life of Jesus, the consummate exemplar for a Spirit-filled life; Pentecostals seek to imitate and extend the life and ministry of Jesus into the current world, and they do so as Christians filled with the Spirit of Jesus.

claims.text: Kierkegaard and Climacus affirm positive silence as both religious life’s beginning and goal, linking it to self, God, inner knowledge, and union with God.
claims.quote: I argue that both authors affirm the necessity of positive silence as both the beginning and goal of religious life and a learned practice that can be distinguished from potentially harmful forms of silence, that it is linked to the nature of self and God, and leads to inner knowledge and unitive experience with God.

claims.text: Their shared Christian language of silence has distinct emphases concerning attaining silence, divine silence, guidance, and asceticism.
claims.quote: The authors speak a common "language of silence" which is inherited from the ongoing conversation on contemplative silence in Christianity, but their respective emphases reveal two distinct accents: they differ in their advice on how to acquire silence, how closely one can approach divine silence, whether one can look to others for guidance, and the nature and role of asceticism in cultivating silence.

claims.text: The Society of Free Quakers was animated by the principle that individuals should hold their sentiments without censure or attack.
claims.quote: The movement's primary founder, Samuel Wetherill, once proclaimed that the grand "principle" which animated the religious association "was that every man should enjoy his sentiments without being censured at smote at."

claims.text: Hannah’s pregnancy is secondary evidence of her healing from sadness and distress, rather than the story’s central point.
claims.quote: For me, the crux of the story is not that Hannah is granted a child, but that she is healed of her bitter sadness and distress. Her pregnancy is simply a secondary sign of her being healed.

claims.text: Second Isaiah’s divine voice answers Lamentations’ appeals by breaking the divine silence found there.
claims.quote: She urges that Second Isaiah’s emphasis on the divine voice constitutes a structural reinforcement of such allusions and reveals its intention to be an answer to Lamentations’ appeals that breaks the divine silence in that text.

claims.text: Spiritual and psychological visions are important because they restore the sacredness of a disenchanted world.

claims.text: The perfect human has precedence over angels because that person possesses all divine names.

claims.text: God’s kenosis is an essential key to loving union with God according to John of the Cross’s spirituality.
claims.quote: la necesidad de crear un sentido particular de la kenosis de Dios como clave esencial para llegar a la union amorosa con Dios; un camino que Juan de la Cruz trazo a lo largo de su espiritualidad.

claims.text: The Sadducees’ problem assumes that life in the world to come is fully continuous with present life.
claims.quote: The assumption, of course, is that the life of the world to come is fully continuous with the life of the present.

claims.text: Those worthy of resurrection neither marry nor die, because they are equal to angels and children of God.
claims.quote: The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. (20.34–6)

claims.text: Jesse’s visualization of his daughter’s possible suffering is solidarity and love rather than masochism.

claims.text: Facing the brutal truth about Becca becomes integral to Jesse’s piety and worship.

claims.text: God’s hiddenness challenges theism because an omnipotent and morally good God could make God’s existence and nature known.
claims.quote: Surely it is well within the abilities of God to let God's existence and nature be known to us. Why isn't the existence and nature of our Heavenly Father as apparent as, say, the existence of our various earthly fathers?

claims.text: The question is whether theists can plausibly explain why God’s existence and nature are hidden.
claims.quote: How can theists explain God's hiddenness, and how plausible are their explanations?

claims.text: If God is omnipotent, God has the power to reveal his existence with enough clarity to eliminate doubt.
claims.quote: For if God is omnipotent, as the tradition maintains, it seems that he would have the power to reveal himself to us and, for that matter, with sufficient clarity that we would be left with no doubt about the matter.

claims.text: If God wants people to accept his existence and reject false idols, God has a significant reason to reveal himself.
claims.quote: And if, as the tradition maintains further, it is important to God that we accept his existence and reject false idols who would pretend to divine status, it would seem that he has a significant reason to reveal himself to us.

claims.text: God's hiddenness is puzzling if God can make his existence obvious and doing so would serve an important purpose.
claims.quote: In short, given that God can make his existence obvious to all, and that doing so would fulfil an important purpose, why does he remain hidden from us?

claims.text: Given divine omnipresence, God is hidden only by withholding unmistakable signs and wonders of his existence from most people.
claims.quote: Consideration of the implications of the omnipresence of God shows that there can be only one sense in which God is ‘hidden’: he does not present human beings with (or at least presents very few of them with) unmistakable evidence of his existence in the form of ‘signs and wonders’.

claims.text: The chapter offers a response to the hiddenness argument parallel to its response to the global argument from evil.
claims.quote: This chapter presents a response to this argument that is parallel to the response to the global argument from evil in Chapters 4 and 5.

claims.text: The world's religious ambiguity permits reasonable secular interpretations as well as interpretations from several religious traditions.
claims.quote: Since the world is religiously ambiguous, it may reasonably be interpreted either in secular terms or in terms provided by any one of a number of religious traditions.

claims.text: Some theistic accounts maintain that the benefits of divine hiddenness outweigh the benefits of clearer knowledge of God.
claims.quote: Theists have made many attempts to account for God's hiddenness, some of which contend that the advantages of God's hiddenness (“goods of mystery”) outweigh whatever benefits would result if God's existence and nature were clear to us (“goods of clarity”).

claims.text: Other theistic accounts explain divine hiddenness by appealing to human defectiveness or divine transcendence.

claims.text: If mystery's goods outweigh clarity's goods, no particular good of clarity, including more immediate theistic belief, is likely very important.

claims.text: Theists should deny that holding theistic beliefs here and now is likely part of human life's goal.

claims.text: If essential human flourishing depended on present belief in God, God would provide more evidence and would not remain hidden.

claims.text: Schellenberg argues that a perfectly loving God would ensure sufficient evidence for nonresistant people capable of believing, but such evidence is unavailable, so no perfectly loving God exists.

claims.text: Edwards accepts Schellenberg's first two premises but denies the premise that sufficient evidence is unavailable.

claims.text: Edwards holds that intrinsically clear and compelling evidence is available, but sin blinds people to its force.

claims.text: Heidegger adopted Lutheran hidden-God themes, which later post-theological continental thinkers misappropriated.

claims.text: Luther's philosophical relevance lies in integrating the hidden-God theme into his wider theology and historical context, rather than adopting Heideggerian revisionist readings.
claims.quote: Finally, I will propose that the appreciation of Luther’s legacy and his relevance for philosophy lies not in popular ‘Heideggerian’ revisionist readings of the reformer but, alternatively, through integrating the Deus absconditus theme into the rest of his theological thought, including his historical context.

claims.text: God's hidden yet multifaceted presence creates narrative space for dramatic development and interpretative exploration in cinematic flood retellings.

claims.text: God's hiddenness and presence make the narrative more compatible with contemporary enlightened and postmodern sensibilities.

claims.text: Game theory can be used in attempts to solve aspects of the problem of divine hiddenness.

claims.text: A game-theoretic approach may improve modern biblical hermeneutics.

claims.text: Formulating philosophical ideas in simple monotheistic terms as ordinary believers understand them comes at a cost.
