claims.quote: his criticism aimed particularly against a faction of educated members who regarded their knowledge as evidence of social superiority.

claims.text: Paul countered superiority claims by distinguishing worldly wisdom from God’s secret wisdom.
claims.quote: He countered these types of claims to superiority by proposing a dichotomy of wisdoms—“the wisdom of this world” and “God's wisdom”:

claims.text: God’s absence and hiddenness prevent direct access to God and direct people toward their neighbors.
claims.quote: The absence and hidden of God renders that people cannot access to God and have to go to the neighbor,i.e.,the other.

claims.text: Responsibility toward one’s neighbor is the detour to God, making ethics the first theology.
claims.quote: Therefore,the relation with the neighbor,that is,the responsibility,becomes the detour to the God.Thus ethics is the first theology.

claims.text: Levinas emphasizes independently undertaking responsibility for the other without relying on God.
claims.quote: He lays emphasis on undertaking responsibility for the other independently and no relying on God.

claims.text: With God’s grace, the speakers will become rulers.
claims.quote: With His grace we shall become rulers.

claims.text: Psalm 44 emphasizes righteous suffering and anguish at God’s apparent hiddenness.
claims.quote: Psalm 44 underscores the suffering of the righteous and their anguish when faced with the apparent hiddenness of God.

claims.text: Paul uses Psalm 44 typologically to portray Christ as fulfilling the psalmist’s plea and grounding God’s faithfulness amid suffering.
claims.quote: I will argue that Paul uses Ps 44 typologically to depict Christ as the fulfilment of the psalmist’s plea, establishing the ground for God’s faithfulness, the inseparability between God and His people, and the ultimate victory even through temporal sufferings.

claims.text: Arnauld’s conception of God is more radical than scholars have generally allowed.
claims.quote: In this paper, I argue that Arnauld’s conception of God is more radical than scholars have been willing to allow.

claims.text: Arnauld rejects not only transparent divine wisdom but also the distinction between divine will and wisdom, even if wisdom is hidden.
claims.quote: Arnauld’s objections to Malebranche are directed not only at the claim that God’s wisdom is transparent to human reason, but at the whole distinction between will and wisdom in God, even if that wisdom were “hidden.”

claims.text: Arnauld’s God approaches Descartes’s extreme voluntarist God and transcends practical rational agency.
claims.quote: Arnauld’s God, in fact, approaches the extreme voluntarist God of Descartes, and thus transcends practical rational agency altogether.

claims.text: The nameless and hidden Jewish God appears to support Jesi’s study of religious belief without presupposing God’s existence.
claims.quote: Being nameless and hidden, the God of the Jews seems also to legitimize and justify Jesi's attempt to develop his research on religious beliefs without assuming the existence of a god.

claims.text: Rabbi Shapira explores God’s hiddenness to support perseverance under the dreadful conditions of the Warsaw Ghetto.
claims.quote: Based on studies of the Hebrew Bible and the Jewish tradition, the Hasidic rabbi explores the problem of God’s hiddenness in order to support perseverance in this dreadful environment.

claims.text: Shapira’s concepts of divine hiddenness are theologically focused on the unity of God and God’s people.
claims.quote: These concepts find their theological focus in the unity of God and his people.

claims.text: Genuine transformation occurs only through being drawn into sacred liminal space.
claims.quote: Richard Rohr suggests that the only way out of a person's entrapment in "normalcy, the way things are," is to be drawn into sacred space, often called liminality, where he believes all genuine transformation occurs.

claims.text: Liminality is an in-between state in which the old world has been left but the future has not yet arrived.
claims.quote: Liminality, from the Latin word for threshold, is the state of being betwixt and between where the old world has been left behind but we have not yet arrived at what is to come.

claims.text: Liminal times present both God’s apparent hiddenness and an opportunity to see God in new ways.
claims.quote: It seeks to reconcile the paradox of the apparent hiddenness of God and the concurrent opportunity to see Him in new ways that occurs in these times.

claims.text: Psalm 69:18 expressly refers to the hiddenness of God’s face.
claims.quote: One of the Psalm texts which expressis verbis refer to the hiddenness of the face of God is Psalm 69; and specifically Psalm 69:18.

claims.text: The Psalm 69 scribes or theologians experienced desolation and divine hiddenness, giving witness to their isolation.
claims.quote: They laboured under the plight of their feeling of isolation. They therefore gave witness of the feeling of the hiddenness of God.

claims.text: God’s hiddenness has traditionally meant that finite creatures face an inescapably mysterious, transcendent Creator.
claims.quote: Usually, though not always, God has been seen as ‘hidden’ in the sense that the inherent gulf between the finite creatures and the infinite Creator has made God inescapably mysterious, Wholly Other, transcendent of our puny grasp.

claims.text: Divine hiddenness does not make knowledge of God impossible, but makes it necessarily limited and enigmatic.
claims.quote: To say that God is hidden has not been to say that we could not know of God, but to insist that what we know of God is necessarily limited and enigmatic.

claims.text: Seven identified areas, including God’s hiddenness, are crucial to developing a contemporary Christian doctrine of salvation.
claims.quote: The ‘shape’ of salvation is presented as an exposition of what one is saved from and for, by whom/what one is saved, and what one is saved into. In filling in this ‘template’ the seven areas which need exploring are: a broad definition of sin; the affective dimension of salvation; salvation is a present (and not just a post-death) experience; whether human action contributes to the experience of salvation; social salvation; institutional forms of social salvation; the hiddenness of God.

claims.text: For Luther, God is hidden from unbelievers, who require the law, gospel, and Holy Spirit to know God properly.
claims.quote: For Luther, God is hidden, firstly, from unbelievers. In order to know God properly, sinners should learn properly the law and the gospel with the help of the Holy Spirit.

claims.text: God is hidden from theologians of glory, so believers need a theology of the cross to reveal and overcome sin.
claims.quote: Secondly, God is hidden from theologians of glory who pursue God in their sinful desires. Believers should have theology of the cross that reveals and overcomes their sins.

claims.text: Because God remains hidden even from true believers, every believer should cling to Christ as God’s revelation amid existential crises.
claims.quote: Thirdly, God is hidden even from all true believers. Every believer should hold tight to Christ the revelation of God, experiencing existential crises in this world.

claims.text: The testing and fear motifs in Genesis and Exodus are not yet linked to a Deuteronomistic understanding of law.
claims.quote: In Gen 22:1, 12 and Exod 20:20 the motifs „testing by God“ and „fear of God“ are not yet connected with a Deuteronomistic understanding of the law, as they are in Deut 5:29; 8:2-3.

claims.text: Moses is presented as a prophet leading Israel from Egypt rather than as a lawgiver.
claims.quote: Further, Moses is not yet understood as a lawgiver but as a prophet, who leads Israel out of Egypt (cf. Hos 12:14).

claims.text: The relevant Genesis and Exodus passages derive from northern Israelite judgment-prophecy circles rather than the post-exilic period.
claims.quote: Gen 22:1-14*, 19 and Exod 20:18-21 should, therefore, not be dated in the post-exilic period, but go back to circles that transmitted northern Israelite judgement prophecy (cf. the concept of the hiddenness of God in Gen 20-22*).

claims.text: Waltraut Stein’s characterization of Edith Stein as hidden in a convent and in God is only partially true.
claims.quote: This statement is only partially true.

claims.text: Although cloistered, Stein directly responded to Nazism through her convent writings and died for that revelation.
claims.quote: For while Stein spent the last decade of her life cloistered, to her mind she was responding to the “conagration” in the most direct way she knew how: she came out of “hiding” by way of the words she wrote from the convent, and she paid for this revelation with her life.

claims.text: Contemporary political and social oppression is undergirded by the logic of identity.
claims.quote: the author utilizes the work of the political philosopher Iris Marion Young, who argues that contemporary forms of political and social oppression are undergirded by “the logic of identity.”

claims.text: Luther’s theology supplies grounds for theological and ethical resistance to these forms of oppression.
claims.quote: the article contends that Luther’s theology provides ground for theological and ethical resistance to these forms of oppression.

claims.text: Luther’s theology of the cross, justification, and hiddenness of God constitute elements of a theology of otherness.
claims.quote: the author gives a detailed reading of three elements of the Reformer’s theology—Luther’s theology of the cross, Luther’s doctrine of justification, and Luther’s notion of the hiddenness of God—as three elements of a theology of otherness.

claims.text: The proposed reading construes Esther as a product of Diaspora Judaism.
claims.quote: The first and most important premise for the reading of the book of Esther proposed in this chapter is to construe it as a product of Diaspora Judaism.

claims.text: Postcolonial and ritual concepts highlight the narrative Jews’ struggle to maintain religious and ethnic identity against others.
claims.quote: Concepts from postcolonial studies and ritual theory (specifically ritualization) are employed in order to highlight the struggle of the “Jews” in the narrative to maintain their religious and ethnic identity vis-à-vis “others” from within and without.

claims.text: Gendered interactions function as identification, representation, and embodiment for the suppressed or marginalized group as a whole.
claims.quote: The reading is supplemented by insights from gender studies, approaching the various interactions between male and female protagonists not simply as the struggle between the sexes, but more broadly, as a means of identification, representation, and embodiment for the suppressed or marginalized group as a whole.

claims.text: Traditional Judaic obligations of female presence and the Shekhinah's accompanying Israel into exile contradict post-Holocaust theologies of divine absence.
claims.quote: But traditional Judaic obligations of female presence, together with the traditional image of the Shekhinah as a figure of God's 'femaleness' accompanying Israel into exile, seem to contradict such theologies of absence.

claims.text: God was revealed at Auschwitz through women’s morally protesting material and spiritual care for assaulted others.
claims.quote: God's face, says Melissa Raphael, was not hidden in Auschwitz, but intimately revealed in the female face turned towards the other as a refractive image of God, especially in the moral protest made visible through material and spiritual care for the assaulted other.

claims.text: Montessori’s metaphysics and moral philosophy do not depend on God's existence, though theism may enrich them.
claims.quote: It then shows how neither her metaphysics nor her moral philosophy depend on God’s existence, even as both make room for being enriched by theism.

claims.text: Religion is essentially embodied practice, supporting a philosophy of religious practice.
claims.quote: Finally, it emphasizes Montessori’s notion that religion is essentially an embodied form of life, showing how this should support a turn toward a philosophy of religious practice.

claims.text: Religious ambiguity and the lack of an adequate explanation for it suggest that belief in God is unimportant even if God exists.
claims.quote: The extent of the ambiguity that surrounds God's existence, and indeed all important religious matters, combined with our lack of an obviously correct and adequate explanation of this lack, suggest that, even if God exists, it is not important that people believe in God.

claims.text: Religious diversity gives adherents reason to critically scrutinize and tentatively hold their beliefs.
claims.quote: The character of this diversity is such that it provides people who take a position on religious matters with reason to adopt the “Critical Stance” – which requires people in all the religious traditions to subject their religious beliefs to critical scrutiny and hold those beliefs in a tentative way.

claims.text: Tentative belief can sustain many forms of religious commitment despite claims that faith requires complete confidence.
claims.quote: Some contend that religious faith requires complete confidence in what is believed but tentative belief actually is sufficient to sustain many forms of religious commitment.

claims.text: Seventeenth-century Lutheran writers emphasized continuous divine care amid tribulations, which call believers to repentance.
claims.quote: They affirmed the fundamental goodness of creation and extended the doctrine of creation into a strong emphasis on God’s creatio continua, his providing care in the midst of tribulations that serve to call believers to repentance.

claims.text: Lutheran dogmaticians attempted explanations defending God against the charge that he causes evil.
claims.quote: Although the Lutheran dogmaticians tried to avoid detailed theodical argument they did attempt explanations that defended God from the charge that he causes evil.

claims.text: A modified Christian dualism can be applied to the natural world.
claims.quote: The chapter then argues that a modified Christian dualism can be applied also to the natural world.

claims.text: Animal suffering belongs to a corrupted world that will eventually be overcome.
claims.quote: If the world is inexplicably both good and bad, perfect and corrupted, and telling these apart is often fraught, then animal suffering can be understood in the same way that human suffering is, as a part of a corrupted world which will eventually be overcome.

claims.text: Divine transcendence makes all theological speech intrinsically limited, and sin makes those limits especially salient.
claims.quote: While the confession of divine transcendence entails that all theological speech faces intrinsic limits, the problem of sin brings theology’s limits into focus in a very particular way.

claims.text: Christians do not claim that Christ’s unique revelation explains sin’s place in the divine economy.
claims.quote: insofar as they do not claim that even this revelation explains the place of sin in the divine economy, the ongoing mystery of sin and evil presents the theologian with a stark alternative.

claims.text: Theologians face a tension between emphasizing grace revealed in Christ and emphasizing sin hidden in God.
claims.quote: On the one hand, if the grace of God revealed in Christ is emphasized, less attention will be given to the mystery of sin that remains hidden in God; on the other, if theologians emphasize what is hidden, the light of Christ will be obscured.

claims.text: In Hermetic thought, unaided intellect cannot grasp true notions of God and needs a teacher’s assistance.
claims.quote: True notions of god, are hidden to the unaided intellect in the Hermetic scheme, and the assistance of a teacher is necessary for attaining any knowledge of the divine.

claims.text: Hermetic God is concealed from the uninitiated but progressively revealed through study and contemplation guided by a master.
claims.quote: God is considered completely concealed from the uninitiated, and progressively less hidden the further a Hermetic pupil would pursue his study. A god, who is simultaneously everywhere and nowhere is almost by definition hidden from normal perception, and according to Hermetic beliefs, must be revealed through diligent study and divine contemplation, as instructed by a master.

claims.text: Human experience and belief are embodied and conditioned by intentional practices such as prayer, liturgy, ritual, and charismatic activities.
claims.quote: Human experience and belief are embodied and as such are conditioned by intentional practices: for example, in daily prayer, liturgy, ritual, and charismatic activities.

claims.text: Cognitive science of religion and neurobiology suggest that the brain is malleable and changes in response to lived experience.
claims.quote: Research in cognitive science of religion and neurobiology suggests that the brain is essentially malleable, constantly changing in response to lived experience.

claims.text: Scientifically informed tools can deepen understanding of embodied human participation in divine presence and absence.
claims.quote: This article argues for the possibility of using scientifically‐informed tools to work with psychological and neurobiological realities to provide a deeper understanding of the cooperative, participatory nature of our embodied human engagement with Divine presence and absence.

claims.text: True theology is revelatory rather than speculative.
claims.quote: the theology of the cross teaches us that true theology must be a theology of revelation that stands in sharp contrast to speculation;

claims.text: God’s hidden revelation dismantles fallen preconceptions, thereby humbling and correcting human knowledge of God.
claims.quote: God’s revelation and workings are hidden under their opposite, and this hiddenness of God breaks down all our fallen human preconceptions of God, makes us humble, expands and corrects our knowledge of God, and helps us to have confidence in our knowledge of God;

claims.text: For Luther, knowing God is salvific rather than merely theoretical: it is being loved by God.
claims.quote: for Luther, the knowledge of God is not merely theoretical knowledge but rather a matter of salvation: to know God is to be loved by God.

claims.text: According to Ibn Arabi, the human heart is humanity’s true essence and manifests God’s attributes.
claims.quote: The truth of Human being according to Ibn Arabī is heart (qalb) that enslaves all man's inner and outer potentialities. Heart is the perfect manifestation of God with all its attributes, such as the First and the Last, the Apparent and the Hidden.

claims.text: Because God is limitless, the heart likewise has neither limits nor a true definition.
claims.quote: As God has no limits, heart also has no limitation and true definition.

claims.text: Isaiah 45:15 depicts a God who hides himself, rather than a passively hidden God.
claims.quote: The main point lies with reading the often misunderstood text of Is 45:15, where the verb satar is used, not in the passive form, i.e. the hidden God, rather in the reflexive form, i.e. a God who hides Himself.

claims.text: Knowledge that God is hiding depends upon God’s revelation.
claims.quote: If we know that He is actually hiding, it is because of His revelation.

claims.text: Readers have treated Shakespeare’s avoidance of explicit divine allegiance as choosing aesthetics over theology.
claims.quote: While many readers have taken this avoidance as an opting for aesthetics over theology,

claims.text: God’s hiddenness in Shakespeare heightens theological tension rather than eliminating it.
claims.quote: this introductory chapter argues that the opposite is in fact the case: the hiddenness of “God” serves to heighten rather than expel theological tension.

claims.text: God’s absence can be interpreted as an unstaged presence through theological categories including providence, transcendence, repetition, and excess.
claims.quote: Using some of the most suggestive work in contemporary theology, this chapter develops the interpretive categories of pressurized providence, non-competitive transcendence, repetition, and excess as keys to reading the absence of God as an “unstaged” presence.

claims.text: Readers have treated Shakespeare’s avoidance of explicit divine allegiance as choosing aesthetics over theology.
claims.quote: While many readers have taken this avoidance as an opting for aesthetics over theology,

claims.text: God’s hiddenness in Shakespeare heightens theological tension rather than eliminating it.
claims.quote: this introductory chapter argues that the opposite is in fact the case: the hiddenness of “God” serves to heighten rather than expel theological tension.

claims.text: God’s absence can be interpreted as an unstaged presence through theological categories including providence, transcendence, repetition, and excess.
claims.quote: Using some of the most suggestive work in contemporary theology, this chapter develops the interpretive categories of pressurized providence, non-competitive transcendence, repetition, and excess, as keys to reading the absence of God as an “unstaged” presence.

claims.text: Scholars often characterize Clement as an esoteric author who used miscellany to conceal teachings selectively.
claims.quote: Clement’s motif of concealment has often led scholars to describe him as an ‘esoteric author,’ who chose the miscellany genre in order to hide some things from some people, in imitation of scriptural concealment by aenigma.

claims.text: Clement’s esoteric tropes instead foreground a widespread discourse of hiddenness grounded in God’s hiddenness.
claims.quote: This chapter begins to respond by arguing that Clement’s esoteric tropes draw attention to the theme of hiddenness , which is a widespread imagistic discourse in his work. Five major modes of hiddenness are discerned in Clement’s theology: theological, anthropological, exegetical, social and cosmic; in practice, all of these are grounded in the hiddenness of God.

claims.text: Miscellanism is the necessary and normative form of gnostic life.
claims.quote: Miscellanism emerges as the necessary and normative mode of gnostic life.

claims.text: Rea holds that God authorizes and validates lament and protest, including impious protest arising from negative responses to apparent injustice.
claims.quote: In The Hiddenness of God, Rea defended the view that God authorizes and validates lament and protest from human beings—including impious protest, which emerges from outright anger, sorrow, or other negative emotions in response to apparent divine injustice.

claims.text: Authorizing impious protest appears incompatible with the universal duty to worship God.
claims.quote: But this view apparently stands in tension with widespread assumptions about worship and prayer. In particular, it is hard to see how God can authorize and validate impious protest if it is always true that everyone ought to worship God;

claims.text: Impious protest may be defective prayer that God should neither authorize nor validate.
claims.quote: it is also tempting to think that impious protest is an instance of what Lauren Winner calls the ‘characteristic deformation of prayer’, which, in turn, suggests that it is defective prayer that should neither be authorized nor validated by God.

claims.text: Any physical system’s total state is governed by all its foundational components, whether or not they are observable.
claims.quote: We assert that the total state of any physical systemis governed by its complete set of foundational components, regardless of their observational status.

claims.text: The infinite product of unobservable hidden variables collapses into a stable finite constant.
claims.quote: we demonstrate that the infinite product of unobservable “hidden variables”naturally collapses into a stable, finite constant.

claims.text: The Observer Unity Identity establishes that observer and system form one continuous mechanism.
claims.quote: This validates the Observer Unity Identity (CObs = 1), proving that the observer and the system are a single, continuous mechanism.

claims.text: Luther offers a framework that confronts evil, affirms God’s goodness, and values creation’s multiplicity.
claims.quote: This dissertation argues that Martin Luther provides a framework for contemplating evil in its diverse manifestations, offers a profound account of faith in the goodness of God, and also affirms and rejoices in the multiplicity of values in creation.

claims.text: Luther holds these positions together through the dialectical interrelationship of faith, creation and justification, and sin and evil.
claims.quote: Luther's ability to hold these positions in tension depends on the dialectical interrelationship between three concepts: first, a new concept of faith grounded in the promise of God; second, a theological distinction between creation and justification in which creation maintains its own integrity against distinctively Christian claims about justification; third, a concept of sin and evil based on both the lived experience of evil and theological reflections on the depth of sin and the hiddenness of God.

claims.text: The interplay of these concepts permits Luther to face evil while retaining faith in God’s incomprehensible goodness.
claims.quote: The interplay of these three concepts allows Luther to confront the horrors of evil while maintaining a profound faith in God's goodness, even beyond human comprehension.

claims.text: Pascal argues that non-believers should investigate Christianity from self-interest.
claims.quote: Pascal argues that the non-believer should, as a matter of sheer self-interest, seek for God; that is, in the first instance, investigate the truth-claims of Christianity.

claims.text: Pascal replies that atheists dismiss Christianity because they misunderstand its claims about God’s hiddenness.
claims.quote: Atheists’ dismissal of these claims, he argues, rests on a misunderstanding of the claims themselves.

claims.text: Pascal’s probability theory supports seeking God despite divine hiddenness.
claims.quote: Although God is hidden, it is in our interest to seek for him, as Pascal explains on the basis of his theory of probability.

claims.text: Previous explanations of the Son of Man’s preexistence are inadequate, though Psalms 72 and Isaiah 49 retain limited validity.
claims.quote: I discuss these three proposals, rejecting the first entirely and suggesting that the latter two have some validity but fall short of explaining the key reason behind the Son of Man’s pre-creation existence.

claims.text: Isaiah 51:16 is the most important scriptural source for the Son of Man’s pre-creation existence.
claims.quote: I then propose that the most important scriptural source for this idea is Isa 51:16, which has a syntactical ambiguity that allows it to be read as describing a figure hidden by God before the creation of the world.

claims.text: Isaiah 51:16 and Isaiah 49:2 were combined in Enoch to portray the Son of Man as preexistent.
claims.quote: This verse shares significant parallels with Isa 49:2, and these texts were combined in 1 En. 48:6 and 62:7 in order to depict the Son of Man as a preexistent figure.

claims.text: Podmore proposes a Kierkegaardian theology of spiritual trial centered on the self’s kenosis before God.
claims.quote: Podmore proposes a Kierkegaardian theology of spiritual trial that elaborates the kenosis of the self before God in terms of Spirit's restless longing to rest transparently in God.

claims.text: The book rehabilitates spiritual trial to renew theological interpretation of human struggle amid spiritual darkness.
claims.quote: Offering an original rehabilitation of the temptation of spiritual trial, this book strives for a renewed theological hermeneutic that speaks to the enduring human struggle to realise the unchanging love of God in the face of spiritual darkness.

claims.text: Theistic philosophers have not ruled out alternative monotheisms or shown them less probable than classical theism.
claims.quote: We find that theistic philosophers have not successfully eliminated these and other possibilities, or argued for their relative improbability.

claims.text: Current evidence about divine hiddenness and gratuitous evil makes many alternative god hypotheses more probable than theism.
claims.quote: In fact, based on current evidence – especially concerning the hiddenness of God and the gratuitous evils in the world – many of these hypotheses appear to be more probable than theism.

claims.text: Given infinitely many alternative monotheisms, classical theism is a very improbable conception of God.
claims.quote: Also considering the – arguably infinite – number of alternative monotheisms, the inescapable conclusion is that theism is a very improbable god-concept, even when it is assumed that one and only one transcendent god exists.

claims.text: The paper examines divine hiddenness and human incompleteness in Oscar and Lucinda through Pascal’s wager.
claims.quote: This paper aims to examine the hiddenness of God and the incompleteness of a man in Peter Carey’s Oscar and Lucinda in light of Blaise Pascal’s concept of wager.

claims.text: Pascal argues that people should believe in, serve, and respect God despite their wretched and corrupt condition.
claims.quote: Pascal argues that, despite his condition of wretchedness and corruption, he should be convinced that God exists, he is saved by God, and thereby he respects and serves God with all his heart.

claims.text: Oscar is portrayed as weak and imperfect because he knows God without recognizing his own wretchedness.
claims.quote: With this approach, Oscar is shown as a weak and imperfect man who knows God without realizing his condition of wretchedness, by sinking himself encaged inside of the glass church.

claims.text: Joy indicates closeness to God and directs even sinners toward goodness, whereas evil produces heaviness and despair.
claims.quote: Joy, even in sinners, shows closeness to God and leads toward goodness. Evil is marked by heaviness, despair, anything blocking liveliness.

claims.text: Kierkegaard challenges Schellenberg's claim that awareness of God's accepting presence is the best basis for a mutual relationship with God.
claims.quote: One can, i.e. suppose that Kierkegaard would cast doubt on Schellenberg’s claim that the best evidence allowing the development of a mutual relationship between God and the human being is an experience of an accepting presence of God in human consciousness.

claims.text: Only God's hiddenness can secure a free and selfless relationship between humans and God.
claims.quote: Kierkegaard argues in his works that only the hiddenness of God guarantees a free and a selfless relationship between men and God.

claims.text: Podmore proposes a Kierkegaardian theology in which spiritual trial involves the self's kenosis and Spirit's longing to rest transparently in God.
claims.quote: Podmore proposes a Kierkegaardian theology of spiritual trial that elaborates the kenosis of the self before God in terms of Spirit's restless longing to rest transparently in God.

claims.text: The book rehabilitates spiritual trial to develop a theological interpretation of human struggle to realize God's unchanging love amid spiritual darkness.
claims.quote: Offering an original rehabilitation of the temptation of spiritual trial, this book strives for a renewed theological hermeneutic that speaks to the enduring human struggle to realise the unchanging love of God in the face of spiritual darkness.

claims.text: In the Hebrew Bible, fertility is ultimately controlled by God and forms an important element of the relationship between God and humanity.
claims.quote: From the perspective of the Hebrew Bible, fertility is ultimately controlled by God and is one important element in the relationship between God and humanity.

claims.text: Psalm 139 presents conception and prenatal growth as God's creative work, which is not hidden from God.
claims.quote: The Psalmist recognizes that conception and growth even before birth are part of the creative work of God. The phrase within the earth is a parallel to the growth deep within the body of the mother, but this growth is not hidden from God.

claims.quote: This paper introduces the Fifth Law of Thermodynamics, or the Law of Observational Completeness, which asserts that the total state of any physical system is governed by its complete set of foundational components, regardless of their observational status.

claims.quote: By applying the Geometric Harmonic of 9 to the Brook Density Identity and integrating with Euler’s Number (e), we demonstrate that the infinite product of unobservable “hidden variables” naturally collapses into a stable, finite constant (0.949).

claims.text: Contemplating Christ's suffering cannot transform him because it leads to self-pity and pleasure rather than compassion.

claims.text: Easter's message is salvation through absence rather than pain.

claims.text: Christ's redemptive resurrection ensures eternal glory and life for those called to faith.
claims.quote: Jesus Christ, as man, both continues our original humanness as those made “from the void,” while yet ensuring in His redemptive resurrected life, eternal glory and life for those so called to this destiny of faith.

claims.text: Exodus xxiv 9-11 is an independent and distinctive theophany tradition rather than a covenant tradition.
claims.quote: The tradition in Exodus xxiv 9-11 neither knows of nor implies the existence of a covenant between Israel and 'the God of Israel'. It is a theophany tradition.

claims.text: “They ate and drank” means that witnesses rejoiced or worshipped in God’s presence after the manifestation.
claims.quote: the expression at its conclusion, 'they ate and drank', is best understood, as in other cultic contexts in the Old Testament, as meaning that those who experienced this remarkable manifestation of God 'rejoiced' or 'worshipped' in the presence of God.

claims.text: The tradition lacks standard Sinai theophany features and substantially reduces Moses’s role.
claims.quote: This theophany tradition is unique among and independent of other theophany traditions contained elsewhere in the Sinai narrative: it knows nothing of the mountain of the theophany being enwrapped in cloud, smoke, etc.; though it implies that the usual consequences of seeing God were fatal (verse 11a), it states in the most direct manner that a delegation of Israel's ancestors saw God, whereas in other theophany traditions in the Sinai narrative the hiddenness of God from human view is emphasised; finally, the figure of Moses in this tradition is strikingly 'reduced' when compared with the dominating role he plays in other theophany traditions.

claims.text: Kierkegaard’s apophaticism developed independently of classical apophatic theology.
claims.quote: The present article argues for the first approach by providing a survey of the apophatic motifs of Kierkegaard’s authorship organized around the notions of “objective apophaticism” and “subjective apophaticism.”

claims.text: God is hidden both by transcendence and by human existential misalignment.
claims.quote: It is not only God’s transcendent nature that conceals God from human beings but also the “existential misalignment” of human beings.

claims.text: Kierkegaard’s apophatic strand is best categorized as existential apophaticism.
claims.quote: the article concludes with the claim that the apophatic strand in Kierkegaard’s authorship is best categorized as “existential apophaticism.”

claims.text: Aristotelian causality and epistemology reshaped medieval exegesis and elevated Scripture’s literal sense.
claims.quote: Aristotelian theory of causality encouraged exegetes to adopt a new type of prologue organized around the four main causes described by ‘the Philosopher’, an approach which encouraged new attitudes to such matters as authorship and authority, and literary style and structure. Aristotelian epistemology gave the human faculties and human perception a new dignity; late medieval scholars afforded the ‘body’ of Scripture, its literal sense, a corresponding dignity.

claims.text: Late medieval semantics located biblical meaning in the literal sense expressed by human authors.
claims.quote: Meaning was no longer believed (as in twelfth-century exegesis) to have been hidden by God deep in the biblical text; rather it was expressed in the literal sense by the human authors of Scripture, each in his own way or ways.

claims.text: Luther uses masks to explain how the hidden God accomplishes plans in believers’ lives.
claims.quote: Luther depended greatly on the concept of masks to explain how the hidden God works out His plans in the lives of His people.

claims.text: Luther’s doctrine of the hidden God is practical, pastoral, and helpful amid life’s trials.
claims.quote: This paper then concludes with the proposition that Luther's hidden God was meant to be practical and has much to offer us in the trials of life.

claims.text: The New Testament deconstructs rather than reinforces retributive punishment.
claims.quote: Continuing this argument I shall try to show that the New Testament, far from underscoring retributivism, actually deconstructs it.

claims.quote: The story of the crucifixion, I have argued, plays an indisputably important role in shaping the mentalities and sensibilities of Western culture. As such it has also helped shape Western attitudes to the punishment of offenders.

claims.text: Christians often treat the cross’s meaning as self-evident, overlooking learned interpretive frameworks.
claims.quote: For many Christians the ‘meaning of the cross’ is simply selfevident. They do not reflect that they have been taught to understand it through hymns and paintings, and through the way it is described in the liturgy – ‘a full, perfect and sufficient sacrifice, oblation and satisfaction’.

claims.text: Vatican I holds that God can be known with certainty from created things through natural reason.
claims.quote: that God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason

claims.text: Catholic teaching distinguishes natural reason from divine faith and recognizes divinely revealed mysteries beyond reason.
claims.quote: The perpetual agreement of the catholic church has maintained and maintains this too: that there is a twofold order of knowledge, distinct not only as regards its source, but also as regards its object. With regard to the source, we know at the one level by natural reason, at the other level by divine faith.

claims.quote: It is only via the results obtained due to the phenomenological scrutiny over openness, hiddenness and existence that it becomes clear to what extent Schellenberg’s argument is founded upon solid grounds.

claims.text: The paper uses phenomenological descriptions of hiddenness, openness, and existence to assess Schellenberg’s argument.
claims.quote: The means to this end is a phenomenological description of hiddenness, openness and existence.

claims.text: Phenomenological insights make critical assessment of Schellenberg’s conception available.
claims.quote: It is only at this point; that is, on the fringes of the reflection supported by phenomenological insights, that the ways of critical assessment of Schellenberg’s conception become available.

claims.text: Spiritual perception is possible and can receive a constructive philosophical and theological account.
claims.quote: Perceiving Things Divine seeks to make philosophical and theological sense of spiritual perception. Reflecting the results of the second phase of the Spiritual Perception Project, this volume argues for the possibility of spiritual perception.

claims.text: Human brokenness can distort spiritual perception through dispositions such as pornographic sensibility and racist prejudice.
claims.quote: However, spiritual perception is often distorted due to the general brokenness of the human condition. The volume explores such distortions as pornographic sensibility and racist prejudice.

claims.text: Spiritual disciplines, virtues, sacramental life, and divine grace can purify, train, transform, and heal spiritual perception.
claims.quote: Since perceiving spiritually involves the whole person, the volume proposes that spiritual perception could be purified by ascetic discipline, healed by contemplative practices, trained in the process of spiritual direction and the pursuit of virtue, transformed by the immersion in the sacramental life, and healed by opening the self to the operation of divine grace.

claims.text: Belief in God cannot be understood without understanding what it means to become nothing before God.
claims.quote: The original title of the manuscript was “God as Nothing,” in which it was argued that we cannot understand belief in God without understanding what it means to become nothing before him.

claims.text: Early medieval belief in divine omniscience produced a distinctive ethics of secrecy and culture of scrutiny.
claims.quote: Looking to law codes and religious architecture, hagiographies and riddles, Bonds of Secrecy shows how legal and monastic institutions harnessed the pervasive and complex belief in God's omniscience to produce an intense culture of scrutiny and a radical ethics of secrecy founded on the individual's belief that nothing could be hidden from God.

claims.text: Concealing a secret from God was sinful, whereas concealing it from the world while submitting to divine observation could be virtuous.
claims.quote: In other words, to attempt to hide from God was to become ensnared in a serious sin, but to hide from the world while deliberately and humbly submitting to God's constant observation was often a hallmark of spiritual virtue.

claims.text: This ethics of secrecy shaped medieval conceptions of mind and literary interpretation in ways relevant to contemporary reading.
claims.quote: According to Saltzman, this ethics of secrecy not only informed early medieval notions of mental activity and ideas about the mind but also profoundly shaped the practices of literary interpretation in ways that can inform our own contemporary approaches to reading texts from the past.

claims.text: Traditional theism can withstand the traditional problem of evil by affirming law-governed nature and human free will.

claims.text: God's hiddenness creates a further problem of evil, and proposed explanations of its place in divine purposes fail.

claims.text: The appeal to a divine law written in human hearts faces cases where God's will remains uncertain.

claims.quote: Many of the interpretations arose from polemical concerns, whether political, ecclesiastical, or theological.

claims.text: The theological reception of Luther was, in many respects, a struggle for authority.
claims.quote: In many respects, the story of Luther’s theological reception is also a struggle for authority.

claims.text: The hiddenness of God gives no strong support to naturalism, but neither does the theist position establish a conclusive result.

claims.text: In the Hebrew Bible, fertility is ultimately controlled by God and is integral to the God-human relationship.

claims.text: Psalm 139 presents conception and prenatal growth as part of God's creative work.

claims.text: Each threshold enables an epiphany of the invisible through analogy of being and visualized verbal symbols.

claims.text: The Word becomes embodied by revealing itself as a visual sign-bearer.
claims.quote: Revealing itself as a visual sign-bearer, the Word acquires a body.

claims.text: Most studied narrations have continuous chains supported by other transmission lines that strengthen them.

claims.text: The hadith texts contain no irregularities or hidden defects and contradict neither scripture, stronger hadiths, reason, nor history.

claims.text: The evidential weight of reason, experience, testimony, and revelation depends on reliability, independence, alternatives, error, counterevidence, and defeaters.
claims.quote: Their evidential weight instead depends on reliability, conditional independence, alternative explanations, shared sources of error, counterevidence, and resilience to defeaters.

claims.text: Insufficient or balanced evidence permits suspension of judgment.
claims.quote: It permits suspension of judgment where the available evidence is insufficient or balanced.

claims.text: Unified Categorical Basis Panpsychism reconciles microphysical fundamentality with a unified divine categorical ground.
claims.quote: This paper develops a third option, Unified Categorical Basis Panpsychism (UCBP), which preserves the fundamentality of microphysical entities with respect to physical structure and composition while locating ultimate unity at the level of categorical grounding.

claims.text: A single irreducibly mental categorical basis explains physical dispositions and makes conscious experience possible.
claims.quote: The view openly posits a novel primitive: a single, irreducibly mental, internally differentiated categorical basis—identified with God—in virtue of which physical properties have the dispositional profiles they have and conscious experience is metaphysically possible.

claims.text: UCBP avoids the combination problem of micropsychism and the decomposition problem of cosmopsychism.
claims.quote: The paper argues that this posit is theoretically motivated, internally coherent, and explanatorily principled, and that UCBP thereby avoids both the combination problem facing micropsychism and the decomposition problem facing cosmopsychism.

claims.text: The coin-in-the-fish narrative is a specific Christological and providential event, not a general doctrine of supernatural financial provision.
claims.quote: The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision.

claims.text: Universalizing miracle money doctrinally lacks sufficient epistemic warrant and exceeds Matthew's hermeneutical intention.
claims.quote: It further argues that while belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant.

claims.text: Responsible theology must distinguish divine possibility from doctrinal normativity.
claims.quote: The study concludes that responsible theological reflection requires a careful distinction between divine possibility and doctrinal normativity, thereby preserving both the integrity of Scripture and the rational coherence of religious belief.

claims.text: The vagueness problem follows only if absolute perfection is the sole minimally sufficient threshold for worship-worthiness.
claims.quote: I argue that this problem arises only if absolute perfection is the single minimally sufficient threshold of greatness for worship-worthiness.

claims.text: A gradable dual-threshold account separates ordinary worship-worthiness from maximal worship-worthiness.
claims.quote: On this account, a sufficient inequality in value establishes the lower threshold for worship-worthiness, while absolute perfection marks the intrinsic maximum of worship-worthiness.

claims.text: Nagasawa's maximal God approach risks denying God's supreme worship-worthiness or making any modally greatest being supremely worship-worthy.
claims.quote: Nagasawa’s approach therefore risks implying either that God is not supremely worship-worthy or that whichever being happens to be greatest in the available modal space is supremely worship-worthy.

claims.text: Without a non-derivative, non-coercive, necessary ground, intelligibility, agency, and explanation respectively fail.
claims.quote: Without a non-derivative ground, intelligibility is brute and contingent; without a non-coercive ground, originating agency collapses into conditioned transmission; without a necessary ground, explanatory deferral is indefinite.

claims.text: Finite experience requires a necessary, self-existent, intelligible, relational, and non-coercive ground.
claims.quote: The argument concludes that finite experience, taken seriously as a source of metaphysical constraint, requires a ground that is necessary, self-existent, intrinsically intelligible, relational, and non-coercive — the same structural characterisation the ARM series reaches by transcendental elimination from the other direction.

claims.text: Rejecting the ARM ground phenomenologically eliminates the reasoning and inquiry needed to articulate that rejection.
claims.quote: The philosophical significance is architectural: the ARM ground cannot be declined from the metaphysical direction without denying that anything determinate exists, and it cannot be declined from the phenomenological direction without eliminating the very practices — reasoning, inquiry, explanation — by which the denial would have to be articulated.

claims.text: Contingent reality provides explanatory contrasts and supports continued explanation-seeking over brute contingency.
claims.quote: It argues that contingent reality gives us genuine explanatory contrasts and that there are reasons to continue seeking explanations rather than terminating in brute contingency.

claims.text: Cosmological reasoning more strongly supports a necessary ground than the full classical conception of God.
claims.quote: The paper argues that cosmological reasoning provides stronger support for necessary grounding than for the full classical conception of God, while leaving open the possibility that further philosophical arguments could justify additional attributes.

claims.text: Minimalist Agnostic Deism provisionally affirms a necessary ground while remaining agnostic about its further nature.
claims.quote: The conclusion is a position described here as Minimalist Agnostic Deism: a provisional commitment to a necessary ultimate ground of contingent reality, combined with agnosticism about its further nature.

claims.quote: From the standpoint of materialism and its worldview companions, the world is, in principle, knowable, since humans occupy the highest position in the hierarchical ladder of being, whereas in idealism, they do not occupy such a position, which means that materialism is associated with epistemological optimism, and idealism with epistemological pessimism.

claims.text: The doctrine of absolute and relative truth may conceal that knowledge is an eternal pursuit of a receding horizon.
claims.quote: However, materialism does not deny the infinity of knowledge about the material world, and one of the author's conclusions, representing the novelty of this work, is the assertion that the doctrine of absolute and relative truth is possibly a masked acknowledgment of the knowledge process as an eternal pursuit of a receding horizon, as a result of which epistemological optimism turns into epistemological pessimism.

claims.text: The actuality of change requires temporality, spatiality, and physicality, so time, space, and substance are necessarily instantiated.
claims.quote: It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change requires temporality, spatiality, and physicality, borne by time, space, and substance, and that these three are necessarily instantiated.

claims.text: No modal ground can confer the domain of possibility it already inhabits, including a divine intellect.
claims.quote: From there it argues that no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. The result blocks grounds specified as occupants of that domain, a divine intellect among them, while leaving essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals standing as burdened rather than refuted.

claims.text: Nature, rather than God, possesses eternity, self-existence, and status as the source of all possibility.
claims.quote: The greatness classical theism reserved for God—eternity, self-existence, being the source of all possibility—is relocated to Nature itself, and no determinate, active ground is left able to stand wholly outside Nature while retaining the classical attributes.

claims.text: Private evidence can rationally lift agnostic suspension when independently grounded and not opposed by overwhelmingly symmetric public evidence.
claims.quote: Based on this study’s findings, private evidence can be valid and effective in epistemic dilemmas that incline toward agnosticism, provided two conditions are met: it possesses independent epistemic grounding (evidence supporting evidence), and the opposing public evidence is not so overwhelmingly strong as to create a perfect symmetry.

claims.text: Agnostics suspend judgment because evidence may be ambiguous, individually inadequate, or equally balanced between opposing positions.
claims.quote: Unlike theists and atheists—who interpret evidence to favor their own beliefs — the agnostic regards the evidence as neutral, whether due to ambiguity about what counts as evidence, the failure of individual items to establish the claim, or the equal weight of opposing evidence.

claims.quote: However, this quantitative-objective approach fails to resolve core paradoxes, as it treats yearning as a continuous variable, ignoring its internal architecture and relation to consciousness.

claims.text: Whether yearning is virtuous or vicious depends on its conscious architecture and the worthiness of its object, rather than its amount alone.
claims.quote: Consequently, virtue or vice is determined by its architecture (is yearning sovereign [F] or co-opted [B]?) and the worthiness of the object (defined by absoluteness, limitlessness, and transcendence).

claims.text: Sufi Shawq is the pinnacle of Sovereign Yearning rather than an Aristotelian vice of excess.

claims.text: A kenotic interpretation of naturalism supports a theology of God's self-limitation in an independently developing, non-predetermined world.
claims.quote: Рассмотренный кенотически (на основании кенотической методологии) натурализм открывает перспективу теологии самоограничения (кенозиса) Бога в процессе творения мира, развитие которого не предопределено, то есть в некотором смысле самостоятельно, и включает развитие как физических, так и ментальных событий.

claims.text: This kenotic interpretation requires critically rethinking naturalism's philosophical foundations.
claims.quote: Разумеется, указанная интерпретация возможна только на основании критического переосмысления философских оснований натурализма.

claims.text: The Moral Purity Industry is a hybrid moral-commercial regime, not reducible to either progressive ideology or capitalism alone.
claims.quote: The volume argues that this formation cannot adequately be reduced either to progressive ideology or to capitalism considered in isolation.

claims.text: In the Moral Purity Industry, moral categories become socially exchangeable resources managed through institutions, markets, and reputational systems.
claims.quote: The concept of the Moral Purity Industry (TMPI) designates a social field in which moral categories cease to operate solely as standards of conduct and become socially exchangeable resources: guilt is produced and managed, innocence must be publicly demonstrated and periodically renewed, legitimacy is symbolically conferred, and moral standing is mediated through institutions, markets, bureaucracies, platforms, therapeutic vocabularies, and reputational systems.

claims.text: Woke capitalism names a structural conjunction of moral symbolism and economic organization, not a partisan political target.
claims.quote: In this sense, the term “woke capitalism” is employed analytically rather than as a partisan political label: it identifies a structural conjunction between moral symbolism and economic organization rather than a specifically conservative or left-wing object of critique.

claims.text: Harrison argues that ancient Greek atheism is a scholarly mirage because atheism could not emerge in Socrates and Plato's era.
claims.quote: Harrison reasons that atheism could not have emerged in the age of Socrates and Plato: all we have from this period are empty accusations of atheism, a religious mentality which was incompatible with total unbelief, and a society in which religion dominated every sphere of personal and public life.

claims.text: Greek atheism was real, with some Athenians in the fifth century BCE and later believing in no gods.
claims.quote: This article, conversely, will argue that Greek atheism was a reality: in the fifth century bce and beyond, there were some Athenians who believed in no gods at all.

claims.text: Evidence from Plato and Classical Athens suggests atheism had limited upper-class currency as a life option.
claims.quote: Reasoning from the testimony of atheism in Plato’s Republic and the Laws , and also the intellectual and social conditions of Classical Athens, it will be argued that atheism probably had some limited currency in the upper classes of Athens as a life option.

claims.text: A theistic framing of life's meaning can be compatible with a kind of naturalism.
claims.quote: This paper defends a theistic framing of the problem of life’s meaning, albeit one which is intended to be compatible with a kind of naturalism.

claims.text: Atheists who embrace evolution can provide a robust and satisfying account of human life's main kinds of meaning.
claims.quote: In this paper, I argue that meaning of the main kinds associated with human life can be described and illuminatingly discussed by atheists who reject all things religious and embrace evolution.

claims.text: Evolutionary considerations can source meaning when meaning-related facts emerge through human development and meaning itself evolves.
claims.quote: Indeed, by considering the different forms evolution can take and with sensitivity to how distinctive meaning-related facts emerge at different stages of macroscale human development and also to the fact that meaning itself evolves, atheists are in a position to show that the evolutionary considerations available to them, rather than an obstacle to a robust and satisfying account of meaning, can be its source.

claims.text: Historiography holds that scientific atheism disappeared with the Soviet system in the early 1990s.
claims.quote: Historiography has established the opinion that scientific atheism as a whole shared the fate of the entire Soviet system and became a thing of the past in the early 1990s.

claims.text: Archival and published sources show scientific atheism actively adapted to lost ideological monopoly and religion's public return.
claims.quote: An appeal to archival sources reflecting internal discussions among atheist ideologists, as well as to publications in scientific atheist publications of the late 1980s, shows that scientific atheism during this period went through a stage of active self-reflection and adaptation to the loss of ideological monopoly and the return of religion to the public space.

claims.text: Scientific explanatory success alone does not entail a metaphysical conclusion about God's non-existence.
claims.quote: The paper argues that the epistemic success of a scientific explanation does not, by itself, entail any broader metaphysical conclusion.

claims.text: Scientific propositions do not automatically transfer to metaphysical conclusions, and scientific explanation is insufficient for such conclusions.
claims.quote: The paper further offers a fourfold typology of this error - Functional, Explanatory, Optimization, and Epistemic Gap Atheism - and derives two methodological principles: the insufficiency of scientific explanation and the non-automatic transfer from scientific propositions to metaphysical conclusions.

claims.text: Couples should practice faithfulness, mutual understanding, and effective coping strategies to improve marital health and quality of life.
claims.quote: The research concludes that couples should be faithful to their partners, ensures mutual understanding and never allows family pressure and customary laws and practices to interfere in their marriages. However, where there are stressors, couples should endeavour to adopt effective coping strategies to promote marital health and improve quality of life.

claims.text: Residents identified communication challenges arising from management, services, users, and professionals themselves.
claims.quote: The categories generated showed challenges related to management (abuse of hierarchies, moral harassment), services (pressure for productivity, overload of activities and limited time), users (resistance, low education, religious beliefs), and the professionals themselves (lack of technical preparation, emotional exhaustion, boundaries in bonding).

claims.text: Residents reported difficulty giving clear instructions and regulating emotions despite positive assessments of their social and communication skills.
claims.quote: The residents positively evaluated their social and communication skills but pointed out difficulties regarding clarity in giving instructions and emotional regulation.

claims.text: The study’s data can support education actions that humanize hospital services and improve communication quality.
claims.quote: It is hoped that the data generated by studies such as this can support professional education actions capable of contributing to a greater humanization of services in the hospital setting and improving communication quality in healthcare.

claims.text: The stelae’s owners were not necessarily Egyptian but were clearly influenced by ancient Egyptian religious concepts.
claims.quote: The analysis indicates that the owners of the two stelae were not necessarily Egyptian; however, they were clearly influenced by ancient Egyptian religious concepts, including the depiction of funerary deities such as Anubis.

claims.text: The orans posture expressed moral identity and successful divine judgment in accordance with Greco-Roman pietas.
claims.quote: Furthermore, the study shows that the orans posture served as a visual tool, expressing the moral identity of the deceased and their successful passage through divine judgment, in line with Greco-Roman notions of pietas.

claims.text: Roman-period Mendes preserved Egyptian funerary practices by consciously adapting traditional symbols and techniques.
claims.quote: In conclusion, the artistic culture in Mendes during the Roman period maintained the continuity of Egyptian funerary practices through the conscious adaptation of traditional symbols and techniques.

claims.text: Visible Sikh articles of faith may heighten diaspora youths’ vulnerability to discrimination and bullying.
claims.quote: Many Sikh youth navigate complex intersections of religious identity, family expectations, migration experiences, and minority stress, particularly in diaspora contexts where visible articles of faith may increase vulnerability to discrimination and bullying.

claims.text: Family cohesion, community support, and religious values often provide important resilience for Sikh youth.
claims.quote: At the same time, strong family cohesion, community support, and religious values often function as important sources of resilience.

claims.text: Awareness of Sikh cultural context can improve trust, reduce misinterpretation, and produce more culturally responsive care.
claims.quote: Greater awareness of Sikh cultural context can help clinicians build trust, reduce misinterpretation of culturally normative behaviors, and provide more effective, culturally responsive care.

claims.text: African feminist cultural hermeneutic can transform negative cultural phenomena while promoting socially beneficial cultural values.
claims.quote: It posits African feminist cultural hermeneutic as a fundamental process through which the gospel can elevate and transform negative cultural phenomena, advocating for the promotion of cultural values that positively influence society while critically rejecting harmful narratives.

claims.text: Cultural heritage should not be wholly abandoned because some narratives are integral to African and women’s identities.
claims.quote: However, it recognizes the importance of preserving certain cultural narratives integral to African and women’s identities, resisting the notion of wholesale abandonment of cultural heritage.

claims.text: Gendered contextualization should foster inculturation that promotes justice, equality, and communal flourishing.
claims.quote: Ultimately, the article calls for a renewed commitment to gendering contextualization, fostering inculturation that promotes justice, equality, and communal flourishing.

claims.text: Mainstream Christian churches are negotiating between doctrinal integrity and evolving expectations of inclusion and equal treatment for lesbian and gay communities.
claims.quote: The study concludes that mainstream Christian churches remain engaged in an ongoing process of negotiating the balance between preserving doctrinal integrity and responding to evolving societal expectations for inclusion and equal treatment of lesbian and gay communities.

claims.text: Churches' disputes over sexual diversity reflect tension between traditional theology and an inclusive constitutional democracy.
claims.quote: These issues reflect the broader tension between adherence to traditional theological doctrines and the demands of an inclusive constitutional democracy.

claims.text: The informational intervention significantly increases deceased organ-donor registration.
claims.quote: We find that the intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive evidence of positive spillover effects on the control group.

claims.text: The intervention increases knowledge, donation-supportive religious beliefs, and institutional trust, rather than attitudes or social expectations.
claims.quote: The survey data provides little support for changes in attitudes and social expectations as potential mechanisms. Instead, it reveals large and statistically significant increases in medical and legal knowledge, religious beliefs supportive of donation, and institutional trust among treated students.

claims.text: The intervention's registration effects are driven by male students and students whose families likely support donation.
claims.quote: Finally, we show that treatment effects on organ donor registration are driven by male students and those whose families likely support organ donation.

claims.text: Chinese identity in Malaysia is continuously negotiated and evolves rather than remaining fixed.
claims.quote: The findings reveal that Chinese identity in Malaysia is not fixed but is a continuously negotiated and evolving process.

claims.text: Chinese identity is shaped by dynamic interactions among individuals, communities, and the state.
claims.quote: These findings demonstrate that Chinese identity in Malaysia is shaped by dynamic interactions between individuals, communities, and the state.

claims.text: Understanding Malaysian Chinese identity requires attention to both structural forces and lived experiences.
claims.quote: A comprehensive understanding of this identity thus requires attention to both structural forces and lived experiences.

claims.text: Loneliness among respondents is high, with widowers experiencing more loneliness.
claims.quote: The data shows that the level of loneliness falls in high category in which widowers are more.

claims.text: Loneliness significantly correlates with coping mechanisms, support networks, time spent with others, and gender.
claims.quote: The study shows that there is significant correlation between loneliness, coping mechanism, support network, time spent with and gender.

claims.text: Widows and widowers need improved professional and community psychosocial support.
claims.quote: The study highlights the need for improved psycho-social support both at the professional and community level for widows and widowers.

claims.text: Despite high awareness, family-planning utilization is limited by spousal disapproval, religious beliefs, and fears about infertility, promiscuity, and side effects.
claims.quote: Findings revealed that awareness of modern family planning methods was high in the study area, but actual utilization was limited by spousal disapproval, religious beliefs, fear of infertility, fear of promiscuity and fear of side effects.

claims.text: Negative perceptions of family planning contribute to high fertility and rapid population growth.
claims.quote: The study further established a significant relationship between women’s perception of family planning and their fertility behavior, indicating that negative perceptions contribute to high fertility rates and rapid population growth in the area.

claims.text: Conflict arises when a character's religious habitus encounters a social field governed by different norms.
claims.quote: Conflict emerges when the character’s religious habitus encounters a social field governed by different norms, while support from the Muslim community serves as social capital for maintaining identity.

claims.text: Identity negotiation involves rejecting belief-conflicting practices, adapting social relationships, and participating in the Muslim community.
claims.quote: Identity negotiation occurs through rejecting practices that contradict religious beliefs, adjusting to social relationships, and participating in the Muslim community.

claims.text: A finding at one epistemic layer warrants revision at another only through a specified dependency connection.
claims.quote: Its scope-dependency principle states that a finding at one layer warrants revision at another only through a specified connection; once such dependence is established, layer distinctions do not insulate the dependent claim.

claims.quote: The contribution is a typed assessment record and a criterion of diagnostic adequacy: an assessment of revision must identify its target, dependency, required response, and residual uncertainty.

claims.text: Whether the proposition-centered checklist performs comparatively as well remains untested.
claims.quote: A proposition-centered checklist is equivalent only insofar as it represents these same distinctions and links; comparative practical performance remains to be tested.

claims.text: Both Hinduism and Buddhism identify attachment or craving as a source of suffering.
claims.quote: Both religions have been found agreeing with attachment or craving as a source of dukkha.

claims.text: Hindu and Buddhist non-attachment rests on different metaphysical understandings.
claims.quote: However, there are significant differences in their ideas on the metaphysical aspect of non-attachment.

claims.text: Non-attachment is morally shared but ontologically distinguishing between Hinduism and Buddhism.
claims.quote: Consequently, in spite of being identical from the standpoint of morality, there exists an ontological gap between both religions concerning nonattachment. Thus, it may be said that non-attachment is both the common with distinguishing feature of the two religious beliefs.

claims.text: Parental understanding, religious attitude, and social support significantly predict parental acceptance.
claims.quote: The findings reveal that parental understanding (β = .34), Religious Attitude (RA) (β = .29), and social support (β = .25) significantly predict parental acceptance, jointly explaining 48% of the variance.

claims.text: Parental acceptance is shaped by cognitive, social, and faith-based resources in Muslim family environments.
claims.quote: These results indicate that parental acceptance is not solely determined by cognitive factors but is also shaped by social and faith-based resources within Muslim family environments.

claims.text: Integrating Islamic values, parental understanding, and social support can improve family adaptation and well-being.
claims.quote: The study implies that integrating Islamic values, strengthening parental understanding, and enhancing social support systems can contribute to more adaptive family processes and improved well-being among families of children with disabilities.

claims.quote: Religious coping may serve as a source of emotional strength, offering meaning, hope, and resilience during periods of strain.

claims.text: Religious coping can foster guilt, self-sacrifice, and reduced pursuit of external support.
claims.quote: However, when caregivers feel spiritually inadequate, religious coping may also reinforce self-sacrifice, limit the pursuit of external support, or contribute to guilt.

claims.quote: The analysis underscores the need for holistic approaches in domestic care practices that integrate spiritual resources with practical and psychosocial support systems

claims.quote: The findings show that the Panel of Judges transferred ḥaḍānah to the father by placing the mother’s apostasy and her parenting practices, which were considered potentially influential on the child’s religious beliefs, as dominant considerations.

claims.text: These considerations insufficiently balanced religious protection against the child’s safety, psychological development, and maternal relationship.
claims.quote: However, from the perspective of Maqāṣid al-Syarī‘ah, these considerations did not fully balance the protection of religion with the child’s safety, psychological development, and continuity of the relationship with the mother.

claims.text: Apostasy alone should not transfer custody; custody should serve the child’s welfare and best interests.
claims.quote: Therefore, apostasy should not, in itself, constitute the sole basis for transferring ḥaḍānah without concrete evidence of a threat to the child’s religion, safety, and development; the determination of custody should instead be directed toward the child’s welfare and best interests.

claims.text: Religious beliefs, rituals, and communal practices help families reinterpret trauma, sustain hope, and rebuild cohesion.
claims.quote: It emphasizes the significance of religious beliefs, rituals, and communal practices as coping tools that help families reinterpret trauma, sustain hope, and rebuild social cohesion.

claims.text: Religious coping can intensify guilt, helplessness, or fatalism through spiritual interpretations.
claims.quote: At the same time, the article acknowledges the limitations of religious coping, particularly when spiritual interpretations intensify guilt, helplessness, or fatalism.

claims.text: Existing conflict-resolution mechanisms often fail to produce enduring outcomes.
claims.quote: Although various conflict resolution mechanisms have been employed to settle disputes, they often fail to yield enduring results.

claims.text: Interfaith dialogue is a promising approach to conflict resolution and reconciliation.
claims.quote: In this regard, the paper proposes interfaith dialogue as a promising approach for conflict resolution and reconciliation.

claims.text: Jaina non-absolutism and qualified assertion provide a framework that transforms conflict through dialogue.
claims.quote: Against this backdrop, the paper introduces the Jaina philosophical tradition, specifically the principle of ‘non-absolutism’ (anekāntavāda) and the doctrine of ‘qualified assertion’ (syādvāda), as a coherent framework for dialogical engagements. Focusing on epistemic decentring, conditional articulation, and non-violent involvement, the Jaina framework pushes interfaith dialogue beyond conflict resolution towards conflict transformation.

claims.text: Persian termite terms linguistically represent biological traits through concepts of eating, cutting, and destruction.
claims.quote: The etymological analysis reveals that concepts such as “eating,” “cutting,” and “destruction” are directly inspired by termites’ biological characteristics and are mirrored in their linguistic representation.

claims.text: Persian termite terminology has been shaped by interaction with local dialects and ancient religious beliefs.
claims.quote: The findings indicate that some of the terms associated with termites have been shaped by the historical interaction between the Persian language and local dialects. Additionally, the study highlights the influence of ancient religious beliefs on the naming of creatures like termites, which are often perceived as pests.

claims.text: The mosque's ornaments integrate Islamic aesthetics with distinctive traditional Acehnese art.
claims.quote: The findings reveal that the mosque's ornamental decorations are predominantly composed of geometric, floral, and vine motifs, reflecting the integration of Islamic aesthetics with the distinctive characteristics of traditional Acehnese art.

claims.text: The motifs convey religious, historical, aesthetic, and cultural-identity values and illustrate Acehnese cultural acculturation.
claims.quote: Beyond their decorative function, these motifs convey religious, historical, aesthetic, and cultural identity values while illustrating the process of cultural acculturation in Aceh.

claims.text: University students' family-planning knowledge, attitudes, and practices may be shaped by interpersonal, sociocultural, economic, and structural factors.
claims.quote: Family planning knowledge, attitudes and practices among university students may be influenced by interpersonal, sociocultural, economic and structural factors, including relationship dynamics, gender norms, social approval, access to methods and services, concerns about side effects and future fertility, and beliefs about the acceptability of contraception.

claims.text: Domestic sacredness differs from formal worship and depends on continuing religiously grounded meanings, practices, and behaviors.
claims.quote: The findings demonstrate that the manifestation of sacredness in the home differs from that in formal places of worship and, within domestic space, depends on the continuity of meanings, practices, and behaviors grounded in religious beliefs.

claims.text: Intergenerational continuity of domestic sacredness can be understood as intangible cultural heritage.
claims.quote: The results further indicate that the continuity of this experience, through intergenerational transmission, continuous re-creation, self-identification, and the safeguarding of authenticity, can be analyzed within the framework of intangible cultural heritage.
